title: Could Trump really not own a mobile phone? Albanese's claim doesn't stack up
content:
Welcome back to your daily election wrap. Leigh Tonkin will catch you up on news from the campaign trail.
Some days, it really feels like we never leave the playground.
High-stake election campaigns and high school popularity politics have a lot more in common than you'd hope for grown men vying to run the country.
Who has whose phone number? Did you call him first or did he call you? Why didn't he call you back? Do you follow each other on Truth Social?
OK, maybe not that last one.
But Donald Trump's mobile phone number — if it exists — has taken up more air than you'd expect in an apparent cost-of-living campaign.
Donald Trump’s mobile phone number – if it exists – has taken up more air than you’d expect in an apparent cost-of-living campaign.   (Reuters: Craig Hudson)
In the final debate on Sunday night, in the context of the PM not being able to secure a third phone call with Trump, Anthony Albanese suggested the US president didn't have a phone.
"I'm not sure that he has a mobile phone, the US President. Or Joe Biden. It's not the way it works when you have, with any global leader," he said.
"We text each other, we do," he said.
"But global leaders, you set up, there are people taking notes from either side, it's not something that's a casual relationship."
But could Trump really not have a phone? Have you seen how much time he spends on Truth Social?
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
Albanese picked up the conversation in his press conference on Monday morning, saying it's not a bad sign that Trump's mobile isn't in his contact list.
"Not at all," he said.
"I don't have Donald Trump's number. I didn't have Joe Biden's number. It is not the way it works between the Australian prime minister and the US president," he said.
"There are formal processes that take place. I have had two very warm conversations with President Trump."
Perhaps the more pertinent question is whether Albanese has been added to any Signal chats by Trump's team, since it seems that's where the juicy stuff is happening.
While campaigning in Melbourne yesterday Dutton called the ABC and Guardian Australia "hate media".  (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)
And then there's the name-calling merry-go-round.
You have to have thick skin when you're in politics — and when you're in the media covering politics.
At a rally of party faithful in Melbourne on Sunday, Opposition Leader Peter Dutton had some of the media coverage of the campaign in his sights.
He suggested people should "forget about what you have been told by the ABC, in the Guardian and the other hate media".
It was left to frontbencher Jane Hume to roll it back Monday on ABC News Breakfast.
"I have appeared on the ABC so many times I doubt you would hear that from me," she said.
"I think you can safely say that that was a tongue in cheek comment by Peter Dutton yesterday."
She was asked whether the comment echoed similar stances taken by Trump.
"I don't think so," she said.
Later in the day at his press conference, Dutton was asked about the Liberal candidate for Fowler who has had to apologise for social media posts where he repeatedly used derogatory terms to refer to Indigenous Australians.
He also made insensitive and offensive remarks about Tanya Plibersek's family.
Dutton was asked if this was the standard he would accept for Liberal candidates running in this election and "indeed if elected for your government, and do you not have a better candidate?"
"He has apologised for the comments and so he should have," Dutton said.
"They were inappropriate and shouldn't have been made. He has apologised for them."
Dutton could have stopped there. But this is an election campaign.
Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Brett Worthington
"I am not going to take a lecture from the prime minister," he said, accusing the ALP candidates for his own seat of Dickson, and for Flynn, of conducting themselves "appallingly".
"[Albanese] is preferencing a Green number 2," he said.
"This is an antisemitic, Jew-hating party.
"They have been involved in all sorts of horrible doxing and comments online that are repugnant but not repudiated by the prime minister."
And then Greens leader Adam Bandt stepped up to the plate.
Speaking on Seven, the Greens leader said his party had "always opposed antisemitism, Islamophobia [and] any form of racism".
"I'm not going to take lectures from someone who has made a career out of punching down and hurting marginalised communities in an attempt to win votes," he said.
Key moments from final leaders debate
There's a national talking point that's been noticeably absent for much of the campaign: China.
When the Coalition announced its increase to defence spending last week, Dutton was quick to pivot away from China to focus on the Middle East and Europe.
"China under the CCP is a very different country and has ambitions in relation to Taiwan and a naval blockade in the region is not out of the thinking of the defence experts," he said.
"Let's be frank about it but it's not just that, it's the fact that, when you look at what's happening in Europe, the prospect of Russia, emboldened, going into countries beyond Ukraine in Europe that has NATO countries deeply concerned, at the moment, and, as you know, in Germany and Italy and other countries, they're ramping up their defence investment."
It's sensitive politically even when you're not in a campaign where key city seats — including Reid, Chisholm, Bennelong and Menzies — and their large Chinese-Australian communities are vital to the end result.
The federal election campaign battle on Chinese social media platforms has intensified, with a surge in candidates seeking to win over Chinese-Australian voters.
So when Seven's Mark Riley asked, in Sunday night's debate, which country poses the biggest threat to Australia's security, we waited with bated breathe.
Dutton went first and played a straight bat.
"If you are to believe the intelligence that I received as defence minister and as the leader of the opposition — and no doubt the prime minister receives as well — the biggest concern from our intelligence agencies … is in relation to the Communist Party of China," he said.
"[Our intelligence agencies] are worried about [the potential of] conflict in our region, and what that will do to impact on our trade, and what it will do to our own security settings and what we would need to do to respond to a cyber-attack on our country."
Albanese, on the other hand, tried to nick it into the slips.
China is a major power in our region, he said, and is "seeking to increase its influence".
Riley wasn't happy with that and pressed him to answer directly.
"I am the prime minister of a country and how you deal as prime minister is diplomatically and that is what we continue to do," he said.
Clear as mud.
Electric vehicle (EV) owners. After the Coalition's transport spokesperson Bridget McKenzie floated the idea of EV owners contributing to road maintenance on ABC's Insiders, given that other motorists do so through the fuel excise, Dutton said the Coalition does not have any plans to impose a road user charge.
Dutton's bus driver. No one likes manoeuvring out of a tight spot when there's an audience. When you get stuck on a divider and that audience is the nation's press gallery? Awful.

title: Traditional owner says 'over my dead body' to the Coalition's nuclear policy
content:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are warned that this article contains images and names of people who have died.
In the 70s, Aunty Janine Smith protested against nuclear power on foreign shores.
"The contamination and the consequences of the bombings in Hiroshima, and then the Vietnam War and chemical warfare. There were always meltdowns somewhere," she said.
"You know, it just reaffirmed my opinion of the safety of [nuclear] and the effectiveness of it."
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
Today she is prepared to once again fight that battle, but now it's at home on her own traditional lands — the site of one of the Coalition's proposed nuclear power plants.
The Bujiebara traditional owner is worried the proposed plant at Tarong, north-west of Brisbane, could impact on culturally significant sites that lie only 4 kilometres away.
"Bujiebara were makers of stone axes and there is a large sandstone rock in the Tarong precinct that was used to grind the edge of these axes, that is our culturally significant site."
The coal-fired power station at Tarong in Queensland's South Burnett Region is one of the proposed sites for a nuclear power plant. (Supplied)
She also holds concerns about the lack of water resources in the town given nuclear plants require more water than any other power source aside from hydropower.
"Because of the water limitations here, we just can't. We haven't got access to that kind of water," she said.
"There is not enough water in the South Burnett to even supply all the towns with water."
At the recent leaders' debate hosted by the ABC, Peter Dutton insisted there was enough water for all seven of the proposed nuclear plants.
This claim was contradicted by one of his own senior frontbenchers, Nationals MP Darren Chester, who said the question of water requirements needed further scientific assessment that could take up to two and a half years.
Queensland Premier David Crisafulli is opposed to the Coalition's nuclear policy. Mr Dutton will also need to overturn a federal parliament ban on nuclear power if he wins the election.
Aunty Janine Smith said she won't ever give consent for nuclear power on her country.
The mushroom cloud from the Marcoo nuclear bomb test at Maralinga in outback SA in October 1956. (Creative Commons)
For many First Nations people, anti-nuclear sentiment runs deep.
Passed down generation to generation, the enduring impacts of nuclear testing in the South Australian outback are front of mind for second-generation survivor Karina Lester this election.
Her late father, Yami Lester, was just 10 years old when he watched the British government drop an atomic bomb on his traditional country in 1953.
"Dad's witness account [was] of the black mist rolling, and the ground shaking over his Walyatjatjara country," said the Yankunytjatjara-Anangu woman.
"Four years after that test, my late father's own world turned into complete darkness."
Just a teenager, he went blind.
Yami Lester lost his sight from the impacts of nuclear testing and spent his life protesting. (Supplied: Jessie Boylan)
But loss of eyesight wasn't the only impact worn by the Anangu people after the radioactive dust settled.
"Anangu died after those tests. Anangu still feel the effects of it through autoimmune diseases, through health issues, respiratory skin rashes, eye infections. The list goes on," she said.
The Anangu people were not adequately warned about the test's dangers.
It has taken decades and millions of dollars to clean up the radioactive fallout from the nuclear bombs, and tests show the contamination of the land remains highly active.
Ms Lester is now an ambassador for the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons.
Karina Lester honours her father's legacy by continuing to fight against nuclear weapons internationally. (Supplied)
As the proposed rollout of nuclear power stations remains a cornerstone of the Coalition's energy policy this election, she wants Australians to remember the lived experiences of her people when they head to the polls.
"We have the heavy burden of having to remind fellow Australians that this is not the way to go for nuclear power. We are standing up for our people and country."
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
The Coalition's proposal has identified seven locations around the country for nuclear plants, all on the sites of current or former coal-fired power plants.
Indigenous businessman and non-executive director of uranium exploration company Aura Energy Warren Mundine supports the Coalition's proposal.
Of Bundjalung, Gumbaynggirr, Yuin and Irish descent, Mr Mundine said that he understands the concern of communities, especially those with connections to Maralinga, but said nuclear power has come a long way since the 50s.
"These are genuine issues that did happen back in the 1950s and that was in regard to very high-grade nuclear weapons and nuclear testing. That type of thing doesn't happen anymore."
Nuclear energy supporter Warren Mundine says First Nations communities could benefit from the Coalition's policy. (ABC Illawarra: Gavin Coote)
He said it's about talking with First Nations communities about safety and educating them on the potential benefits.
"The jobs that can come out of it, the future training in science that could help those Aboriginal communities," he said.
"The dollars which can help their communities grow and have economic independence and development as well as looking at how they protect the environment and their cultural heritage."
But not all are convinced.
In towns across Australia, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities are divided over the proposal.
For both Karina Lester and Janine Smith, the issue of where the nuclear waste from these seven sites would be stored is also of major concern.
Across Australia, an estimated seven Olympic swimming pools' worth of radioactive waste is stored in hospitals and universities.
Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app.
Under the Coalition's plan, the radioactive waste generated by the power plants would be stored on site. At the end of each plant's life the waste would be moved to a permanent home, yet to be established.
Over the decades, successive governments have attempted to establish a national nuclear waste repository — all have failed.
And part of that failing has been over a lack of consultation with relevant traditional owners.
Protesters opposing the proposed National Radioactive waste dump in Muckaty in the NT mounted a barrel depicting radiation outside Parliament House in Canberra in 2011.

 

  (AAP )
Over a decade ago, the Howard government signed a deal with the Northern Land Council (NLC) to develop Australia's first purpose-built radioactive waste dump in Muckaty Station, north of Tennant Creek in the Northern Territory.
The NLC withdrew the nomination after some traditional owners took the case to the Federal Court, arguing they were not consulted and did not give their consent.
In 2023, the Barngarla people won a Federal Court case blocking a similar facility for low-and intermediate-level waste storage near Kimba in South Australia.
Traditional owners argued the facility would interfere with a sacred site and that they too were excluded from consultation.
The determination concluded seven years of negotiations. Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King at the time said the government was searching for other options — but they are yet to be identified.
Barngarla Traditional Owners protested the nuclear waste dump at Kimba, outside the Federal Court of Australia in Adelaide in 2023. (AAP)
For nuclear energy to be successful in Australia, Mr Mundine said it must include adequate consultation with First Nations communities.
"It's about sitting down with Aboriginal people and having transparency about the whole process … We do have to make sure that we're meeting these environmental, cultural heritage and important Indigenous issues."
But for Karina Lester, the time for consultation has passed for her community.
"We have been consulted for decades now, and South Australian Aboriginal people have said no.
"What's not right is the fact that [governments] continue to come and pressure First Nations people to have nuclear power on our traditional lands," she said.
"They are not listening to the voices of First Nations peoples."

title: Queensland still 'youth crime capital of the country', premier says
content:
The Queensland government says new data shows the state's 'adult crime, adult time' laws are working, but a criminologist believes it is a "premature" claim.
Under the Making Queensland Safer laws, which passed in December, juveniles who are found guilty of particular crimes such as murder, serious assault and break-ins are subject to the same penalties as adults.
According to data released by the Crisafulli government, there was a 32 per cent drop in related cases before the courts in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year.
Bond University Associate Professor Terry Goldsworthy said while the reduction was good news, it is "far too early" to link it to the new laws.
Dr Terry Goldsworthy says it's "too early" to know if the laws are working. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
"You would need at least 12 months of data with these laws being in place to make any kind of claim as to effectiveness or non-effectiveness."
Dr Goldsworthy said youth offending across the state began to decline early last year, with the latest Queensland crime report showing a 7.5 per cent reduction in the youth offender rate in 2023-24.
"This was a trend occurring before the LNP even came to government to be honest," he said.
Pressed on the data on Monday, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli rejected claims he was cherrypicking statistics.
"If you have a look at the statistics, you'll see in the case of north Queensland that there's been some improvement in some areas, but there's a long way to go," he said.
Mr Crisafulli says the issue of youth crime is "a big mountain to climb". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)
He said he was pleased about "some of the green shoots", but was "far from satisfied".
"It's a big mountain to climb, which is why we're not popping the champagne corks yet."
Public hearings for the government's Making Queensland Safer Bill will continue today.
Mr Crisafulli said statistics released last month showed there was a reduction of around 8 per cent in both stolen cars and in break and enters.
"We've had fewer people who have had their lives torn apart by youth crime," he said.
The March data showed 453 fewer people had their car stolen and 1,033 had had their home broken into in the state, he added.
Last year Mr Crisafulli said he had tasked the relevant ministers and government agencies to establish "clear and accurate targets".
"Once established, those targets will be made public," he said.
Asked about the targets on Monday, Mr Crisafulli said he wants to see "fewer victims of crime per head of population".
"I want to see fewer victims of crime year on year," he said.
Will 'adult crime, adult time' reduce youth offending?
Expansions to the Making Queenslander Safer laws are set to be debated next month, with a further 20 charges set to be included.
Dr Goldsworthy said he was supportive of the additional offences — which include arson, torture, attempted murder, rape and trafficking dangerous drugs — being added to the legislation.
"There are serious offences that weren't included in the first draft of offences that came out, and that's probably because it was quite rushed," he said.
He said there would be other offences "that may raise their head as time goes on".
"It would have been simpler just to put in a single mechanism that could apply this principle across every offence and criminal code under certain circumstances," Dr Goldsworthy said.
"That would have been a logical way to do it."

title: $3m lifeline for dairy farmers out of pocket as processor liquidated
content:
In a rare move, the South Australian government has thrown a financial lifeline to dairy farmers left millions of dollars out of pocket by the collapse of a major milk processor.
The state is providing a $3 million fund for dairy farmers owed money after the collapse of South Australian processor Beston Global Food, which went into liquidation earlier this year owing farmers $11.6 million for milk they had already supplied.
The fund will provide grants to struggling dairy farmers, many of whom have been hit with the “double whammy” of ongoing drought.
South East dairy farmer John Hunt is owed about $700,000 and welcomes the support, as he doubts he'll get much of it back through the liquidation process.
John Hunt believes there should be support for farmers caught short-changed through no fault of their own. (ABC Rural: Jemima Burt )
"For them to step in and just give a bit of relief over what has been quite a stressful time over the last six months.
"We've been affected by higher costs and the dry conditions … so to get this is real relief."
The funding announcement will allow Mr Hunt to get back on top of expenses on the farm.
About 22 farmers and 159 workers at the company's Jervois and Murray Bridge sites will be affected by the development.
"The overdraft has taken a real hiding," he said.
"We've taken a real hit, this long, drawn-out autumn is certainly taking a toll.
The South Australian Dairyfarmers Association will administer the $3 million support scheme.
President Robert Brokenshire said the state "couldn't afford to lose any more dairy farmers".
Robert Brokenshire says the funds will help dairy farmers remain sustainable and pay off some debt. (Supplied: South Australian Dairy Association)
"It's a package now that will help those 43 milk suppliers remain sustainable, pay off some debt, pay some creditors, and importantly, help us keep the billion dollar SA dairy industry going," Mr Brokenshire said.
"Every farmer is doing it tough at the moment, but the exception here was that these farmers are dealing with drought, high input costs, interest rates that are still high, and on top of that, hundreds of thousands of dollars in many of those cases that were not paid after milk was provided to Bestons.
"The government realised this was an unusual but high-risk area for our industry if those farmers can't survive."
Up until they were placed into voluntary administration late last year, Beston Global Food Company Limited and Beston Pure Dairies purchased about 20 per cent of milk produced in South Australia.
A processing plant at the Beston Global Food Company, which went into liquidation in Febraury. (ABC News: Carl Saville)
South Australian Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said the funds could be used by farmers to "get back on their feet", including for farm modifications or reducing debt.
"There's been a real double-whammy for dairy farmers — like most farmers across the state, they are very impacted by drought, but also having the impact of the Bestons closure has meant that it's magnified so many times," Ms Scriven said.
"We do not want to see large numbers of our very large dairy industry not able to continue, and that was perhaps a reality for some people until now."

title: Labor demands Coalition costings and claims $1b in deficit reduction
content:
A crackdown on consultants will help fund the lion's share of Labor's $10 billion in election commitments, according to government pre-election costings released on Monday in a bid to pressure the Coalition to publish its own accounts.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the budget would be about $1 billion better off over four years compared to the March budget, which forecast more than $150 billion in deficits over the same period.
The updated figures include a claimed saving of $6.4 billion through reduced use of consultants, and $740 million in additional revenue from student visa application fees.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
The savings come on top of $4 billion in offsets accounted for in last month's budget.
Released on the same day that one of the world's top ratings agency warned both sides of politics that spending roaring towards post-war highs could threaten Australia's coveted AAA rating, the figures again confirm the nation faces a decade of ongoing deficits caused by increased promises on welfare, military outlays and tax benefits.
"We call on the Coalition to release their costs and cuts immediately," Mr Chalmers told reporters in Brisbane on Monday.
"It is long past time for the Coalition to come clean on their secret cuts to pay for nuclear reactors.
"We've made it very clear what our costs are and how we will pay for the commitments that we have made in this election campaign."
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the government spent about $100 billion a year on procurement and contracts and that it saw "room to make further reductions in that area".
That suggests the savings on consultants announced on Monday would be equivalent to about 1.6 per cent of those outlays.
"That's a significant commitment and it shows that responsible economic management that we've brought to our budget processes," Senator Gallagher told ABC's Afternoon Briefing.
"We want to find further whole-of-government savings."
However, she added that they were "modest in the overall spending of government services".
"They don't affect programs or people, and that's a real contrast, I think, with what the opposition are saying, which is … in the order of $28 billion worth of cuts and 41,000 jobs they want to sack from the public services. We've taken a different approach."
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Labor's demand for immediate Coalition costings follow the traditional political pantomime of election campaigns in their dying days. Three years ago Labor held off releasing its costings until the Thursday before polling day.
The Coalition has made a series of major spending and tax promises during and prior to the campaign, but has yet to reveal a full picture of its likely budget outcomes if it wins government.
Figures released by Labor's campaign claim the Coalition's election promises amount to more than $62 billion, including plans to allow mortgage interest deductions and fuel excise cuts.
Shadow Treasurer Angus Taylor said Labor's costings revealed it had "no plan for the budget and no plan for the economy".
"There is a better way. We can get this country back on track and that means we need to beat inflation by cutting waste and slashing red tape," he said.
Ratings agency S&P warned Australia's AAA credit rating may be at risk if a swathe of spending promises lead to larger budget deficits and greater debt.
S&P analyst Anthony Walker said the budget is "already regressing to moderate deficits" as spending hits "post-war highs, global trade tensions intensify, and growth slows".
Labor and the Coalition have now laid out nearly all their major commitments for what they would do if they win the May 3 poll. Find out what Anthony Albanese and Peter Dutton are promising.
"How the elected government funds its campaign pledges and rising spending will be crucial for maintaining the [triple-A] rating," he wrote in a note on Monday.
S&P also cautioned that the increased use of "off-budget" funds for investment in projects such as the NBN and clean energy is "increasingly obfuscating" Australia's budget position and borrowing needs.
Mr Chalmers said Labor has "demonstrated" in Monday's costings that it has "found the room for our election commitments".
"The budget is stronger at the end of the campaign than it was at the beginning."
He said the biggest risk to the triple-A rating "is Peter Dutton and the Coalition".

title: Dutton won't say if Liberals should dump candidate over offensive posts
content:
Opposition Leader Peter Dutton has refused to say whether a Liberal Party candidate who apologised for derogatory social media posts should be disendorsed ahead of Saturday's federal election.
The ABC uncovered a series of offensive comments made by Vivek Singha, who is running for the Western Sydney seat of Fowler that is currently held by independent MP Dai Le.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
In the posts from 2023, Mr Singha used a derogatory term for Indigenous Australians and made disparaging comments about federal Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek amid reports her daughter had experienced domestic violence.
Mr Dutton declined to say on Monday if the Liberal Party should disendorse the candidate for the high-profile seat.
"He has apologised for the comments and so he should have. They were inappropriate and shouldn't have been made," he said.
Peter Dutton has refused to say whether Vivek Shinga ought to be disendorsed from the Liberal Party. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)
The opposition leader pointed to the apology as a means to move on from the conversation, going on to criticise Prime Minister Anthony Albanese for preferencing the Greens across Australia and in his own seat.
Mr Dutton accused the Greens of being an "antisemitic, Jew-hating party".
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Another reporter asked if Mr Dutton would call on a Labor candidate to be stood down in a similar situation to that of Mr Singha.
"I answered that question earlier," he replied.
Mr Singha issued an apology for his social media posts to the ABC, saying he should "not have expressed myself in that way" and regretted doing so.
Tanya Plibersek says she is disappointed by Mr Singha's comments. (AAP: Lukas Coch)
Ms Plibersek lambasted Mr Singha's remarks, saying in a statement that she was disappointed to see victims of violence blamed "for not protecting themselves".
"As a parent there is nothing more devastating than knowing one of your children is hurting," she said.
"It is the strongest urge of any mother to protect her children, and to question herself when something goes wrong."
Ms Plibersek further condemned the "victim-blaming attitudes which excuse the behaviour of perpetrators".
Mr Singha is not expected to claim the seat of Fowler, which is seen as a contest between independent MP Dai Le and Labor candidate Tu Le.

title: Towns with no doctors say election health promises a 'bandaid' approach
content:
For those living in the small busy rural town of Yarraman, 180 kilometres north-west of Brisbane, medical help can be hard to come by if something goes wrong.
The town of about 1,200 people has been without a regular doctor since 2018 and the nearest GP in Blackbutt, a 30-minute drive away, has closed its books to new patients.
Yarraman farmer and yoga teacher Jane Hodgkinson said residents were travelling long distances to see a doctor in Kingaroy, Toowoomba or even Brisbane or opting out of general health check-ups because it was too difficult to access without public transport.
Yarraman is on the intersection of the D'Aguilar and New England Highways. (Supplied: Jane Hodgekinson)
Ms Hodgkinson said many people also could not afford to take a day out of their schedule to travel out of town for a general check-up.
"If you can get to the surrounding towns, then they've often closed their books and not taking any new patients, so it's actually a bit of an issue because people put off their regular checks and making health a priority," she said.
"They end up with complex issues and that just compounds again."
Jane Hodgkinson says it is a struggle to see a GP. (ABC Southern Queensland: Aisling Brennan)
Ms Hodgkinson said she travelled to Brisbane for her medical appointments in order to get consistent care but she was "fortunate" she could stay with family overnight, otherwise the trip would be costly.
Rural Doctors Association of Australia chief executive Peta Rutherford said Yarraman was not the only community facing this "real challenge" of accessing medical support.
"When you're having to travel hundreds of kilometres to access a GP service, a lot of people actually choose to not go and have the service," she said.
There are five contests in regional Australia that could influence the overall result of the federal election. Here's why they matter.
"What that means is we often see them present to hospitals with really serious illness but something that could have been prevented and should have been managed in community."
Royal Flying Doctor Service Federation chief executive Emma Buchanan said more than 32,000 people across the country did not have access to a GP within a 60-minute drive.
More than 100,000 people do not have access to mental health resources.
"We know that people who live in very remote areas are likely to die 14 years earlier to their urban counterparts and that they're dying from causes that are largely preventable," she said.
The number of bulk billing GPs has dropped over the past five years, especially in rural areas. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)
As the federal election campaign enters its final week, Ms Hodgkinson said she was disappointed rural health had not been a major talking point and believed party proposals were a "bandaid approach".
"I actually think it needs a fair bit of leadership. I think it needs grassroots leadership but it also needs help to get there," she said.
"It's not going to happen without some investment in time as well as money."
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
Both major parties have put forward policies to tackle GP shortages, with the Coalition promising 200 training places specifically aimed at regional, rural and remote health.
Labor has pledged to expand the GP workforce to 2,000 a year from 2028, as part of its $8.5 billion bulk-billing pledge.
This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat.
Ms Rutherford said there had been a lot of interest in graduates looking to specialise in general practice medicine in rural communities.
"It's not all doom and gloom," she said.
"What we need to do is make sure the system is ready to support these young doctors coming through and that we provide job opportunities for them and we provide an appropriate level of incentive and support to facilitate them relocating into our rural communities where we need them most."
It comes as Darling Downs Health Service hired the total 108 nursing graduates from the University of Southern Queensland last year to secure staff for the region.

Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the state government had also committed to providing "homegrown staff" by employing 46,000 new staff into Queensland Health by 2032.
"We know we need more specialists and we need more doctors in our rural and regional areas and we believe that one of the best ways is a grow-your-own program," he said.
Tim Nicholls says the government will add 46,000 staff to Queensland Health by 2032. (AAP: Darren England)
Ms Rutherford said rural communities and all levels of governments needed to work together to retain doctors, whether that was councils providing housing opportunities, state government ensuring it supported recruitment and retention and the federal government providing supportive training pathways.
"It's something we may need to be a little bit innovative on," she said.
"If you want someone to move to your community and you want a medical service — that's a really important pillar to ensure you've got a vibrant and sustainable community — we need to look at how as a community do we attract these people and retain them in the longer term."

title: Union says police change flat batteries in GPS trackers in regional WA
content:
Western Australia's police union says serving officers are increasingly frustrated with the Department of Justice's electronic monitoring program due to a lack of resources and "unnecessary" delays responding to breaches of high-risk criminals and defendants.
"It's indicative of a common public amongst the public sector, everyone is trying to run on the smell of an oily rag," WA Police Union vice-president Peter McGee said.
Police concerns come amid the fallout from the Department of Justice's repeated courtroom admissions it cannot provide GPS tracking in regional areas.
Last week, WA Premier Roger Cook told ABC Perth Radio he had not been advised there was a resourcing issue within the department.
He acknowledged there were "some technical limitations" of electronic monitoring in regional areas due to poor network coverage.
There have been multiple courtroom admissions that the Department of Justice cannot carry out electronic monitoring in WA's regions. (Supplied: wa.gov.au)
When mandatory GPS tracking laws came into force in December, then-police minister Paul Papalia said in a ministerial statement that "any breach of an offender's restricted movements generates an immediate alert and officers will respond rapidly."
Mr McGee said the reality of implementation had fallen short of that announcement.
"The monitoring system is a great idea, but it relies on the Department of Justice to monitor it and raise, but then also we can't access it until a warrant is issued by the Department of Justice to apprehend these offenders," he said.
Mr McGee said WA police officers were also being called on for routine maintenance of tracking devices in regional areas, which commonly involved replacing flat batteries.
"It's another example of our members being called on to fill holes in a lack of resources from other departments, to do routine things they should be doing," he said.
Earlier this month, the Department of Justice sought to revoke bail of a Denmark man accused of rape, whose bail was conditional to electronic monitoring.
In an affidavit provided to the Albany Magistrate Court, Adult Community Corrections' (ACC) chief executive said: "Electronic monitoring cannot be adequately facilitated to maintain continued tracking. The issues with the monitoring at this location are not able to be overcome at this stage."
Magistrate Erin O'Donnell noted there was "no detail" about what the precise issues with electronic monitoring were.
An Albany magistrate said the electronic monitoring gaps appeared to be related to resourcing. (ABC News)
Police prosecutor Sergeant Gary Simpson told the court his office had not had a definitive answer from the ACC on why electronic monitoring could not be facilitated.
He said the revocation of bail was "out of the abundance of caution".
"If the monitoring equipment were to fail out of hours, they couldn't respond in a timely manner," Sergeant Simpson said.
Ms O'Donnell said while there were scant details, the issue with electronic monitoring appeared to be related to resourcing.
"I don't think that it is a case where the court ought to be constrained by resourcing issues or whether it's the fact that the government did not consider things adequately when passing the legislation they did," she said.
Ms O'Donnell decided to release the accused on bail with a $5,000 surety and a protective condition to not be within 100 metres of the alleged victim, her home, or her workplace.
Mr Cook said the government had initially committed $27.8 million over four years for 35 full-time equivalent staff but will provide money for an additional 12 full-time equivalent positions in the upcoming state budget.
Under the Family Violence Legislative Reform package, the government has provided $35 million of funding for the employment of extra correction officers.
He said the government will continue to provide additional funding to the program as it rolls out, with more funding expected in the next state budget.
"Police sit alongside correction officers at the state operation centre and they work together literally shoulder to shoulder in that room, monitoring all those people that are subject to electronic monitoring," Mr Cook said.
He claimed everyone was still getting used to the system, under the new law, and working together to address the "limitations".
The Department of Justice recently posted a job pool advertisement for electronic monitoring officers tasked with 24/7 monitoring within the State Operating Command Centre, a centralised hub for policing operations and intelligence.
The Department of Justice did not respond directly to questions about police frustration with resourcing or the lengthy delays for the issuance of warrants.
In a statement to the ABC, a Department of Justice spokesperson said electronic monitoring continued to be used effectively in conjunction with other bail conditions.
"The department has sufficient staff embedded in the State Operations Command Centre working alongside WA police to effectively monitor all persons who are subject to electronic monitoring — including in the regions — 24/7," the spokesperson said.
In December, the state government enacted laws making GPS monitoring mandatory for serial family and domestic violence offenders.
"In anticipation of this increase, the department was allocated $27.8 million over four years," the spokesperson said.
That funding led to an immediate increase of 35 full-time positions, and a further 12 full-time roles in the next financial year, according to the department spokesperson.

title: With the election days away, what can be done to engage fed-up young voters?
content:
When asked which voter group they think is most fed up with Australian politics, many people are quick to point to Gen Z.
"We've been raised in a world that's left worse off for us," 21-year-old Zach Mead told the ABC.
His partner, Catherine Ferry, 21, shared a similar sentiment.
"I feel like Gen Z is just upset with everything and they don't want to live in a world where it's been screwed over for us," she said.
Catherine Ferry, 21, believes Gen Z is disillusioned by the political process.  (ABC News: Tabarak Al Jrood)
While younger Australians are increasingly tuning out of politics, Australian National University senior politics lecturer Dr Jill Sheppard said the most disengaged group was actually millennials or people aged in their 30s to early 40s.
"It's really [these] voters who are getting to a point in life when they haven't created enough of a deposit to buy a house, they don't have job security, they're working contract to contract, they're renting, or they're steeped in mortgage payments," she said.
"People for whom the system really doesn't seem to be working that well, people who look at their parents at the same age and think they had it better."
Dr Jill Sheppard says more voters in general are tuning out of politics.  (Supplied)
But Dr Sheppard acknowledged it was a growing trend, with more voters of all ages switching off from the political process.
The May 3 federal election will be the first where Gen Z and millennial voters aged under 45 will outnumber baby boomers in every state and territory.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
But Dr Sheppard said most major parties have relied on older cohorts as their "path to victory".
"The problem with this two-party system is that there are plenty of voters, particularly aged 40 and under, who don't feel like they're getting ahead, and there's no real electoral incentive for parties to talk to those voters, because they can build enough of an electorate without having to talk to them," she said.
"That's where parties like the Greens and then increasingly independents are finding a path to victory, because they can talk to these voters who don't feel heard by the major parties."
Researchers say people aged in their 30s and early 40s are the most disengaged with politics.  (Supplied: WA Electoral Commission )
With a record 542,141 votes cast in the first day of early voting, it's clear many voters have made up their minds long before the official polling day.
In Western Australia, the first-day result of 59,000 votes marked a notable 115 per cent increase on 2022 — a figure not surprising to Dr Sheppard.
More than a million people have already cast their ballots for the federal election early. Some experts say the polling day has just become the last day to vote.
"We do want someone to promise us the world, sometimes we want someone to let us know that they hear our concerns and that they will respond to them," she said.
"And if you don't feel like you're being heard in those three years between elections, then you can't fix that in the 33 days of the actual campaign."
A new web-based tool is hoping to change that, by helping voters cut through the political noise and make informed decisions.
Created by climate-focused charity Project Planet, the Build a Ballot website walks voters through a series of questions to see how they would tackle issues like housing, cost of living, climate change and education.
From there, users receive a personalised voting plan and can see which of their local candidates and parties reflect their own views and preferences.
"People are starting to think, 'oh, maybe I shouldn't just vote how my parents have always voted, maybe I should actually understand a little bit more about what I'm doing,' and we've tried to design the tool in a way that really invites people into that process," co-founder Lizzie Hedding said.
Build a Ballot co-founder Lizzie Hedding is hoping the tool helps voters to make informed decisions.  (ABC News: Marcus Simpson)
Ms Hedding said despite the political power younger generations held this election, she had noticed a significant divide when it came to engaging them.
"But the reality is that these young people are smart, they do jobs in our economy, they're very switched on [but] they just don't see themselves represented in the political conversation, and they don't see that conversation talking about the issues that actually matter to them."
Zach Mead believes engaging disconnected voters could be as simple as talking to them.
"Come ask us questions, ask us what we want because I see so many politicians out there that just assume what we want and do whatever and then we hate them for it," he said.
Zach Mead, 21, says politicians need to engage young voters by talking to them.  (ABC News: Tabarak Al Jrood)
Meanwhile, Catherine Ferry feels younger voters would connect more with people they look up to or regularly follow, such as influencers.
"For a lot of voters they just don't know where to start … so it would be a lot better if we had good examples out there to actually show us the parties and what they're offering," she said.
"Everyone's so focused on cardboard signs [but] it's not the way that a lot of the younger generation is raised on, so having that technology-based advertising would be absolutely amazing,"
While Ms Hedding hopes disengaged voters will switch on at the last minute, Dr Sheppard believes it's too late to change their minds.
"The parties can't come to them now, with [one] week to go after three years of this electoral cycle, and tell them convincingly that they care," she said.
"I think if you're disengaged at this point, you're going to stay disengaged until the 3rd of May."

title: Parties vow no horse-trading for power, as Greens leader reveals 2010 Abbott plea — as it happened
content:
Labor frontbencher Tanya Plibersek, outgoing Liberal MP Paul Fletcher and Greens leader Adam Bandt joined Menzies Institute CEO Georgina Downer and Sydney Morning Herald political editor Peter Hartcher for the final Q+A panel before the federal election.
An occasionally fiery panel descended into disbelief as Bandt revealed he'd had a "very short" conversation with Tony Abbott during crossbench negotiations following the 2010 election.
Take a look back at how the day's events unfolded with our live blog below.
Or, if you would like to explore how your views compare to those of the parties and candidates, you can check out the ABC's Vote Compass tool.
By Joshua Boscaini
This is where we'll leave our live blog for today. A massive thank you for joining us on another day of the election campaign.
Make sure to join us again tomorrow as we get ever closer to election day on May 3.
You can check out the rest of today's online coverage at our Australia Votes page and you can try out the ABC's Vote Compass tool, to see how you align with the political parties.
By Maddy Morwood
Here's the full video of Tanya Plibersek calling out Greens leader Adam Bandt for the Greens' lack of support for Labor's environmental policies.
Q+A: Tanya Plibersek attacks the Greens on blocking environmental protection
By Jason Whittaker
And that's it for Q+A tonight. If you missed it, you can scroll down and catch up below, or head over to iview and watch the program there.
Q+A is live in Sydney next Monday for all the election wash-up. You can join the audience by registering on the website.
Journalist Paul Kelly, editor-at-large at The Australian, and social research Rebecca Huntley will join the panel, plus politicians from all sides of the new parliament.
Come along or watch at home at 9:35pm (AEST) on ABC TV and ABC iview.
By Joshua Boscaini
Q+A host Patricia Karvelas has asked the panel to share something positive.
Adam Bandt says he's happy that millennials and Gen Zs will be the biggest voting block this election.
Georgina Downer says she's glad that this Saturday "we get to vote in a free and fair election".
Tanya Plibersek says she's proud that her government has moved to protect an additional 100 million hectares of land and oceans.
Peter Hartcher says he agrees with Downer's comments and points out there's only 21 full democracies left on planet earth.
"We really need to nurture it and thank people who put their lives on the lives on the line to represent us," he says.
By Maddy Morwood
Robert Menzies Institute Georgina Downer says that there's a lack of understanding of the context, history and importance of the Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country.
"I do think that overuse of the Acknowledgement of Country tends to reduce its impact," she said.
Watch the full video here:
Q+A: Welcome to Country show of respect for traditional owners or 'overdone'?
By Jason Whittaker
Paul Fletcher's seat of Bradfield — held by the Liberals on a margin of just 2.5 per cent — has been under siege since the last election by well-funded 'teal' independent  Nicolette Boele.
Or as Fletcher calls it, a "giant green left con job". This is what he said to the Sydney Institute in December:
"The Teals, then, are very much in the tradition of front groups established by left-wing political operatives which are designed to lure votes away from the Liberal Party by tricking voters about their bona fides.  As with other such groups over time, many of the campaign volunteers are members of unions or the Labor Party or the Greens Political Party, and have simply put on a different t-shirt for a few weeks."
By Andrew Thorpe
Our next question is from Phil Schulz.
He asks:
As a Bradfield resident, I am wondering why Liberals are on the run, they have never lost in my electorate. But now Bradfield is now one of the most marginal seats in Australia. How have the Teals managed to put the Liberals on the run in their own heartland? And does this diehard Liberal constituency, now on a marginal knifes edge, sound the death nell for the Coalition?
Paul Fletcher acknowledges the Coalition is facing a "tough fight" in Bradfield, but "there is an enormous amount of money being spent by the teal machine".
"It really is the Americanisation of Australian politics," he says, prompting jeers from the crowd.
Rather than any issue with the Liberal Party or its candidate specifically, he says the shift to third-party candidates in general is "the nature of modern politics".
Phil, our questioner, is brought back into the conversation, and says that isn't the case — it's the Liberals' policy on nuclear energy and climate change, in particular, that has him looking at the best alternative.
Peter Hartcher backs him up, pointing out there's a reason the teals made their inroads in Liberal seats.
By Joshua Boscaini
Fomer Liberal prime minister Tony Abbott called Greens leader Adam Bandt to seek his support on forming minority government following the 2010 federal election, which produced a hung parliament.
Bandt has told Q+A he received a call from Abbott after the election.
"He rang me. He said: 'Hi, Adam, it's Tony Abbott here. I've always considered myself a bit of an environmentalist. I think we should talk,'" Bandt says.
Bandt says it was a "very short conversation" and that Peter Dutton would get the same response if the situation was repeated after this year's election.
By Andrew Thorpe
Patricia Karvelas now goes to one of your questions from this very blog.
Josh asks: What policies would the majors be willing to trade to govern in minority?
It's a great question — essentially the reverse of what's usually asked of the crossbench, that is, what they'd demand.
Neither Plibersek nor Fletcher look keen to answer.
Eventually, the environment minister simply says "none".
"We're determined to win a majority government, and he's made clear that there's no deals," she says.
Fletcher is similarly unwilling to entertain the hypothetical — only saying that the Coalition's message to the Australia people is that "majority government is a good thing".
"We have had majority government in Australia since World War II with one  exception, 2010 to 2013. Which was a chaotic disaster," he says.
By Joshua Boscaini
Audience member Debbie Dunn has our fifth question.
She wants to talk Salmon farming, which has divided Tasmania's Huon community.
She asks:
"Yesterday at the 'vote salmon out' rally in Hobart Tasmania, 6000 of us joined together to say we do not want those toxic fish farms polluting our waterways any longer. Enough is enough. So Labor and Liberal how many of us have to stand up before you will not only hear us but take action to remove these farms from our waterways?"
Tanya Plibersek is responding first and she says Tasmania's salmon industry is an important employer in the state and should be able to operate in an "environmentally sustainable way".
Adam Bandt has been asked what he thinks and he says Tasmania is facing an "extinction crisis".
"We know two things. One is that Australia's environment laws are now weaker at the end of the parliament than they were at the start," she says.
But Plibersek has jumped on Bandt's comments and says the Greens teamed up with Coalition to block environmental law reform.
Paul Fletcher says Labor and the the Greens are fighting for votes in inner city Melbourne and Sydney.
But Q+A host Patricia Karvelas points out that the Coalition voted for the government's salmon laws.
"An 18-month period under which this process went on and on and there was no certainty given to that industry," he says.
By Jason Whittaker
Two-thirds of Australians say the United States can't be trusted as a security ally and want to develop a more independent defence capacity.
Q+A commissioned research from YouGov on what the country thinks of the US relationship with Donald Trump firmly back in charge, and there was worry on national security and the economy.
The number of Australians now calling for more independence from the US - 66 per cent according to the weighted poll of 1,500 voters - has shot up since Trump took office.
As YouGov's Paul Smith told us:
"A 25 per cent change of opinion in the course of nine months is about as big a swing as you can get."
The poll also showed more than 7 in 10 Australians are concerned Trump will make them worse off financially.
And more voters think Anthony Albanese (55 per cent) will handle the US relationship better than Peter Dutton (45 per cent).
By Andrew Thorpe
Sydney Morning Herald political editor Peter Hartcher is next to weigh in.
He says Sam Roggeveen's contention is essentially that Australia is painting a "Donald Trump-shaped" target on itself, and giving China reasons to attack us — but in fact China has "decided it's on a historic mission to dominate the region and the world and break Australia's sovereign will".
He points to Chinese covert campaigns targeting politicians, trade bans, and the recent live-fire exercise in the Tasman Sea — "something that even the Soviet Union didn't do at the height of its powers".
"China has decided it is going to be the  dominant power. We are already a  target. Nothing we can do will  change that," he says.
By Joshua Boscaini
Our expert tonight, director of the Lowy Institute’s International Security Program Sam Roggeveen, says that China's growth has forced the US to ask whether being a top dog in Asia is really worth it.
"America’s becoming a less reliable ally, but that’s mainly because of China, not Trump," he says.
Watch the full clip here:
Q+A: International Security expert says US is becoming a less reliable ally because of China
Tanya Plibersek has joined the conversation and says the Labor government has stabilised the relationship with China.
While acknowledging that the US is an important security partner, Plibersek says she thinks Australia should become more self-reliant as a country, both in defence and economically.
Adam Bandt has also jumped into the conversation and has used the oppurtunity to criticise AUKUS and has called for Australia to "detach" from Donald Trump.
Plibersek and Paul Flecther have clashed about the Coalition's defence policy.
"When you [Paul Fletcher] were in government you made $42 billion worth of announcements that weren't funded," she says.
"If we have to protect the country with press releases we'd be find."
Fletcher responds and says: "If we were attacked while Labor was in government the answer would be to the attacker to wait until we get to the forward estimates because that's when the money comes".
By Maddy Morwood
Do you have a question for the Q+A panel?
You can ask a question right here in the blog by submitting a comment or question in the section at the top of the page.
We’re monitoring comments and will feed the best questions into Patricia Karvelas's ear.
Your question could be next! Jump to it!
By Joshua Boscaini
Oliver Zhang is our next audience member with a question.
He's curious about our national security and the ongoing tension between the US and China.
"Australia's national structure has long relied on security from the United States and economic prosperity from China. As competition between these two powers escalates and pressure mounts from both sides, has this dual dependence now become a systemic risk to our sovereignty and strategic autonomy?"
Peter Hartcher answers first and he says that Australia has over-relied on both powers and thinks it does limit Australia's political autonomy.
Hartcher says Australia is too dependent on China for trade and on the US for security.
"If we don't act now, to change those dependencies, we're fated to permanent paralysis," he says.
Georgina Downer has tuned into the question and says Australia's continued dependence on exports to China opens up the possibility of further economic coercion.
"This is a highly dangerous time and we need to be using all our diplomatic statecraft to build those alliances to ensure that they are strong and to have a trading and economic relationship that is flexible," he says.
By Andrew Thorpe
Adam Bandt is now asked whether immigration is at least "part of the story" on the housing crisis.
He says no — if immigration was driving it, then "why didn't house prices fall during COVID when we didn't have people coming into the country?"
He then leans into what has essentially become his housing stump speech this campaign — a history lesson on the crisis, that puts the blame squarely on John Howard's tax changes in the late 1990s.
"I'm worried about my kids and my  grandkids being able to buy a home. With 7 million renters and with gen Zs and millennials the biggest voting bloc at the election, you  have a chance to make your voice  heard," he says.
Karvelas notes that gen Zs and millennials seem to be everybody's best friend these days.
By Andrew Thorpe
Our second question is from Candice Philliponi.
She says housing has become a "rigged game".
Housing has become a rigged game. Investors win, renters lose, and politicians pretend they’re fixing it. When will any of you admit the systems broken because you benefit from keeping it that way?
Tanya Plibersek takes the question first, and says the housing crisis has been a long time in the making.
She talks about serving as housing minister in the Rudd government, and seeing the way social housing investments changed people's lives — and then "we went into a decade of Liberal government," she says.
Patricia Karvelas asks Paul Fletcher if he accepts that the housing crisis has been building up for a long time — both of them no doubt aware the Coalition's tactic during this campaign has been to cast the crisis as an invention of the past three years.
Fletcher says "some problems" of the past three years have exacerbated the crisis, including high levels of migration, and infrastructure bottlenecks.
Our questioner, Candice, says both parties have offered some great ideas — but she'd prefer if they worked together, then kept trying to make the problem belong to the other side.
"Work together. Get it done," she says.
Plibersek then jumps in — to correct Fletcher on immigration numbers.
By Jason Whittaker
On Friday, after a speech from an elder was heckled by a prominent Neo-Nazi, the opposition leader said the Welcome to Country was "an important part of official ceremonies and it should be respected":
"We have a proud Indigenous heritage in this country and we should be proud to celebrate it as part of today."
But in the leaders' debate last night, Mr Dutton suggested Australians are tiring of the recognition:
"... for the start of every meeting at work or the start of a football game, I think a lot of Australians think it's overdone and it cheapens the significance of what it was meant to do."
And he expanded on that today from the campaign trail:
"Listening to a lot of veterans in the space, Anzac Day is about our veterans — about 103,000 Australians who have died in the service of our country.
"I think if you are listening to their sentiment, and we are respectful of that sentiment on Anzac Day, I think the majority view would be that they don't want it on that day."
By Joshua Boscaini
Our first question is from Peter Strohkorb.
He's asking about the Welcome to Country.
"The Voice referendum divided the nation. Now the Welcome to Country ceremony is becoming a new point of contention. What ideas does the panel have to resolve the issue amicably and in the interest of all parties concerned?"
Paul Fletcher responds first and says there is a sentiment in the community that there are too many Welcome to Country ceremonies.
"I think it's a sentiment across many in the community that we are having too many Welcome to Country ceremonies and so I think that can tend to reduce the significance," he says.
But Tanya Plibersek says she's proud to take part in the ceremonies.
"Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians have served in our defence force since the Boer War. Acknowledging that on Anzac Day is perfectly appropriate," she says.
Adam Bandt has chimed in and has clashed with Fletcher and has criticised Peter Dutton.
Today, Dutton suggested Anzac Day dawn services should not involve Welcome to Country ceremonies.
Bandt says Dutton is "playing from the Trump play book" because, in his words, his campaign is in "free fall".
By Jason Whittaker
Q+A hosted by Patricia Karvelas has started on ABC TV and iview.
Join us as we live blog this program.
Here are the politicians in the hot seat this evening:
Voters haven’t seen a lot of Tanya Plibersek this election campaign, a former deputy leader of the party and a popular figure among the Labor faithful. There was that awkward hug at Labor’s launch and apparent division in cabinet on environmental policy.
Paul Fletcher represents the Liberals tonight - though he’s not running for re-election in his marginal Sydney seat of Bradfield. That leaves a contest between Lib candidate Gisele Kapterian and ‘teal’ independent Nicolette Boele, who got close to Fletcher in 2022.
Adam Bandt leads the Greens, who are defending their three Brisbane seats from all-out attack from Labor and the Liberals, while also hoping to turn new seats green around Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth and on the NSW north coast.

title: Does South Australia matter this federal election?
content:
As Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Peter Dutton jet-set across the country to make last-ditch political pitches, some South Australians could be questioning if a federal election is even on the horizon.
It is not just the absence of corflutes on the state's colloquially-known Stobie poles that has spurred such indifference (the state having banned such advertisements last year), but also the relative infrequency of visits paid by the major party leaders.
Mr Albanese and Mr Dutton have only made fleeting visits to the southern state since campaigning officially began four weeks ago.
But SA still has some sway this election, with the state home to two key battleground seats that could play a crucial role in shaping the country's political future.
In SA, the southern Adelaide seat of Boothby and the eastern Adelaide seat of Sturt are considered key litmus tests for the major parties.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
Both electorates are marginal: Sturt is currently held by Liberal MP James Stevens on a 0.5 per cent margin, while Boothby is held by Labor's Louise Miller-Frost on a 3.3 per cent margin.
Boothby is where Mr Albanese and Mr Dutton have spent much of their time campaigning during their whistle-stop visits to SA, with both major parties considering it a lineball contest.
Despite its marginal footing, Boothby was held by the Liberal Party for decades, with the seat only changing to Labor in 2022.
Boothby is one of the SA's two marginal seats this federal election. As part of the ABC’s “Your Say” campaign, we spoke to local voters about their biggest concerns.
Any so-called incumbency advantage Ms Miller-Frost might have this election has been muted to a degree by her Liberal opponent, Nicolle Flint, who previously held the seat before deciding not to recontest the last election.
The Liberals are confident Ms Flint's strong name recognition and profile in the community will help them claw back the seat, while Labor claims Mr Dutton has been a hindrance to Ms Flint's campaign.
Labor MP Louise Miller-Frost (left) is trying to hold onto Boothby against Liberal candidate and former MP Nicolle Flint. (ABC News)
While Boothby is shaping up to be a two-party race, Sturt has a wider playing field.
Challenging incumbent Mr Stevens is Labor's Claire Clutterham, who would be buoyed by her party's recent victory at the Dunstan state by-election (the seat is within Sturt’s boundaries).
The Greens are also bullish about their chances in Sturt after a 5.2 per cent swing in 2022, while teal independent Dr Verity Cooper is a newcomer.
The Liberals are confident of maintaining their stronghold over the seat, arguing any votes against them would effectively be split between Labor, the Greens and Dr Cooper.
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Since its creation, Sturt has only spent two terms in Labor hands, but the Liberal vote has shrunk in recent years.
Labor could benefit from any swing to the Greens through preference votes, but the contest between the two major parties is still considered tight.
There are six senate spots up for grabs in SA.
Among the 40 South Australian candidates in the running are long-time Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, Liberal Alex Antic, and Labor's Marielle Smith.
Shadow health minister Anne Ruston was relegated to second place on the Liberals' SA Senate ticket after struggling to fight off a factional battle with conservative Mr Antic.
Anne Ruston is up for re-election in the senate this year. (AAP: Dominic Giannini)
One Nation's Jennifer Game — the mother of South Australian upper house MP Sarah Game — has a chance of securing the sixth senate spot.
But that seat is also being contested by former senator Rex Patrick, who is vying for re-election under the Jacqui Lambie Network banner.
Labor holds a comfortable majority in the SA Parliament, with Premier Peter Malinauskas currently enjoying broad popularity — particularly off the back of the AFL's Gather Round in SA earlier this month.
Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app.
Photographs of Mr Malinauskas are heavily featured on federal election campaign material and the premier has been at Mr Albanese's side during press conferences in SA.
On the other hand, Mr Dutton's state Liberal colleagues have had little presence on the campaign trail in SA.
The state Liberals have had a tumultuous 12 months, book-ended by former leader David Speirs's conviction on drug charges last week, and the loss of two seats at by-elections.
The Coalition have attempted to shift attention in SA to issues such as cost of living and energy, but it remains to be seen how much brand damage the state party has caused their federal counterparts.
Premier Peter Malinauskas has featured prominently in Labor's federal campaigning in SA. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)
Polls are pointing to a close result on May 3, so seats like Boothby and Sturt could play a key role in deciding which party forms government.
But much of the focus is likely to fall on the eastern states, where there are more crucial electoral battleground electorates.
Opposition Leader Peter Dutton flanked by Boothby candidate Nicolle Flint, Mayo candidate Zane Basic and Barker MP Tony Pasin. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)
By the Electoral Commission's definition, New South Wales has 14 marginal seats, there are 13 in Victoria, 11 in Queensland and seven in Western Australia.
So, while South Australia's role in the election will not be insignificant, the state is unlikely to be a major focus in the campaign sprint to the finish line.

title: A private hospital opens in Melbourne with no out-of-pocket costs
content:
I've seen the future of an important part of Australia's healthcare system — it's called Adeney Private.
It's a new private hospital in the Melbourne suburb of Kew that's 51 per cent owned by 42 doctors and 49 per cent owned by health insurance company Medibank.
There are zero out-of-pocket expenses for anyone who goes there.
That is, if you're privately insured and you go to this hospital, it's like being in a public hospital — none of the procedures cost extra, the anaesthetic is free and so is any pathology, radiology and drugs from the pharmacy, and of course the stay itself is covered by the insurance.
This hospital is the start of a quiet revolution in Australian healthcare.
Most of the political attention on healthcare, especially during the election campaign, is on primary care — on GPs and bulk billing — which is fair enough since it's where most hardship occurs and where the system falls down most egregiously.
The average cost of going to the GP is now $40 above the Medicare subsidy per visit, and the national bulk-billing rate is down to a record low of 77 per cent.
The Labor government and the Coalition have promised $8.5 billion and $9 billion respectively to get that bulk-billing rate back up to 90 per cent by increasing incentive payments for the bulk billing of children and the disadvantaged.
All of which is fine and overdue, but the other way in which Medicare falls short is with more serious and expensive medical procedures than GP visits.
At Adeney Private there are no out-of-pocket expenses for patients, because the health insurer and the hospital itself cover the gaps. (Reuters file photo)
Anyone who has private health insurance and has shown up at a private hospital for, say, a knee replacement, expecting their expensive policy to cover it, will have had a rude shock when presented with a succession of bills — from the surgeon, the anaesthetist, radiology, pathology and the chemist.
I'm due to have a routine procedure next week and last week I got an email from the anaesthetist demanding $500 at least two days before he sticks the needle in, and that's on top of what he'll get from Medicare, of course, which is not disclosed.
Goodness knows what the surgeon will charge, but it certainly won't be bulk billed and nor will he disclose what he gets from Medicare on top of what I pay him.
Step up Professor Michael Grigg, retired vascular surgeon and former president of the Royal College of Surgeons.
He decided five years ago that something needed to be done about this, or the private health system would collapse, and bring the entire health system crashing down — and it's no good waiting for the government to increase Medicare payments sufficiently to cover costs.
Just like Oprah's iconic "you get a car" moment, Labor is throwing urgent care clinics to punters like confetti.
At that point, non-primary care subsidies, which represent the great majority of the 7,000 item numbers in Medicare, had been frozen for a decade while inflation increased clinicians' costs, and even if they were unfrozen they would never catch up.
So he approached Dr Andrew Wilson, chief medical officer at Medibank, with the idea of collaborating in an experimental hospital that would have no out-of-pocket expenses for patients, because the health insurer and the hospital itself would cover the gaps.
They agreed on a 51/49 ownership split so the doctors would have control and they put in $20 million between them for the fit-out and the equipment.
Centuria Healthcare Property Fund agreed to a three-year rebuild of an existing hospital for $100 million with a 20-year lease from the joint venture operating company (called Curanda Vita, which is Latin for "take care of life"), and Louise O'Connor, the head of operations at Cabrini Hospital, and before that a long-time executive at Epworth, was hired to run it.
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
The key to making the business model work is that stays in Adeney Private Hospital are shorter than usual. O'Connor calls it "right stay" and says that most patients prefer to recuperate at home as long as they are supported.
She says supporting recuperation and rehabilitation at home is cheaper for the hospital and better for the patients.
That lower cost has allowed her to negotiate contracts with radiology company i-Med, Melbourne Pathology, Slades Pharmacy and individual deals with 154 doctors. That's on top of the 42 who are shareholders in the hospital in which they agree to provide their services at no extra cost to the patients because they are satisfied with what they get from Medicare plus the hospital.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
She wouldn't tell me the details of the contracts but says everyone is contributing to the success of the model because they all have a stake in it working.
She has also struck a deal with another health fund, BUPA, so their members can go the hospital for free as well, and is working on getting all other health insurers signed up.
She told me: "This is the hardest thing I've ever done, but we need a revolution in the healthcare sector otherwise it won't be sustainable. Gone are the days when we can allow medicine to get a bit more expensive every year."
Could the Adeney Private model apply across the private hospital sector, including existing hospitals, not just new ones?
Professor Grigg said this experiment had to become profitable first: "It normally takes five years for a new hospital to make a profit, but we're hoping for 12 to 18 months."
Louise O'Connor said it was "not unachievable" for existing private hospitals like Cabrini and Epworth to provide zero out-of-pocket care, but they would have to completely pull apart their businesses to do it.
Andrew Wilson from Medibank told me the company had asked other hospitals if they would participate in a trial, but they weren't enthusiastic. "It's not for everybody," he said.
However, he said Medibank is planning to roll out the Adeney Private model more widely with other part-owned hospitals.
Rafael Epstein
Patricia Karvelas
Richard Willingham
Annabel Crabb
Laura Tingle
Matt Garrick
I asked all of them what the government could do to make it work, and the answer was unanimous: money. Medicare bulk-billing payments for all 7,000 item numbers, not just GP visits, need to increase.
Unless that happens, and gap payments for procedures continue to increase and whack privately insured people who thought they were fully covered, then fewer and fewer people will bother taking out health insurance.
If that keeps going it will make the billions of dollars in government subsidies for private health insurance a waste of money and put increasing pressure on the public system.
The excellent new urgent care clinics and extra incentive payments for bulk billing will help take pressure off public hospital emergency departments, but the queues for elective surgery are also getting out of hand and need attention.
The Adeney Private model is how health insurance, and therefore the public health system as well, could be made sustainable.
Alan Kohler is finance presenter and columnist on ABC News and he also writes for Intelligent Investor.
