title: 'Don't give them a cent': Chinese netizens boycott US goods in trade war
content:
Calls to boycott American brands like Starbucks and KFC are gaining traction on Chinese social media, as Chinese people react to the United States' latest tariff hike with a wave of patriotic fervour.
On Douyin — China's domestic version of TikTok — users are urging their community to reject US goods and support domestic products instead.
"Let the whole nation unite, boycott American brands, not give the US a single cent, support Chinese products, and strengthen our Chinese nation," one user said in a video.
A meme on Douyin shows how traders would monitor the market in the past, and how they do it now. (ABC: Bang Xiao/Screenshot from Douyin)
Thousands of Chinese netizens have also flooded the US embassy's Weibo account to criticise the US government.
Users accused the embassy in Beijing of disabling comments after a barrage of earlier comments called for an end to "American imperialism."
A US embassy spokesperson told the ABC it "does not remove comments from its social media accounts on the basis of viewpoint".
The hashtag "This is China's attitude" — highlighting China's defiance — received 950 million views, and "Trump Tower is almost entirely made in China" was trending as one of the most read topics last night.
"If Trump came to China, his credit score wouldn't even let him rent a shared bike, let alone borrow a power bank," one user wrote.
China's ambassador suggested Australia should stand in "solidarity" with China against tariffs, but Deputy PM Richard Marles said Australia would stand up for its own interests.
"We're suffering from deflation, they're suffering from inflation. But who's more afraid of hardship — us or them?" said another user.
Dr Wang Pan, a China studies expert at the University of New South Wales, said many Chinese netizens are closely watching how Beijing responds to what they see as a heavy blow from Washington.
"There's strong support online for the Chinese government to retaliate," Dr Wang told the ABC.
Chinese netizens haven't responded with just fury — but with a flood of sarcastic, AI-generated memes, as US President Donald Trump ramps up trade tensions with Beijing by slapping a hefty 145 per cent tariff on Chinese goods.
As they take to the internet in defiance, the Chinese government has responded to the US in kind — another tariff of 125 per cent.
One of the most widely shared parody videos on Douyin puts a cheeky superhero spin on the situation.
In it, Marvel and DC characters are re-imagined as factory workers.
Memes show American superheroes doing hard labour.
"Bring manufacturing back to the US!" wrote the account owner Weijinfengdu in the caption.
The video is set to Our Workers Are Powerful, a patriotic anthem from the 1950s that became a rallying cry for China's working class during the Cultural Revolution — adding a rich layer of irony to the ongoing trade spat.
"The humour lies in the irony — even with superpowers, the West is still playing catch-up in manufacturing," one user commented.
"Send the American superhero squad to the factories," another chimed in.
What began as frustration has now evolved into a full-blown "meme war", with Donald Trump and his advisers becoming regular punchlines across Chinese social media.
One viral meme features an AI-generated, bald, orange-tinted Trump dressed in traditional Chinese robes, bowing to a Qing dynasty emperor under the caption: "Please reduce the tariffs, Your Majesty."
Another video casts US officials as characters in a low-budget martial arts drama, pleading for market access while fighting each other in exaggerated slow motion.
These memes have exploded in popularity.
On Douyin, videos mocking the tariffs have racked up millions of views.
Some users declared their own "personal sanctions" against the US — vowing to boycott KFC's Thursday specials or ditch their iPhones — prompting cheers and laughter in the comments.
Chinese memes mock the idea of US manufacturing.
"Whether it's an international incident or a domestic issue, people often respond with humour — playful, satirical, and exaggerated," Dr Wang said.
"That kind of format leaves a strong impression.
"With images and videos, the message spreads widely — and sometimes, it even slips past the censors," she said, adding that political content is often treated as sensitive material on the Chinese internet.
Beyond the memes and mockery, a quieter anxiety runs through Chinese social media — particularly among exporters and small business owners who stand to lose the most from the escalating trade war.
China's export-reliant industrial sector, which helped power decades of economic growth, is no stranger to trade shocks.
In the first round of the US-China trade war in 2018, nearly 1.9 million jobs were reportedly lost in manufacturing alone.
Now, with Washington imposing a fresh 145 per cent tariff, many fear history is repeating itself.
Most of these businesses operate on thin margins, relying on stable trade flows and long-term partnerships to survive.
As supply chains freeze and foreign demand dries up, uncertainty is setting in.
Some entrepreneurs have turned to platforms like Weibo and Douyin to voice their frustrations — and to warn others of the storm ahead.
A user from Dongguan, a major manufacturing hub in the southern province of Guangdong, painted a grim picture.
"Sixty per cent of companies here depend on exports. Our goods can't leave the warehouses anymore," he said in a video.
How China is cushioning the blow on its own economy, and how it could hit back against US tariffs.
He described how a nearby Taiwan-funded factory in the city had extended its Tomb-sweeping Festival break from one day to five — not out of commemoration, but simply because there were no orders to fill.
Another user, Li Shan, who runs a small business selling electric motors, shared a similar story.
"Since the tariff war began, I've sent five messages to a US customer who once asked for samples," she said on Douyin.
"Not a single reply."
Some businesses have summed up the mood as a mix of pride and desperation.
"Rather than lower our heads, we'll lose money selling domestically. We'll never give in to [the US]," posted Weitu Group, a Chinese manufacturing company.
Dr Wang added that commentary from domestic experts and social media influencers may reinforce Beijing’s narrative that the US is deliberately trying to sideline China and will ultimately harm its own standing in the world.
"They strengthen netizens' faith in China's position and boost a growing sense of national confidence."

title: China to increase tariffs on US goods to 125 per cent
content:
China will impose 125 per cent tariffs on US goods, up from the 84 per cent previously announced, the finance ministry says.
The new tariffs will start from Saturday, Chinese local time.
China says US tariffs defy "basic economic laws and common sense".
US markets plunge again as optimism over President Donald Trump's tariffs "pause" is overshadowed by his escalating trade war with China.
In his first public comments about the US-China trade war, President Xi Jinping said there were "no winners" in a tariff war.
He called on China and the European Union to jointly oppose unilateral bullying, a reference to US President Donald Trump's tariff regime, while meeting with the Spanish prime minister in Beijing.
The US administration was sticking to its guns on Friday, touting its discussions with a number of countries on new trade deals, which it says will justify its dramatic upheaval in policy.
"We are doing really well on our TARIFF POLICY. Very exciting for America, and the World!!! It is moving along quickly," Mr Trump posted on social media on Friday.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who met with Mr Xi on Friday, said Beijing and Washington needed to hold talks to defuse the situation, and he also called for a more balanced relationship between Beijing and the 27-nation EU, which has its own trade issues with China.
"China has always regarded the EU as an important pole in a multipolar world, and is one of the major countries firmly supporting the EU's unity and growth," Mr Xi told Mr Sanchez during their talks, according to the Xinhua news agency.
"China and the EU should fulfil their international responsibilities, jointly safeguard the trend of economic globalisation and the international trade environment, and jointly oppose unilateral acts of bullying," Mr Xi added.
US markets opened lower on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 100.2 points at the open, while the S&P 500 fell 12.5 points at the bell.
"Recession risk is much, much higher now than it was a couple of weeks ago," said Adam Hetts, global head of multi-asset at Janus Henderson.
The White House clarified earlier that Mr Trump's announcement of 125 per cent import taxes on Chinese goods was in addition to earlier tariffs, bringing the total since he was inaugurated less than three months ago to 145 per cent.
The 125 per cent figure did not account for the 20 per cent tariff placed on China earlier this year, ostensibly to punish it for doing too little to stop fentanyl shipments to the US.
Mr Trump has said he is hopeful of making a deal with Mr Xi.
"He's been a friend of mine for a long period of time, and I think that we'll end up working out something that's very good for both countries," Mr Trump said.
China blasted the US president's tariffs as a "numbers game" that "will become a joke", in a finance ministry statement.
A spokesperson for Beijing's commerce ministry said it had "become a numbers game with no practical significance in economics".
China says it will "fight to the end" with Donald Trump (left) on tariffs. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)
"It will only further expose the United States's bullying and coercion. It will become a joke," they said.
It added that the US "should bear full responsibility" for any global turbulence or tariff war.
China's mission to the World Trade Organization (WTO) said on Friday it had filed an additional complaint to the trade body over US tariffs.
"On 10 April, the United States issued the Executive Order, announcing a further increase of the so-called 'reciprocal tariff' on Chinese products, China filed a WTO complaint against United States' latest tariff measures," the statement from China's mission said.
"Reciprocal tariffs" and countermeasures could have a catastrophic impact, even worse than foreign aid cuts, on developing countries, the director of the United Nations's trade agency Rebeca Grynspan said.
Global trade could shrink by 3-7 per cent and global GDP by 0.7 per cent, with developing countries the worst affected, the International Trade Centre said.
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, the executive director of the International Trade Centre, said this burgeoning war could have a "catastrophic" impact on developing countries.
"If this escalation between China and the US continues, it will result in an 80 per cent reduction in trade between the countries, and the ripple effect of that across the board can be catastrophic," she said.
Donald Trump said he was hopeful of a deal with Xi Jinping as the White House confirmed a higher tariff on Chinese imports.
Reuters/AP

title: Donald Trump's inner circle accused of market manipulation
content:
Democratic senators are calling for an urgent investigation into US President Donald Trump and his inner circle — including senior adviser Elon Musk, intending to find out if any market manipulation took place following his policy shift on "Liberation Day" tariffs.
Global markets plummeted in the days after President Trump announced select trading partners would be charged tariffs of up to 49 per cent on April 2. The S&P 500 shed $5.83 trillion in four days, representing its steepest losses since the index was created almost 70 years ago.
But on the morning of April 9, Mr Trump began offering his followers reassurance in posts to Truth Social: "BE COOL! Everything is going to work out well. The USA will be bigger and better than ever before!"
Minutes later, he elaborated: "THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT"
Finding buying opportunities as markets swing wildly from losses to gains. (Alicia Barry)
It is not common for the US president to sign off with his initials. DJT is also the NASDAQ ticker for Trump Media and Technology Group, the operator of the social media platform Truth Social.
About four hours later, Mr Trump announced a delay of 90 days on the tariffs in another social media post, choosing instead to impose a 10 per cent tariff in the interim.
Within minutes of Mr Trump's social media post, the S&P 500 shot up more than 7 per cent. It finished the day up 9.5 per cent — its biggest one-day gain since 2008. The Nasdaq composite saw its second-largest session surge on record to finish 12.2 per cent higher.
Democratic senators are now calling for an "urgent inquiry", claiming the US president created circumstances where market manipulation could've taken place.
"This sequence of events raises grave legal and ethics concerns," Senator Adam Schiff said in a letter to the US Office of Government Ethics.
"The president, his family and his advisers are uniquely positioned to be privy to and take advantage of non-publication information to inform their investment decisions."
Mr Schiff then cited Elon Musk as an example, claiming his position as a senior government adviser grants him access to information not available to the public that could affect his vast business interests.
"Stock in Elon Musk's company, Tesla, increased 18 per cent immediately following the president's announcement to pause most tariffs," Mr Schiff said.
"The apparent conflict of interest issues President Trump's announcement presents regarding Mr Musk apply to all White House and executive branch employees — including special government employees — who may have access to non-public information regarding the deliberations and ultimate changes in tariff policy."
Chris Murphy fears this could be an "enormous scam". (AP Photo: J. Scott Applewhite)
Democratic senator Chris Murphy said the US president telegraphed to his social media followers that they should buy stocks, alleging "this could be an enormous scam".
"Trump's position changing every single hour gives ample opportunity for any individual who has early access to information … to make boatloads of money, either by investing at the right time or pulling their money out of the market at the right time," he said in a video posted to social media.
The Democratic senators allege Mr Trump's conduct presented opportunities where the market could've been manipulated.
Market manipulation occurs when someone artificially affects the supply or demand for a security, such as causing stock prices to rise or fall dramatically.
According to the United States Security and Investment Commission, it involves techniques that spread false or misleading information about a company, and by making a security appear either more actively traded or in less demand.

title: Bonza boss speaks for first time since collapse as ASIC probe ends
content:
The former chief executive and founder of collapsed airline Bonza has broken his silence after the corporate regulator revealed it would not prosecute the company's directors.
The Sunshine Coast-based carrier suspended all flights and entered voluntary administration in April 2024.
Liquidators Hall Chadwick alleged the company traded while insolvent.
On Friday a spokesperson for the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) confirmed the investigation had finished.
"ASIC has sent no further action letters to Australian and US directors of Bonza, confirming it does not intend to proceed to enforcement action at this stage," they said.
Following the announcement, former chief executive Tim Jordan made his first public comments since the collapse.
"Whilst the recent news from ASIC of no further action is certainly welcome, it doesn't unfortunately change the sad outcome of Bonza's demise in late April of last year or the subsequent negative impacts on communities, customers, suppliers and the former Bonza team," he said in a statement.
Tim Jordan had said the increased competition from the airline would lead to lower prices in the market. (Supplied: Bonza)
The decision does not mean the regulator's options for prosecution are entirely closed.
The decision does not clear the directors of wrongdoing or indicate they did not break the law, rather that the regulator has declined to take action for reasons that could include the cost, time and availability of evidence.
Hall Chadwick has been contacted for comment.
Bonza's planes were repossessed and flights were suspended before 323 employees lost their jobs. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)
Bonza began flying in February 2023 but was plagued with problems and only had four aircraft by the time it collapsed 14 months later.
Bonza's collapse is merely the latest in a long history of failed Australian airline experiments, but it probably won't deter others from going in on a wing and a prayer.
The airline was wholly reliant on funding from its controversial majority owner, 777 Partners.
Last year the ABC revealed the US Department of Justice was investigating whether the investment firm had violated money-laundering laws.
Bonza offered dirt-cheap fares between regional destinations but haemorrhaged money and never turned a profit.
Hall Chadwick's report last year said the company had "significant" solvency issues from November 2023 and may have been insolvent from March 2024 until its collapse at the end of April.
Hundreds of staff and more than 70,000 customers with bookings were among the creditors.
Hall Chadwick's report suggested Bonza was trading while insolvent. (Supplied: Bonza)
Insolvency expert Michael Sloan said he was not surprised ASIC declined to prosecute because it usually only acted in "egregious circumstances".
Bonza's US private equity backers, 777 Partners, is fighting financial and legal fires around the world with its portfolio of budget airlines and financially struggling football clubs.
'The real story is what the liquidators are doing," he said.
"Where you've got a major collapse, it's the liquidators' primary duty to pursue directors on behalf of the unsecured creditors, to hold those who have caused losses to account.
"Liquidators have very muscular powers under the Corporations Act to examine and investigate and prosecute … that's what they're there for.
"Have they got funds available? Have they sought funding?
The union representing flight attendants in Australia labelled the decision "disappointing".
Flight Attendants Association of Australia (FAAA) Federal Secretary Teri O'Toole said it was "concerning" the regulator had decided not to pursue enforcement action.
"This affected an awful lot of Australians that [were] employed by this airline, that have lost their livelihoods," she said.
"It just seems odd that they're not exonerating them and saying … there's nothing to see.
Ms O'Toole said she was worried about the prospect of the former Bonza directors being able to run companies in the future.

title: Confidence in energy minister questioned after explosion at Queensland power plant
content:
Queensland's deputy premier has defended the state's energy minister, after a testing week involving an explosion at a trouble-plagued Central Queensland power plant.
At a major energy speech on Tuesday, Energy Minister David Janetzki failed to mention that one of Callide Power Station's generators would be offline until May 30 after a "pressure spike" last Friday.
Mr Janetzki, who is also the treasurer, was briefed by operator CS Energy about the serious incident on the same day it occurred.
Mr Janetzki will hand down the new government budget in June. (AAP: Darren England)
Forced to front the media in an at-times tense press conference on Thursday afternoon, Mr Janetzki sidestepped questions about when he notified the premier of the blast.
He noted the operator had informed the national electricity market, but conceded he should have told Queenslanders to demonstrate the value of the government's maintenance framework.
"CS Energy notified the market on Friday, it was publicly available information, you've all got the websites and the apps," Mr Janetzki told media.
"But I should have [told the public] because it is the perfect example of why we need the electricity maintenance guarantee."
Today, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said he "absolutely" still had confidence in Mr Janetzki after the incident.
Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie maintained his confidence in the state's energy minister. (AAP: Jono Searle)
"I think in hindsight, as the treasurer said yesterday to the media, that he ought to have mentioned it in his speech — and no doubt going forward, he will," he said.
Shadow Treasurer Shannon Fentiman said Mr Janetzki's defence was "pathetic".
"It is unbelievable that this man stood on stage for half an hour, answered questions, then had a press conference about the future of energy in this state and the future of Callide Power Station — because he wants to keep it open for longer — without actually informing anyone that just days before, there had been an explosion at that same power station," she said.
Shannon Fentiman said Mr Janetzki knew about the issue before he delivered a major energy speech on Tuesday. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)
Mr Janetzki's speech had laid out the blueprint for Queensland's energy future, part of which involved extending the life of the state's coal-fired power stations.
It's not the first time the Callide plant has made headlines, with almost half a million homes left without power in 2021 after an explosion at the facility.
Also detailed in Mr Janetzki's Tuesday speech was an almost $4 billion increase to the price of delivering the CopperString power grid expansion in the state's north-west.
The project will see 1,100 kilometres of overhead power lines established between Townsville and Mount Isa, giving towns in the region the opportunity to connect to the national electricity market for the first time.
A map showing the regions that will be connected through the CopperString project. (Supplied: CopperString 2.0)
Mr Janetzki said the cost blowout meant the eastern link from Townsville to Hughenden would be prioritised, with the remaining western link to be reviewed.
A completion date is yet to be set, and Mr Janetzki sidestepped questions on Tuesday about when he learned of the increased cost.
Mr Bleijie today confirmed he was only told about the blowout on the morning of Mr Janetzki's address, after it had already been reported earlier in News Corp papers.
"The energy minister briefed the premier and I, obviously, on the morning of his speech but — as the treasurer and energy minister said — he wanted to come to the government with a solution," he said.
Ms Fentiman said Premier David Crisafulli had serious questions to answer. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)
Ms Fentiman said Premier David Crisafulli had serious questions to answer.
"Why isn't the premier being briefed on key infrastructure projects before the media, and why is the premier's government and his ministers inflating the cost of infrastructure projects and misleading Queensland?" she said.

title: New mine gets 20-year licence despite fears land will be 'scarred forever'
content:
The Victorian government has given mining company VHM a 20-year licence for its Goschen Rare Earths and Mineral Sands Project near Swan Hill.
The Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action released a statement saying the approval followed a thorough assessment of the miner's application.
Victoria's Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny approved the environment effects statement (EES) for the project in December.
VHM is also licensed to explore thousands of additional hectares' worth of land in the area. (Supplied)
VHM plans to extract mineral sands and rare earth materials such as zircon, rutile, leucoxene and ilmenite at the site.
Those materials are used to produce a range of products such as mobile phones, batteries and medical devices.
An independent inquiry into the mine held in March 2024 received 179 submissions, the majority of which were opposed to the project.
VHM is licensed to operate on 1,500 hectares of land near Swan Hill. (ABC News: Scott Jewell)
Grain farmer and secretary of Mine Free Mallee Farms Craige Kennedy said the community felt devastated and vulnerable following the announcement.
He said he was concerned about possible health implications from contaminated dust and water blowing onto neighbouring properties or seeping into groundwater.
"We just feel that hasn't been given enough weight and the conditions of monitoring these things will just be too late," Mr Kennedy said.
"The damage will be done by the time they pick up these problems.
"Agricultural land will be scarred forever."
Mine Free Mallee Farms has been a staunch opponent of the project. (ABC News: Francesco Salvo)
Resources Victoria's executive director of regulatory operations Chris Webb said the government's assessment focused on whether VHM could deliver what was set out in its proposal.
"Following this thorough assessment of their application, VHM have been awarded the right to exclusively access minerals under the state's mining legislation," Mr Webb said in a statement.
Mining companies are proposing new mineral sands mines in Victoria, but what are they and what does it mean for the environment? (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Else Kennedy)
Mining can start once the state government approves a work plan that adheres to any conditions imposed by the regulator.
VHM is required to continue engaging the community for the duration of its licence and to give the regulator quarterly reports on its responses to feedback and complaints.
VHM has been contacted for comment.

title: Major insurer taken to court over 'egregious' handling of storm claim
content:
Australia's corporate watchdog alleges one of the country's biggest insurers took nearly three-and-a-half years to resolve a claim over storm damage to a property in regional Victoria.
The Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) is suing Hollard Insurance, accusing it of breaching its "duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of the claim.
A regional Victorian couple lodged a claim two days after suffering major storm damage to their home.
In late October 2021, major storms battered the state, resulting in thousands of calls for help to the State Emergency Service and leaving more than half a million properties without power.
ASIC said Hollard — Australia's fifth largest general insurer — deliberated for 18 months before rejecting the claim in April 2023.
The watchdog claims Hollard relied on "a non-expert opinion over prior expert reports" on the cause of the damage to the property and offered the couple a small cash settlement, which was rejected.
ASIC also alleged Hollard delayed decisions over repairs and took nine months to initiate an inspection by a structural engineer and delayed providing temporary accommodation to the couple.
ASIC Deputy Chair Sarah Court says the couple's home is now uninhabitable. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)
ASIC alleges the delays, poor communication and ignoring of expert advice "exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm" and breached Hollard's duty of good faith in handling the claim.
"In the end, because of the excessive delays by Hollard and the failure to undertake make-safe works, the home has become so riddled with moisture, mould and decay that it is uninhabitable and now needs to be demolished and rebuilt," ASIC deputy chair Sarah Court said.
"The egregious delay highlights ASIC's concern about the significant rise in general insurance complaints reported to AFCA since the 2022 floods, particularly those involving claim delays.
ASIC is seeking a civil penalty under the Insurance Contracts Act.
A spokesperson for Hollard Insurance said the insurer acknowledged the Federal Court action.
"We support ASIC's work in driving positive outcomes for consumers and are cooperating with ASIC in this matter," the spokesperson said.
"As this is an ongoing legal matter, we are unable to provide further comment."

title: Cause of oyster spat deaths at research facility remains a mystery
content:
An investigation into fish mortalities at a South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI) facility has found the cause of the deaths to be "inconclusive".
About 70 per cent of the state's breeding line of oyster spat, as well as significant numbers of barramundi broodstock and snapper larvae, died of unknown causes at the facility at West Beach in Adelaide late last year.
South Australia's oyster industry was worth $58 million in 2022–23. (ABC News: Brittany Evins)
The mass deaths were a significant setback to oyster breeding lines but SARDI executive director Mike Steer said what was lost would be recovered.
"We're working closely with the oyster industry to re-establish the production of new family lines to overcome those losses.
"We're effectively overcoming an environmental impact that's impacted our projects but we can recover them."
Mike Steer say what was lost will be recovered. (Landline: Tony Hill)
Dr Steer also played down concerns about the impact on recreational fishers.
The investigation was led by three SARDI researchers, and has been independently reviewed by University of Adelaide professor Michael Goodsite.
Professor Goodsite's expertise is in civil and environmental engineering.
It had been speculated that the fish deaths were caused by dredging conducted by the Department for Environment and Water (DEW) at West Beach, which began in early October.
However, according to the investigation, no direct evidence was identified to link the mortalities to dredged sand placement or dredging activities.
The report found no link between dredging and sand carting at West Beach, and the mortalities.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)
South Australia's oyster industry was worth $58 million to the state in 2022–23 financial year.
"The mortalities of larvae, spat, fingerlings and broodstock were unfortunate, and disappointing for all involved, not least the team at SARDI who dedicate their careers to our world-class research and breeding programs at the West Beach site," Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development Claire Scriven said.
"While there are times when causes for events such as these cannot be conclusively found, learnings can still be applied for future activities.
"SARDI is already implementing mitigation measures for any future events."
The SA Oyster Growers Association declined to comment.

title: Broken Hill icon set to be revitalised after years collecting dust
content:
One of the main questions Shane Goodwin is asked by tourists and locals about the towering mound of ore that overlooks Broken Hill is "do you know what's happening up there?"
Now he can say that after years spent collecting dust the vacant Line of Lode complex is set for a revival.
NSW Crown Lands poured more than $6 million into renovating the site but it remained untouched until recently, when Broken Hill Mines struck a lease agreement with Foundation Broken Hill to establish offices at the site.
Broken Hill Mines is offering to cover the rent for the business prepared to operate at the site. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)
The Australian miner purchased the Rasp Mine last year and has big plans for the city, according to Mr Goodwin, who is the company's head of corporate sustainability.
"We recognise that facility as an important part of town," he said.
"If we can be a big part of getting that up and running and attracting tourists and locals into that facility then we're very happy.
The Broken Earth Complex has remained largely untouched since the previous tenants moved out in 2021.
Foundation Broken Hill chair John Lynch hopes the development will encourage more people to enjoy the views.
"Whether it's the sunset … whether it's the sunrise, if we're open, with a coffee, with something to eat," he said.
"Then I think it's a real boost for the future."
The challenge now will be to find tenants for the office spaces.
Jim Hickey's family were the last people to run a business at the Broken Earth Complex. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)
Deputy Mayor Jim Hickey said a restaurant would not be economically viable but a cafe would be ideal.
"You get a fair [amount of] patronage, but it's very hard to make a full-time living there," he said.
"It will be a great secondary cafe for someone."
Broken Hill Mines is confident an operator will be enticed to move in on a rent-free basis after the office is built in the existing structure.
"We'd talk to them about how we'd share the utilities costs, but the leasing costs will be covered by us," Mr Goodwin said.
Broken Hill Mines would also like to install an observation point that would allow people to watch the operations inside the Rasp Mine.
But for now the company is focused on finding builders to get the complex up and running as soon as possible.
"We'd like to see this done, certainly, within six months and up and open," Mr Goodwin said.
"I need to source a builder and John needs to source a hospitality provider.

title: Australian share market closes lower after week of turmoil
content:
The Australian share market has ended the day 0.8  lower after seesawing through the week. Ultimately the ASX 200 lost 0.28 per cent over the week, which saw huge losses followed by historic gains when the US president hit pause on his tariff plan.
The ASX 200 closed 0.8 per cent lower at 7,646 points, while the All Ords was -0.8 per cent at 7853 points.
Gold miners continued to be the best performing stocks, with almost all sectors in the red on the ASX200.
The uncertainty has seen the price of gold hit a record high as investors flock to the safe-haven asset, with the previous metal ending the week +0.9 per cent at US$3,202.
The Aussie dollar lost some earlier gains to end the day -0.4 per cent at 62 US cents.
US stocks fell overnight, reversing back some of the gains from the previous session's historic rally triggered by US President Donald Trump's announcement of a 90-day pause on some of his "reciprocal" tariffs.
At the time of writing (4:30pm AEST) US futures were in positive territory over 1 per cent higher, pointing to a possible reversal on Friday's trading day.
The RBA governor Michele Bullock delivered a speech last night at the Chief Executive Women Melbourne Annual Dinner, where she said as bad as things were with tariffs and the ensuing market chaos, it wasn’t reminiscent of the global financial crisis in 2008 (yet).
She said the Australian financial system was strong and well placed to absorb shocks from abroad.
But when it came to interest rates? She said it was still too early to know how the RBA was going to respond.
“We are mindful of not adding to the uncertainty, and to that end, it’s too early for us to determine what the path will be for interest rates.

Investment bank UBS has upgraded US stocks to "attractive" (from "neutral"), stating yesterday's Trump tariff pivot has dialled down the risk.
In a note Mark Haefele, Global Wealth Management Chief Investment Officer, UBS AG states:
"President Trump’s 2 April 'Liberation Day' tariff announcements were harsher than expected and have been followed by tit-for-tat escalation between the US and China, with US tariffs on imports from China now totaling 145%. But President Trump on 9 April also announced a 90-day pause on 'reciprocal tariffs' for other countries.
We believe the demonstrated willingness from the Trump administration to change its stance in response to equity and bond market turbulence indicates some sensitivity to market stress, and points to the existence of a “Trump put” in some form.
To be sure, the significant tariffs on China will cause economic disruption if they remain in place. But while downside risks do remain, we believe the risk of a more severe economic downturn is now more limited. We have raised our downside scenario S&P 500 price target to 4,500 (which we consider to be more aligned with a 'normal' recession), up from 4,000 (more consistent with a systemic crisis like the global financial crisis)."
Despite the uncertainty, UBS is optimistic about the future:
"We remain mindful of the greater-than-expected tariff escalation between the US and China, and the risk that incoming data could demonstrate significant supply chain and business disruption from the China tariffs. It is also not certain that the pause in 'reciprocal tariffs' on other trading partners will result in more long-lasting 'deals', and we do expect additional tariffs on pharmaceuticals and semiconductors to be announced.
But with many countries expressing a desire to negotiate with the US, and the Trump administration now more incentivized to demonstrate “success,” we expect a variety of “deals” or sector carveouts to materialize within the 90-day “pause” period. President Trump has even expressed the view that ultimately a deal would be struck with China. We believe that progress on negotiations should provide encouragement for investors to look through near-term tariff-induced economic weakness and toward a return to earnings growth in 2026."

Do we know who started selling American Bonds? Individuals, Funds or Nations? Was it spontaneous or a planned attack?
- Cassandra
Thanks for the question, Cassandra.
I asked Westpac's bonds guru Martin Whetton exactly this question yesterday. Before I go further, a little refresher.
As he explains, government bonds are basically a way of buying into a country's debt. The sell-off of US government bonds that happened during this week's Trump tariff turmoil was, in Martin's view, a signal from the market that investors were feeling less sure about the US economy's ability to repay their debts.
His thoughts:
"US government bonds are held by every country in the world, and they're held by every bank and financial institution because they are deemed to be what's called golden collateral, the simple bottom line structure of financial markets.
"I genuinely think what you observed (with the sell-off), or maybe what financial markets people observed yesterday, is the breaking of this long-standing financial, almost moral, authority of the US dollar and the US government debt."
The question you asked was: who was selling off?
Martin says around 21% of all the US government bonds are held by investors or institutions in Asia: "Japan, China, Asian central banks and sovereign wealth funds", he says.
"They hold that fairly passively. We don't know whether they sold. It'll take some months before the data actually shows. More than likely they did," he adds.
I also posed another question to him, about whether those markets might have sold off US government bonds, not just because they were less attractive, but as a rage move against the US as Trump's administration put higher tariffs on them.
"If you are one of these Asian nations that have just been tariffed, you may feel a little bit of antagonism towards the US government. That's probably right," he replied.
"I'd make the observation that you'd hardly want to go and buy (US bonds) at the moment, when the (US) dollar is challenged, when you're going to have less in US dollars, tax, trade, receipts, and you feel aggrieved about the situation you find yourself in.
"Ultimately, all you've done as a country is produce goods at a low cost (for) the American market or and global markets. Now you've been tariffed and you're hurting your industries."

title: If you map financial stress, you'll find these 'aspirational Australians'
content:
Paris Basra has everything she wants in life: a house with a backyard, her husband, and a young child.
But like many across Australia, the cost-of-living crisis is biting hard.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
"It brings stresses, it brings its loneliness, it brings its struggles," she said.
She lives in Ripley — a suburb of Ipswich, in Brisbane's western corridor.
Paris Basra and her son Simar live in Ripley, a growing suburb west of Brisbane. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)
It is former farmland turned into expanding developments, filled with new estates and first homebuyers like Paris.
Ms Basra's mortgage repayments are about $900 a week. Interest rates remain over six per cent.
It's expensive — and while it is manageable by keeping a very close eye on the budget — her family's ability to live their dream of home ownership comes with major sacrifices.
Her husband Manpreet works fly-in, fly-out on ships as part of the bauxite industry in Far North Queensland — so for two weeks every second fortnight he is away from home.
For half the year, Ms Basra's husband works away on ships in Far North Queensland to help afford their mortgage repayments. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)
"Obviously, there isn't a lot of local jobs [in south-east Queensland] within the shipping industry, and if there is, they aren't as high paying which would probably mean I would have to work full-time," Ms Basra said.
"Simar would have to go into childcare full time and then obviously there's childcare costs, so you're adding onto your budget and monthly expenses.
She's part of what political commentator John Cole refers to as aspirational Australians.
Associate Professor John Cole says many aspirational Australians call the western corridor of south-east Queensland home.  (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
And they're increasingly calling areas like Ripley, in the federal electorate of Blair home.
"If you map financial stress, you'll find it strongest in areas where you find aspirational Australians, people that have a mortgage," said Associate Professor Cole, from the University of Southern Queensland
It's these voters that some, including Associate Professor Cole, believe could be crucial in the upcoming federal election.
A recent ABC analysis found Blair had the highest rate of household stress in Queensland.
Professor Cole says Labor have been spending "a lot of money" in an attempt to hold Blair.  (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)
Over 77 per cent of households were feeling some form of financial stress, including 66 per cent of those with a mortgage, and 91 per cent of renters in the region.
"Blair will be no different to most of urban Australia — cost of living, cost of housing, housing affordability are all big issues," Associate Professor Cole said.
That stress resonates across the generations.
Ipswich resident Margaret Fielder says she wants to see more support for homeless people from politicians at this election.  (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
Retired nurse Margaret Fielder lives in a small cottage she owns just outside the Ipswich CBD.
"I went from rags to riches and back to rags again," the 85-year-old said.

Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
She lost over $1 million in a bad investment during the Global Financial Crisis and had to continue working until very recently.
"Quite frankly, I cannot afford to pay the prices that's demanded of food in the supermarkets these days and pay my bills and maintain this house as well," she said.
Ms Fielder now pays very close attention to every bill that comes in, so she doesn't have to go into debt to pay them off.  (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
She's on an aged pension and receives other government support but still struggles when it's time to pay the bills.
"I just have to be very careful not to get into debt … I don't have any money in the bank," she said.
"If my food's getting low and that sort of thing, I'm not too proud to go to the [Foodbank] and get food that otherwise would be dumped."
A number of other voters the ABC spoke with on the streets of Ipswich feel the same.
Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app.
"[Rents] are too high, property prices are also too high," one woman said.
Another woman said while she was lucky enough to be a part of the social housing program, other cost-of-living issues plagued her and her children.
"Food, electricity, everything," she said.
"I sort of just take it day by day, especially when you have got three kids."
Many voters in Ipswich say they're currently struggling with the cost of living.  (ABC News: Chris Gillette)
Nadia Noye has her own home but is struggling as she's currently unemployed.
"It takes every cent to have a home, and then, you're eating two-minute noodles," she said.
"But slow and steady. I'll get a job soon. It'll get better."
Despite this sentiment, Associate Professor Cole believes Blair is still likely to be won by Labor at the election, with the seat firmly in their heartland.
"I understand Labor is spending quite a lot of money on Blair. It's a seat that … you'd want to see sandbagged, to protect it.
"It's a seat that the opposition would like to win, but there are others more likely to go to the Coalition in the federal election, probably in the Hunter and in Sydney and Melbourne."
Blair has been held by Labor's Shayne Neumann since 2007. He currently holds it with a 5.23 per cent margin.
It was held from its inception in 1998 to 2007 by the Liberal party. The LNP's candidate this year is Ipswich business manager and pastor Carl Mutzelburg.
Ms Basra grows her own vegetables in her backyard to help alleviate some cost-of-living pressures.  (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)
Back in Ripley, Ms Basra just wants to see whoever forms the next federal government do more to address cost-of-living issues for families.
"There are people that are much harder done by than us," she said.
"But our mortgage repayments nearly work out to $900 a week — no average person can afford that.

title: Markets plunge again as US confirms China tariff even higher
content:
US markets have plunged again as optimism over President Donald Trump's tariffs "pause" is overshadowed by his escalating trade war with China.
At the close on Thursday, local time, the S&P 500 was down 3.5 per cent, the Dow Jones was down 2.5 per cent and the Nasdaq had fallen 4.3 per cent.
That represented a wipe-out of about a third of the previous day's record gains, which followed Mr Trump's decision to "pause" his most severe tariffs for 90 days.
The falls worsened after the White House clarified the tariff imposed on China — which will not be paused — equates to 145 per cent, rather than the 125 per cent previously announced.
The 125 per cent figure did not account for the 20 per cent tariff placed on China earlier this year, ostensibly to punish it for doing too little to stop fentanyl shipments to the US.
Mr Trump again said he was optimistic about reaching a deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
"He's been a friend of mine for a long period of time, and I think that we'll end up working out something that's very good for both countries," Mr Trump said.
Hollywood became the latest target in the bilateral trade war when China indicated it would reduce screenings of American movies.
"The US government's erroneous practice of imposing excessive tariffs on China is likely to further diminish the Chinese audience's favourable perception of American films," the China Film Administration said, according to the South China Morning Post.
"We will adhere to market principles, respect audience choices and moderately reduce the import volume of American films."
Meanwhile, the European Union said it would pause its planned retaliatory tariffs on the US as it works to strike a deal with Washington. Mr Trump said the US would negotiate with the EU as a single bloc, rather than individual countries.
Tech and banking stocks were among those hardest hit by the falls on the US markets.
Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting before the close of trade, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated he was not concerned about the market volatility.
"As we go through the queue and settle with these countries who are going to bring their best offers, we will end up in a place of great certainty over the next 90 days on tariffs," he said.
"We had very good inflation numbers today, oil's down, we had a successful bond market. So I don't see anything unusual today."
Mr Trump said "there will always be transition difficulty" but he was proud of "the biggest day in history" on the US markets on Wednesday.
Mr Trump's "pause" means almost all imports are now subject to a 10 per cent "baseline" tariff, which was already the rate set for Australia.
Of all Trump's miscalculations this week, his biggest miscalculation of all may be assuming that China would not hit back, using the economic power that the Chinese Communist Party has been amassing for decades, but until recently, has not fully deployed.
Asked if countries could negotiate to reduce that 10 per cent tariff further, Mr Trump said: "It depends what they're adding."
"Some countries we have massive deficits with or they have big surpluses with us, and others it's not that way," he said.
"We have some that are pretty even, but they hurt us in other ways, and we just want to get that taken care of."
The US has had a trade surplus with Australia for decades, meaning it sends more products to Australia than it imports from Australia.
But early this year, there was a rare — and almost certainly temporary — reversal after an American buy-up of billions of dollars' worth of Australian gold, fuelled by fears of a trade war.
Mr Trump's trade advisers also complain Australia has unfair trade barriers on meat, pharmaceuticals and tech.

title: A super payment went to the wrong account but the fund says it's not to blame
content:
Warning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article includes the name and image of someone who has died (used with the permission of his family).
Annette Riley stands on the jetty at Derby in remote Western Australia as the harsh afternoon sun beats down on the vast body of water known as King Sound.
Her youngest son Warick Deegan was a keen fisherman who worked on boats and knew this Kimberley coastline well
For most of his life, Mr Deegan was "happy go lucky" but a few years ago, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, he hit a rough patch and requested early access to $10,000 of his superannuation.
When Mr Deegan didn't receive the money, he called Australian Super twice to ask why and repeatedly went into his bank.
Australia's largest superannuation fund, Australian Super, is being sued by the corporate regulator for "significant delays" in processing thousands of death benefit claims.
Months later, he died by suicide.
His mother is still grappling with the loss.
Every day she's reminded of him by a framed picture, inside the entrance way of her home.
"He (would have) turned 40 this year. He was only 36 at the time (he died)," she said.
Derby is a tight knit community of just over 3,000 people, more than 40 per cent of whom are Indigenous.
It feels a world away — almost 5,000 kilometres — from the sleek Melbourne high-rise office tower of the country's largest retirement fund — Australian Super.
Ms Riley, is speaking out about her two-year battle with the fund which she believes failed to meet the needs of her son and his beneficiaries.
The Nyikina woman has been fighting to recoup the $10,000 that was sent to an account that wasn't his and she wants her son's death benefit, worth $180,000, reinstated.
The company is refusing both requests.
Mr Deegan's death benefit was cancelled shortly before he died because he had not made contributions for more than sixteen months, so the account was deemed inactive.
Annette Riley with a photo of her son and his family. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)
Australian Super maintains it acted lawfully.
"I think that's the wrong decision," Ms Riley said.
"It's important for my son, but also for his daughter.
"My granddaughter."
Public confidence in the multi-trillion-dollar superannuation sector has been rocked in recent times.
Australia's corporate watchdog calls on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims.
A cyber-attack this month sparked criticism about security and reporting processes, while a blistering review by the corporate watchdog ASIC called for a drastic overhaul of how death benefit claims are handled.
The review singled out the poor experiences of First Nations members and their families.
ASIC is also suing Australian Super over what it alleges were lengthy delays in processing thousands of death benefit claims.
Financial counsellor Alan Gray from Bush Money Mob works across Indigenous communities in remote Western Australia.
He represents Ms Riley and believes the superannuation sector is regularly failing First Nations members.
Mr Deegan earned his money doing hard, physical work on cattle stations, railway lines for the mining industry and on pearling boats.
Since his partner's death, John's been locked in a lengthy battle with one of Australia's largest funds to get her super paid out. He's not alone, with the country's peak advocacy group calling for an end to lengthy delays and further grief for families.
But as the pandemic shut down the country, he was one of three million Australians who requested early access to their super for compassionate reasons.
Mr Deegan was living in the tiny Indigenous community of Pandanus Park about 40 minutes drive from the nearest ANZ branch in Derby.
His mother said he went regularly to the bank to see if the super payment had come through.
After coming up empty at the bank, Mr Deegan called Australian Super twice.
His family has provided recordings of the phone calls to the ABC.
They also allowed us to show his face and use his name.
The first time Mr Deegan called was October 15, 2020 and he told the call centre worker he'd applied for the payment through the tax office.
Warick Deegan spoke with Australian Super twice over the phone about the missing money
"How long ago was that?" the call operated asked.
"About four weeks ago," Mr Deegan replied.
The call operator sounded shocked.
"Four weeks? Okay,"
After looking up his file, the Australian Super call operator delivered bad news.
The money had been paid weeks earlier.
"How much would that be?" Mr Deegan asked.
"Ten thousand," the call operator answered.
"Far out," Mr Deegan whispered.
The operator then checked the ANZ bank account the money went into and Mr Deegan stated it was not his.
"You don't have any other bank accounts?" the call operator asked.
"No, I don't, um, I might have to rush into the bank or something. Someone else's account," Mr Deegan said.
The second call was just days later on October 26.
Mr Deegan asked the female call operator if it had been paid into someone else's account.
"It will bounce back to us if the bank account details is (sic) incorrect it will bounce back to us," she reassured him.
"That's what I was thinking, because it's been awhile," Mr Deegan answered.
He then asked if it was certain the money would bounce back, as she had suggested.
"It will bounce back, for sure, right?" he asked.
"Yeah it will bounce back to Australian Super," she confirmed.
The call operator then said she would get Australian Super to reprocess the payment.
Mr Deegan again said he was concerned the money won't bounce back and for the third time she reassured him it would.
"Look, so far, in my experience, all payments that have been made to the wrong bank account has bounced back to Australian super," she said.
When Mr Deegan died he had only a small balance left in his ANZ bank account.
Ms Riley said her family remains distressed because it believes based on the phone calls that he never received the money.
Financial counsellor Alan Gray is working with Annette Riley and is calling on the fund to reinstate her son's death benefit. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)
She suspects financial hardship may have contributed to his death.
"We were all angry when we found out," Ms Riley said.
When the family asked Mr Gray for help, he in turn questioned Australian Super about the missing $10,000.
At first Australian Super told him it had paid the money to Mr Deegan's ANZ account.
The bank later contradicted that, confirming in an email it was not his account but refused to say more due to privacy restrictions.
"Australian Super have no idea who they are paying that COVID super money to because they don't match the account name with the BSB and account number (known as confirmation of payee technology).
A photograph of Warick Deegan hangs in this mother's home. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)
The ABC asked Australian Super whether it used confirmation of payee technology or if it performed other due diligence on the account prior to making payment but it did not directly answer.
It said the $10,000 was paid to the bank account provided by the tax office and Mr Deegan should have checked the account details when making his early release application with the ATO.
ANZ said it did not comment on individual customers and when money was sent to the wrong account it attempted to recover it.
The taxation office also declined to comment.
Australian Super is also refusing to reinstate $180,000 in death benefits insurance Mr Deegan had until shortly before he died.
The company cancelled the cover about four months earlier, due to his account being inactive — a requirement that was put in place to stop ongoing fees eroding super balances.
But his family said he never knew his insurance cover was at risk and the company missed crucial opportunities to warn him while he was on the phone.
Australian Super did send two warning letters to an old address but the letters were returned to sender.
Alan Gray and Annette Riley say Australian Super had many opportunities to warn Mr Deegan his death benefit was about to be cancelled. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)
The company conceded it did not have his phone number or email address but maintained the onus was on the member to make sure their contact details were up to date.
Australian Super declined to be interviewed but said in a statement it was, "a tragic case" and "we feel deeply for Mr Deegan and his family".
Chief Member Officer Rose Kerlin said Australian Super stood by its position because it had followed its processes and met its legal obligations.
However, Ms Kerlin also said, "the outcome for Mr Deegan and his family is not what anyone would have wanted."
Mr Deegan's family took a dispute to the financial ombudsman, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) but lost.
AFCA found Australian Super had acted fair and reasonably by cancelling his insurance and processing the super payment.
Financial counsellor Alan Gray. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)
However, Mr Gray believes Australian Super should have done more to warn Mr Deegan about the loss of his death benefits and should have offered him additional support as a remote First Nations person.
Mr Gray is calling on Australian Super to reverse its position on the case.
Ms Kerlin from Australian Super said Warick's case showed the need for widespread change.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant says the industry needs to meet "reasonable expectations". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)
"This shows systemic changes to laws and industry standards are needed to better serve vulnerable Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, particularly in remote areas," she said.
The company has a phone line for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander members and those staffing it have cultural training, as have other employees including those in the dispute resolution and operations teams.
Last month ASIC released a highly-critical review of how 10 super funds dealt with death benefits.
It excluded Australian Super due to ASIC's ongoing lawsuit.
The review uncovered lengthy delays — mostly within the trustee's control, poor customer service like phone calls not being returned and claims handling where vulnerability wasn't properly considered.
Email michaelatkin@protonmail.com or contact him via the Signal secure messaging app +61 447 279 901.
ASIC Commissioner Simone Constant said the industry was on notice to "lift their game now," to meet the "reasonable expectations" of grieving families.
The review found outcomes were worse for First Nations members and their families and that was further exacerbated when people lived remotely.
Amongst 34 recommendations, were six related to fixing these chronic issues with Indigenous Australians.
"Something needs to be done here urgently," Ms Constant said.
"The service failings and the gaps were amplified or exacerbated with the First Nations members and their families."

title: Australian weapon trialled by Israel's military ahead of potential sale
content:
Israel's military has completed trials of an advanced weapon made by a Canberra-based defence supplier which boasts its “high precision” and “lethal” product can strike targets up to two kilometres away.
The ABC can reveal the remote weapon system (RWS), designed and built by Australian company Electro Optic Systems (EOS), was one of dozens of counter drone technologies tested by the Israel Defense Forces earlier this year.
A defence industry source claims the Australian-made components were first sent to an EOS entity in the United States for assembly, before being shipped to Israel without an Australian export approval.
For months, the Albanese government has insisted “no Australian weaponry” has been exported to Israel, and the Defence Department has again told the ABC that “Australia has not supplied weapons or ammunition to Israel” since the Gaza war began in 2023.
On Friday morning, the prime minister again insisted that Australia would not sell arms to Israel.
"I am aware of this report that you refer to, we looked into this matter and the company have confirmed with the Department of Defence that the particular system was not exported from Australia," he said.
"Australia does not export weapons to Israel."
In a statement, EOS declined to comment on whether its R400 RWS has been demonstrated in Israel telling the ABC it “does not publicise commercially sensitive information regarding clients, existing contracts or business development campaigns”.
However, documents supplied to the Australian Stock Exchange in February reveal that EOS “supported a local prime to demonstrate counter-drone capabilities in a high-profile local demonstration” in January 2025, but did not specify where it took place.
Australian Army Hawkei fitted with an EOS R400-HD during a counter-drone firing (Defence department image: CPL Michael Currie)
The “Market Development Update” includes a photo of Israeli Ministry of Defense officials standing behind a modified R400 and states that the “EOS’ system performed extremely well, earning high praise from the organisers”.
On EOS’s website the R400 is described as “Lightweight 30mm lethality with precise mobile engagements up to 2 km” and “a high-precision weapon platform with the firepower of a 30 mm cannon”.
“The R400 also supports other weapons, such as machine guns, automatic grenade launchers, and anti-tank guided missiles. It is compatible with other EOS weapon systems through ‘plug-and-play’ functionality.”
Israel’s Ministry of Defence announced in February it had “successfully completed an extensive series of operational trials testing approximately 20 advanced counter-drone technologies”.
“Nine Israeli defence industries and startups demonstrated various drone interception and neutralisation capabilities using both projectile-based systems and counter-drones at a testing field in southern Israel,” the Ministry said in a press release.
An accompanying photograph shows Israeli Defence Ministry officials and industry representative standing behind an R400 system, which is the same image included in the EOS “Market Development Update” provided to the Australian Stock Exchange.
The R400, manufactured by Electro Optic Systems (Supplied by the company, EOS)
In response to questions on whether EOS sought approval to demonstrate its R400, a Defence Department spokesperson insisted Australia had “not supplied weapons or ammunition to Israel since the conflict began, and for at least the past five years.
“As the circumstances of the conflict have evolved, the Government has calibrated its approach and has only approved new export permits to Israel for items for Australian defence and law enforcement that will return to Australia,” the spokesperson said.
“Defence has also been undertaking a process to scrutinise the pre-existing export permits to Israel. These pre-existing permits were all approved before the conflict began and none of the permits relate to weapons or ammunition.”
Asked whether it had sought permission to export the lethal technology, and whether the product had first gone to the United States, an EOS spokesperson told the ABC that that the company “complies with all relevant regulations at all times”.
“EOS operates under the trade control regulations of the countries it is based in, due to the nature of its products and technologies,” the spokesperson added.
“That includes detailed regulations in Australia and other host countries where EOS manufactures products, like the United States.”
Greens Senator David Shoebridge says the involvement of EOS exposes the Albanese government’s “lies” that Australia has not supported Israel’s military campaign against Gaza, a position reinforced this week by the Prime Minister during a leaders’ debate.
"What we can see clearly here is an Australian made weapon in the hands of the Israeli military in Israel in January this year and I think that really puts the lie to these denials we've had from the Albanese government since this appalling conflict started," Senator Shoebridge told the ABC.

title: Prada to buy rival fashion house Versace in $2.2 billion deal
content:
Prada Group has announced a deal to buy Versace from the US luxury group Capri Holdings under terms that value the fashion house at 1.25 billion euros ($2.2 billion).
The deal brings one of fashion's best-known Italian labels back under Italian control after it was sold to Capri Holdings, then known as Michael Kors, for $US2.15 billion ($3.4 billion) including debt in 2018.
Donatella Versace is replaced as creative director of the luxury fashion house Versace.
Prada said the addition of Versace's "highly recognisable aesthetic constitutes a strongly complementary addition" to its portfolio, which includes the Prada and Miu Miu fashion brands.
It said Milan-based Versace offered "significant untapped growth potential.''
The final value of the deal will be adjusted at closing which is expected in the second half of the year.
It will be funded by 1.5 billion euros in new debt and has been approved by the Prada and Capri Holdings board of directors.
"Versace will maintain its creative DNA and cultural authenticity, while benefiting from the full strength of the Group's considerable consolidated platform, including industrial capabilities, retail execution and operational expertise,'' Prada said in a statement.
Versace, founded in 1978 by the late Gianni Versace, has been owned since 2018 by Capri Holdings, which includes Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo.
Capri Holdings paid $US2 billion for Versace, but had been struggling in the recent era of "quiet luxury'.
Last month, Capri Holdings named Dario Vitale as creative director to replace Donatella Versace, who assumed the role after her brother's 1997 murder.
Versace was given the new role of chief brand ambassador in the shake-up, which was widely viewed as setting the scene for the long-running Prada sale.
The deal has revived hopes for a 'Made in Italy' luxury champion after many other family-founded brands ended up in French, Swiss or US hands, and comes as many Italian groups are outperforming the struggling sector.
A model presents a creation from the Prada Fall-Winter 2025/2026 collection during the Milan Fashion Week in Italy. (Reuters: Alessandro Garofalo)
Despite Italy accounting for 50 to 55 per cent of global personal luxury goods production, according to consultancy Bain's estimates, the country lacks a group with a scale that matches up to French players such as LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE and Gucci-owner Kering.
Milan-based Prada, controlled by designer Miuccia Prada and husband Patrizio Bertelli and listed in Hong Kong with a market capitalisation of about 14 billion euros, is the largest Italian luxury fashion group by revenue.
But the group, which also includes the fast-growing Miu Miu label, has been a relative minnow in terms of stock market valuation compared with the likes of Louis Vuitton-owner LVMH.
The Versace deal comes after Andrea Guerra became Prada's CEO in 2023 to bridge a change in generation, with Lorenzo Bertelli, the son of the company's main owners and its chief marketing officer, regarded as the heir apparent.
"Prada's ambition to become a leading Italian luxury conglomerate is a significant move in a market that is dominated by French groups," said fashion and luxury industry adviser Achim Berg.
The combined revenue of the five biggest Italian-owned listed luxury groups still well below Kering's roughly 17 billion euros, even after a big fall in sales at the French group last year.

title: Coalition to abolish 'ute tax' fuel efficiency standards
content:
A scheme to cut the emissions of cars and encourage electric vehicle uptake will be substantially wound back under a Coalition government, with Opposition Leader Peter Dutton dubbing it an unfair car tax.
The New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES) will take force in July after being legislated at the request of several automotive companies in 2024.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
It sets an emissions ceiling on the total car sales of each automaker, with heavy penalties for those who exceed it.
The federal government has detailed its proposal to impose a CO2 standard on new cars. It will have a narrow road to travel to ensure it cuts emissions without driving up car prices.
The Coalition will dump those penalties — keeping the framework of the efficiency standards, but not penalising breaches.
It argues car manufacturers will continue to offer cleaner cars in the Australian market, but costs will not increase for consumers.
The industry had asked to be regulated, saying Australia was alone with Russia in not having a fuel efficiency law — and the lack of one was making it hard to get hold of in-demand electric vehicles or other more fuel-efficient cars.
However, with United States President Donald Trump's tariffs — including a substantial tariff on "foreign automobiles" — the sector is in crisis and some car makers have expressed fears when the NVES takes effect it will compound their uncertainty.
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Industry insiders told the ABC last week that 4x2 variants of the Ford Everest and Mazda M-UX were among ranges due to be pulled from July — while other makers considered baking penalties into their business models and passing on some of that fine to consumers.
The opposition leader claimed industry estimates showed some of the heaviest polluting cars could raise their prices by thousands of dollars in the long run.
"This is a tax on families who need a reliable car and small businesses trying to grow. Instead of making life easier, Labor is making it harder and more expensive," Mr Dutton said.
"A Coalition government will scrap this tax, so Australians can keep more of their hard-earned money when purchasing a new car."
Peter Dutton has dubbed Labor's fuel efficiency standards a "tax" on families.
Labor has denied its NVES will substantially affect prices, pointing to overseas markets with similar schemes that have remained competitive on price.
"Let's be clear on what these standards do: they bring us into line with the rest of the world, so that Australians can have more cars that are cheaper to run," energy minister Chris Bowen told the ABC.
The industry has challenged that, suggesting Australia's late adoption means it is acting harder and faster to reach similar fuel efficiency goals.
However, while there is great uncertainty in the global car market under the cloud of Mr Trump's tariffs, the penalties and credits accrued under NVES don't become payable before 2028.
This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat.
Motoring data insights agency Blue Flag has forecast the industry could be hit with as much as $2.7 billion in penalties by that date, though those who accrue credits would be set to benefit under the cap-and-trade scheme.
The Coalition campaigned on Labor's planned fuel efficiency standards at previous elections, calling it a tax on utes because it dis-incentivised less fuel-efficient cars, and saying it "threatened to end the weekend".
The party says it will work with industry to bring the cleanest cars on the market to Australia, without "punishing" those who cannot afford them.
Shadow energy minister Ted O'Brien said the party will retain the vehicle efficiency standard without penalties, with the aim of ensuring cleaner cars continue to be brought to the Australian market.
"The Coalition backs lower emitting vehicles because more fuel-efficient cars save Aussies money every time they fill up — but we won't back Labor's car tax that drives prices through the roof," he said.
"Labor has got the balance wrong by imposing penalties that will be passed on to Australian families and small businesses."
Mr Bowen said the Coalition would turn the standards "into a toothless tiger" and that this would be "worse than a voluntary standard".
"Peter Dutton wants Australia to be a dumping ground for out-of-date models, that guzzle petrol and cost more to run, putting us in the same basket as Russia when it comes to standards," he said.
"Consumer and motoring advocates, carmakers, and dealers support standards with teeth because they know their customers benefit from cars that are cheaper to run.
"People can by whatever car suits their needs, from 4-wheel-drives and utes to EVs and hatchbacks. Vehicles are getting more efficient every day, and carmakers that offer those up-to-date models won't be impacted."
