title: Wagyu beef producer confident about exports despite Trump tariff threat
content:
Australia's wagyu beef industry is set to capitalise on growth opportunities amid record-low cattle numbers in the United States and less competition for its premium beef product in world markets.
Despite potential tariffs under consideration by the US government, industry leaders and producers remain confident that Australia's high-quality wagyu beef will continue to command premium prices and strong demand.
South Australian producer Scott de Bruin said he was not deterred by the threat of US tariffs.
Mr de Bruin, the managing director of Mayura Station near Millicent on South Australia's Limestone Coast, said its full-blood Wagyu cattle were first imported into Australia in 1997 and the herd's ancestry, bloodlines and pedigree were distinguishing factors in world markets.
Australia's wagyu industry is about four times larger than America's sector. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)
Mr de Bruin said he did not see a 10 per cent tariff significantly impacting his business.
"Overall, the American cattle herd is at 70-year lows … they do really need beef from other countries.
"When you've got a high-quality article, I believe those customers that want to consume high quality are not going to be bothered by another 10 per cent."
Scott de Bruin holds a tomahawk wagyu steak. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)
His comments follow US President Donald Trump singling out Australian beef in early April.
While Australia will be subject to a 10 per cent reciprocal tariff, the president has yet to detail any specific response to Australia's beef sector.
Global AgriTrends meat and livestock analyst Simon Quilty said it was an "outstanding time" for the sector with the opportunities and challenges dependent on the quality of the wagyu.
This class one fullblood wagyu competition entry from Mayura Sation had a nine-plus rating. (Supplied: Australian Wagyu Association)
Within Australia, the quality of a cut of wagyu is determined by its marbling score.
A score of zero indicates no marbling, while a score of nine indicates extraordinary amounts of marbling.
A nine-plus indicates the meat exceeds current Australian standards.
"In the last year we've seen zero-to-three marble score in America really be challenged, so those products tend not to go to America these days because there is no home for them," Mr Quilty said.
"Those that are producing five to seven … those higher marble scores stand out on their own and they today from Australia trade at a significant premium above the best in America.
"That's where the best return for Australian exporters is.
However, North America is not the only opportunity for Australian producers – with Australian exporters already benefiting from American export shortfalls in key markets in the Middle East and South-East Asia.
Mr Quilty said if America implemented further tariffs, it could open the door for Australia to better compete against US beef internationally.
Wagyu beef is high in marbled white intramuscular fat, providing a full flavour and creamy texture. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)
"[American] exports have fallen and as a result of that we have seen less and less of that high-end-choice prime in these markets, which then has created opportunities for Australian wagyu outside of America," he said.
"You're not only getting less product come out of America, but it will be priced higher, therefore making Australian beef more attractive.
"Australia sits in a unique position as a producer of grain fed of a standard that matches America."

title: Live music programs giving regional artists something to sing about
content:
After years of struggling to attract audiences in regional areas, there may be hope on the horizon for Australia's live music performers and small-town venues.
Distance, travel costs and venue adequacy have always been obstacles for bands and solo artists in the regions, but grassroots initiatives in South Australia and New South Wales are looking promising, according to industry experts.
A recent study from the University of South Australia found venue owners and artists are being short-changed as it becomes harder to attract substantial audiences and put on regular shows.
But co-lead researcher Rosie Roberts suggested local grassroots programs could reinvigorate the regional live music industry.
Bianca Feher says there are more opportunities for musicians in the cities. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)
Singer-songwriter Bianca Feher, 20, from South Australia's Riverland region, about 200km north-east of Adelaide,  knows the challenges of the regional music scene.
"There's not as many people [in the Riverland] and the creative industries are not as established," she said.
Ms Feher began playing gigs at local pubs and breweries when she was 16, but has since moved to Adelaide, where there are more live music opportunities.
Finding audiences in her home region that seek out original music has also been a struggle.
"There's not really a defined audience for it and there's not as big of an audience for the stuff I do, which isn't even that niche," Ms Feher said.
Jazz pianist Andrew Casey says musicians cannot make a living in regional areas without support. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)
Jazz pianist Andrew Casey, who performs with the band Auspicion, also moved to Adelaide from the Riverland because, he said, it was "impossible" to make a career playing original music there.
"You cannot be an original music artist and expect to make any money from it if you live in the Riverland," he said.
"Most venues in the Riverland want original artists to hire the venue at ridiculously large costs that are just unrealistic.
"The only way to put on a show is definitely at a loss."
South Australian band Auspicion performs at the Woolshed Brewery at Murtho. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)
But Mount Gambier-based music promoter Stephen Esnouf said a fledgling MusicSA initiative was giving young artists "a bit of hope".
Project: Music South East launched in August 2024 with a focus on venue support, sustainability and activation.
It included the introduction of a regional venue coordinator, who shared industry expertise with venue owners through workshops and masterclasses.
The Woolstore Brewery in Mount Gambier. (Supplied: Woolstore Brewery)
Co-founder of the Woolstore Brewery in Mount Gambier Kylie Ind said the workshops allowed artists, venue owners and promoters to come together to build a better understanding of each other's needs.
Ms Ind said part of the project's value came from formalising the relationship between artists and venues.
MusicSA chief executive Christine Schloithe said the initiative had a holistic approach.
"That has a flow-on impact for being able to support artists, to be able to support the creation of new music in Australia and … to build those audiences for live music," she said.
Christine Schloithe says supporting live music in the regions benefits artists, venues and audiences. (ABC News: Angus Patterson)
Ms Schloithe said one of the foremost issues the industry was facing was the "tyranny of distance".
"Even to hire a truck with some technical gear to put the band on the road, to pay for accommodation, to cover meals and expenses, that's a really significant undertaking," she said.
"Artists really can't be paying out of their own pocket for the pleasure of performing and touring and delivering their job.
"It's not just the venues that benefit — it is the artist, it is the audiences."
The peak body said it was working towards replicating the program in other regions across the state on an ongoing basis.
One of the difficulties for both artists and venues is bridging the cultural gap in understanding what it takes to stage live music.
Despite finding an online audience, the Mount Gambier rapper says finding somewhere to play live in regional South Australia has been a battle. He hopes new local music initiatives will change that.
For artists, this has looked like venues not being aware of the value of hosting an original artist instead of a DJ.
Mr Casey said while it may once have existed, there was no longer a culture of venues supporting live music in his home region.
And for venues, Ms Ind said while customers were crying out for live music experiences, they were often not willing to buy a ticket for a show or spend money on drinks at free events.
Music promoter Stephen Esnouf works in the local music scene in Mount Gambier. (ABC South East: Joshua Brine)
Mr Esnouf said venues were now getting on board and supporting artists.
"What this project has made us as a community realise, and I think made venues wake up to as well … [is that] this is a business relationship," he said.
A similar program was introduced in New South Wales in 2023 by MusicNSW, with a cohort of five "regional coordinators" to provide localised support.
The program includes an online regional touring network to guide artists, promoters and managers to venues outside Sydney.
MusicNSW managing director Joe Muller said artists and industry professionals faced a gap in opportunities between metropolitan and regional areas.
Joe Muller says the coordinators in the regional NSW music program are the "special sauce" of the initiative. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)
"So much of the contemporary music industry is really centralised in metro centres, and so navigating folks towards better outcomes for that as they develop their careers can be challenging in regional and remote spaces," he said.
Mr Muller said he saw the coordinators as the organisation's "superpower".
The positive effects of the program were already being seen, he said.
"On the Mid North Coast, our coordinator there identified a town that was really lacking in opportunities for live music," Mr Muller said.
"She found a young woman who was interested in becoming a promoter and she connected them and that young person has now gone on to book shows in a number of neighbouring towns as well, and created some touring networks."
Bianca Feher began playing gigs at local pubs and breweries in the Riverland region when she was 16. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)
Ms Feher said for regional artists, being able to develop a relationship with venue owners in their home towns would be mutually beneficial.
"I think it's just a really nice environment to be in and celebrate performing arts," she said.

title: There’s never been a better time for NSW unit owners to look towards the sun
content:
Apartment dwellers can now harness the power of the sun thanks to new technology and government support, making it cheaper to electrify high-density housing with solar panels.
The push is part of a broader effort to demystify the often difficult task of installing renewables in strata buildings.
Australia is a world leader in rooftop solar, but while one in five homes in NSW are apartments, only 3.5 per cent of them have solar panels installed, the federal government says.
Comparatively, over 30 per cent of houses in the state use solar.
National campaign director for advocacy group Solar Citizens Joel Pringle said there had "never really been a better time" to install solar.
"As there's more assistance, as there's more funding available from government programs, it gets easier," he said.
Only 3.5 per cent of NSW apartments have solar panels installed. (ABC News: Monish Nand)
The state government's new scheme covers up to half the cost of a shared rooftop solar system for small-to-medium-sized apartment buildings.
Solar for Apartment Residents (SoAR), will divvy out grants of up to $150,000 in matched funding for those living in apartments or multi-dwelling units to install a shared system.
It's a first for the state and should also streamline the process of installing panels on co-owned roof space.
Owners corporations or strata management firms can apply for the scheme on behalf of an entire property for buildings with three to 55 units, but the program is not available for individual units.
Installing a rooftop solar system does come with inherent cost for apartment owners. (ABC News: Monish Nand)
Other states and territories have unveiled similar programs, including Victoria and the ACT, and Queensland recently announced a program for rental properties.
Installing a rooftop solar system does come with inherent costs, which for apartment owners are subdivided between units.
But Cameron Knox from Allume Energy, which installs rooftop solar for apartment buildings, said the financial outcome was worth the up-front cost and would provide a buffer from the volatility of traditional power prices.
Mr Knox said units could now benefit from burgeoning technology.
His company created a product called SolShare that subdivides the energy a solar system generates equally among all of the connected apartments but delivers it dynamically throughout the day.
If one unit needs energy to run the dishwasher around noon, but the others are empty, it can deliver power to that unit alone.
When residents of the other units return, the product sends energy to their properties instead.
New technology means solar power can be equally subdivided between apartments in a strata block. (ABC News: Monish Nand)
The NSW government also finalised changes to strata legislation in 2021 that meant sustainability upgrades — including the installation of solar systems — only require a simple majority of 50 per cent to go ahead, down from 75 per cent.
But questions remain about another grey area in solar capacity — the push for new high-rise, high-density homes in transport corridors across NSW.
Mr Pringle urged the government to ensure new builds consider the inclusion of clean energy options for those who live there.
"We need to get it right in the first place. We can't build all these buildings and then fix them later," he said.
Joel Pringle says solar panel access is getting easier for apartment owners. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)
It could still be difficult for apartment owners to jump on the renewables train because every building has vested interests.
"The strata sector is really diverse," Mr Pringle, who recently installed solar on his strata-managed townhouse, said.
"The first thing is to get to know your neighbours, that helps.
Energy providers and solar installers often have calculators to guesstimate what size system a building may need and how much it can cost.
Those interested in the program can contact a company of choice for an energy assessment. (ABC News: Monish Nand)
Tools like SunSPOT can also help provide other estimates for how many panels could fit on a building's roof.
But Mr Pringle said the most straightforward strategy was to contact a solar consultant for an energy assessment.
About one-third of homes have rooftop solar, but just one in 40 have a battery, according to government figures.
Batteries can be used to store energy generated from solar panels for later use, helping to lower power bills and take strain off the grid.
Household discounts on batteries used for rooftop solar has featured in the federal election. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)
Labor recently pledged to discount household batteries for homes across the country if re-elected, allocating some $2.3 billion to the effort.
The program would subsidise 30 per cent of the cost of a battery, which could in turn save a household up to $1,100 on power bills each year, according to that party's modelling.
Mr Pringle said those discounts would apply for solar systems already in place, meaning houses with panels will largely be the immediate benefactors. But apartment buildings should be eligible once they have a system on the roof, he said.
Opposition Leader Peter Dutton lambasted Labor's plan as a benefit solely for families with high incomes, which he claimed will be subsidised by taxpayers who couldn't afford one themselves.
The Liberal Party instead plans to focus on an increase in domestic gas production and the roll-out of seven new nuclear plants.

title: Builder's collapse leaves years-long fight with insurer in its wake
content:
At 73 years of age, Amarjit Singh Pabla was supposed to be living a comfortable retirement.
"But the way it happened, I'm not very happy. I'm very close to bankruptcy," Mr Pabla tells ABC News.
The West Australian man's investment project, building eight new apartments, turned sour when his builder collapsed, leaving him with hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of repairs to make the dwellings saleable.
Mr Pabla's development was covered by insurance in his building contract.
In fact, the insurance is compulsory for any residential building work worth more than $20,000 in the state.
But his claim has been caught up for years and he is facing mounting legal costs to continue the process.
Lawyers and consumer advocates say builders warranty insurance — just one of the various names the product is known by across Australia — is complex and doesn't offer adequate protection for consumers.
There are calls for national minimum standards, including limits on how long it should take for insurance claims to be settled.
As more builders go bust, consumers face insurance payout delays (Nassim Khadem)
In December 2014, Mr Pabla signed a contract to build eight apartments using about $200,000 worth of his superannuation savings, a $1.6 million loan from the bank, and about $420,000 borrowed from friends and relatives.
But after the builder he contracted went bankrupt in February 2022, the entire building was found to be defective, making all eight apartments unsaleable.
Amarjit Singh Pabla says he may go bankrupt if his insurance claim is not settled.  (ABC News: Julian Robins )
Mr Pabla says he has spent the past three years fighting insurance company QBE to get a payout to repair the building defects, sell the property and move on with his life.
He believes the insurer is dragging out the case rather than paying him out swiftly.
If you have more information about this story please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com
He says while he waits for the defects to be fixed, QBE has appointed third-party lawyers to deal with his claim.
"I have to talk to QBE through their lawyers. And up to now it has cost me $32,000 in legal fees so I can talk to their lawyers."
He believes there is no motivation on the insurer's side to settle the claim as its liability is capped. The maximum payout for incomplete or defective works was $100,000 at the time Mr Pabla entered his building contract.
"There's absolutely no motivation on their [QBE's] side [to settle the claim] because their liability will never, ever go up," he said.
QBE Insurance offers builders warranty insurance in many states.  (AAP: Luis Enrique Ascui)
While QBE has paid out some costs for plumbing repairs, it has not paid the money for the bulk of repairs for other, more costly defects.
ABC put a number of detailed questions about Mr Pabla's case to QBE but a spokeswoman told ABC News they were "unable to comment on the specific details of individual claims due to privacy obligations".
"QBE notes that builders warranty claims that involve a number of issues — including encroachment and structural issues — can be highly complex."
She said matters often required "extensive investigations and coordination with multiple stakeholders, including legal and council authorities, which can affect timeframes".
QBE's spokeswoman also told ABC News: "It is common for settlements to be made in stages as each issue is assessed and resolved."
She also said it was "standard practice for QBE to engage third-party legal representatives in claims of this nature to ensure that legal and procedural aspects are appropriately managed".
"We acknowledge that delays can be distressing, and we are working to progress the matter as fairly and efficiently as possible," she said.
Building contracts contain compulsory insurance designed to cover a builder's client in the event the builder goes bust.
Australia's $270 billion construction sector is facing trouble, with more builders going under and new home builds in decline, leaving many customers in the lurch.
The consumer can then, in theory, claim the cost of incomplete or defective work.
But often the consumer does not even know the insurance exists, nor do they read the lengthy policy documents detailing the limitations of that insurance.
The insurance is there as a last resort. And it goes by different names in each state and territory.
According to consumer group Choice, these names include:
Different states also have different regulations about how much cover a person needs before they can enter a building contract and the maximum liability the insurer is up for if the builder goes bust and fixes to the building are required.
John Berrill, an insurance lawyer and director of Berrill & Watson Lawyers, says builders warranty insurance does not offer consumers adequate protection.
Home indemnity insurance in WA covers lost deposits up to $40,000 and completion costs up to a maximum of $200,000 (the liability threshold was recently raised from $100,000).
In June 2022, QBE's own assessor found the repair costs for Mr Pabla's eight units would be just over $716,000.
The QBE assessor's report listed just over $12,000 in plumbing defects. It also included about another $495,000 for building and guttering encroachments defects, as well as $209,000 for acoustic (soundproofing) defects.
But Mr Pabla says that repair cost has now likely escalated, possibly doubling, due to rising building material and labour costs.
He says in July 2022 QBE paid out just under $12,000 for repairing plumbing defects, but it is stalling on paying out for the repair of the other, more costly, defects.
He says aside from the financial turmoil, the dispute with QBE has taken a toll on his health.
Amarjit Singh Pabla says the dispute with QBE has dragged on and is taking a toll on his health. (ABC News: Julian Robins)
Mr Pabla says he received a letter from QBE's lawyers in November 2023 saying that they would need further quotes for loss or damage resulting from acoustic issues.
It also addressed the damage resulting from units being built outside the property boundaries and encroaching onto the surrounding private and public lands, noting: "Our client [QBE] will issue a further decision on liability for this item once those investigations have been complete."
Lawyer John Berrill says liability caps imposed by the insurer often result in the consumer not having enough funds to pay for costly repairs needed to get their home fixed.
John Berrill says builders warranty insurance is failing to protect consumers.  (ABC News: Billy Draper)
He is calling for the implementation of national minimum standards that include how long insurers should take to settle a claim.
"What we need here is a national approach, and standard terms and conditions, so that people can have peace of mind that when they think they're going to have an event that they're going to need to claim on, that they're not going to be out of pocket hundreds of thousands of dollars."
Mr Berrill says consumers should also have an independent consumer body they can turn to when they have a dispute over a claim, especially in cases where the insurance company uses a third-party lawyer to deal with a claim.
"Apart from going through the court system, which is very expensive, you're dealing with people who are vulnerable," he said.
"They're out of their home, they're in debt hundreds of thousands of dollars … and in no position to take their case to court.
"The vast majority of people simply have no idea what's covered, what's not covered, are there any caps on it. So that's where you need the intervention of regulators, governments or legislation to set out minimum terms and conditions."
Mr Pabla is also calling on state governments to regulate the industry to better protect consumers.
More builders are tipped to collapse over the next 18 months, due to speculation in the recent boom.
"Let's … [estimate] 10 per cent of people end up in unfortunate situations like me — QBE is not even interested in a genuine manner to address that issue," he said.
"They [QBE] want to pay you the bare minimum, and if you don't accept that bare minimum, they will set up a team of their lawyers, which they have in every state.
Mr Pabla says QBE had appointed an assessor to investigate the defects in the building, but he did not get their June 2022 report showing the building defects would cost, at that time, $716,000 to repair until months later.
He says he finally received the report on April 14, 2023, when he made a complaint via QBE's internal dispute resolution process.
Amarjit Singh Pabla looks through insurance documents and building contracts.  (ABC News: Julian Robins)
"QBE did not inform us that they had received an assessor's report when they received it, nor when they settled the plumbing defects' claim, nor when we requested it," he said.
He says after making the plumbing repair payment worth just less than $12,000, QBE had asked him to sign an agreement that he would accept this amount as full and final settlement of all issues, releasing QBE from making payments for the soundproofing and encroachment issues worth another $704,000.
The corporate regulator has launched court action over renewal notices sent to more than 500,000 customers, that promised discounts that weren't always delivered.
Had Mr Pabla not consulted with a family member who advised him not to sign the settlement, he says he would have likely signed because English is his second language and he does not understand legal jargon.
He says after refusing to agree to a settlement, QBE appointed a legal firm, Moray & Agnew Lawyers, to deal with the claim.
Mr Pabla has since appointed his own legal firm to represent him.
In 2015, corporate watchdog ASIC called out QBE's use of third-party law firms when dealing with consumer complaints.
ASIC, at the time, raised concerns that consumers may "feel intimidated and possibly dissuaded from pursuing their complaint", after reports emerged that some QBE clients received communications bearing the letterhead of a law firm rather than the insurer.
QBE had at the time agreed to ensure all communications with customers relating to complaints be made on company-branded letterhead, even in cases where the insurer had received assistance from a law firm in preparing the response.
Mr Pabla says while his debts continue to increase, QBE's maximum liability is capped at $100,000 per unit.
And, because of time stamp of the dated policies he has with QBE, he is unable to claim a higher $200,000 policy threshold recently put in place by the state government due to escalating construction costs in WA.
The limit of the indemnity was increased to $200,000 for policies issued from June 2020. For all policies issued prior to this date, the $100,000 policy limit of indemnity applies.

title: Man pleads not guilty after telling police victim asked him to kill her
content:
A man accused of murder impersonated his dead housemate for financial gain, a court has been told.
Warning: This story contains content that readers may find distressing.
Then 26-year-old Yang Zhao was arrested in July 2021, the same day police found 29-year-old Qiong Yan's badly decomposed body in a toolbox.
Detectives made the discovery while searching Mr Zhao's Brisbane apartment as part of an investigation into Ms Yan's disappearance.
The Chinese national had been reported missing by her friends and family in April that year.
The Newport building in Hamilton, in Brisbane's north, where the woman's body was found. (ABC News: Michael Rennie)
Police alleged Mr Zhao killed Ms Yan by "a blow or a number of blows to the head", followed by strangulation.
He then allegedly accessed her phone and bank accounts, transferring himself hundreds of thousands of dollars while also convincing friends and family that Ms Yan was still alive.
Mr Zhao has pleaded guilty to interfering with Ms Yan's body, but pleaded not guilty to her murder.
In his opening statement to the Supreme Court in Brisbane, Crown prosecutor Chris Cook said it would be alleged that Mr Zhao had killed his former flatmate to gain access to her money.
Qiong Yan was reported missing on April 12, 2021. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)
Mr Cook said Mr Zhao "loved the high life" and regularly gambled on the stock market and at poker, despite having no job and living in Australia on a student visa that had expired in 2020.
Ms Yan had come into "a significant settlement" from the sale of her late father's estate in Shanghai in August 2020, which the prosecution argued formed a motivation for Mr Zhao to murder her.
Mr Cook said the day after the alleged murder, Mr Zhao drove to a Bunnings in Newstead and purchased a De Walt toolbox, gloves and duct tape.
The prosecution alleged Mr Zhao had gained access to Ms Yan's phone and used the social media app WeChat to message her mother Rongmei Yan, sending her more than 2,000 messages over the next 10 months.
During that period, he allegedly convinced the deceased woman's mother to send more than $400,000 in separate transactions.
Crown prosecutor Chris Cook alleged the murder accused sold Ms Yan's computer and cancelled her gym membership. (ABC News)
Mr Cook said Mr Zhao transferred a Porsche Panamera, worth more than $300,000 and belonging to Ms Yan, into his own name in the months after her death.
He said Mr Zhao also sold a MacBook belonging to Ms Yan on Facebook Marketplace and cancelled her membership at Anytime Fitness.
Mr Zhao also allegedly sent Rongmei Yan a video of a woman's hand petting a cat in an effort to convince her that her daughter was alive.
By April 2021, Lu Xu had grown suspicious of the "strange" WeChat messages she was receiving from former flatmate and friend, Ms Yan.
The court heard Mr Zhao used messaging app WeChat to contact the dead woman's mother. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)
She reported her missing to NSW Police, who contacted Ms Yan by WeChat when they couldn't locate her.
It's alleged Mr Zhao responded to the messages posing as Ms Yan, writing "Hi, I'm sorry to waste your time and resources, I'm fine."
Mr Zhao allegedly lied to police multiple times about where Ms Yan was, telling them she owed him money and that she'd moved to Melbourne six months earlier.
In July 2021, Mr Zhao was arrested by NSW Police in Sydney.
The court heard a video recording of the subsequent police interview, in which Mr Zhao described Ms Yan's death.
Police said the accused also asked them "how convincing" he was during the arrest, and whether he would receive the death penalty.
Mr Zhao allegedly told police he and Ms Yan had formed a "suicide pact" and she had asked him to kill her.
Forensic officers and detectives at the scene of a Hamilton apartment block after the woman's body was found. (ABC News)
He described hitting her in the head with a gas canister multiple times, after which her head was "covered in blood" and "deformed".
"If I stop now, she'll look ugly the rest of her life," he said in the police interview.
Mr Zhao said he choked Ms Yan for "about half an hour or an hour".
In evidence to be presented to the court, the Crown alleged Ms Yan's phone and Mr Zhao's phone "moved in unison" after her death.
Mr Cook argued that showed Mr Zhao had taken Ms Yan's phone with him.
After the arrest, the victim's phone — which had duct tape covering the cameras — was found at Mr Zhao's Sydney home.
The murder trial is expected to hear from roughly 20 witnesses, including Rongmei Yan, friends, police officers and experts.

title: Being financially prepared before ending a relationship
content:
Thinking about ending a relationship can come with a lot of apprehension.
As well as dealing with the emotional side of things, you will likely be considering the practicalities of single life, including finances.
It's helpful to be as prepared as possible — especially if you're a woman, says Lacey Filipich, a financial educator based in Perth/Boorloo.
While everyone's circumstances will be different, she says on average women have fewer financial resources than men because of the gender pay gap and motherhood penalty.
"There are more cases of women being financially dependent on a man than in reverse," Ms Filipich says.
And whether you're in a marriage or de facto relationship, kids or no kids, splitting up can cost money.
"If you are living with a partner, at some point your finances became entangled," says Bomikazi Zeka, an assistant professor in finance and financial planning at the University of Canberra.
"And when things fall apart, even if amicably, there is still that process of distancing those finances."
If you are experiencing financial abuse and/or other forms of domestic and family violence, you should seek support.
For help, you can contact 1800 RESPECT, the national body for supporting people impacted by sexual assault, domestic or family violence and abuse.
This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.
Your Toolkit is designed to provide women facing domestic and family violence with a road map towards independence, including managing finances.
"It's designed for people escaping violence, but it's a really good list for anyone to look at," Ms Filipich says.
If you have some time before you plan to leave the relationship, Ms Filipich recommends creating an "escape fund".
"Escape money" or a "get out fund" is typically designed to provide someone with the financial freedom to leave a relationship if things break down.
"It doesn't need to be a secret, but having some cash set aside to help you get set up [if you leave] that is only yours can be a bit of a buffer."
'Escape funds' may seem less relevant than they were for our mothers and grandmothers, but some experts say they are common sense and a way to feel 'safer' in relationships.
It's common in relationships for one partner to take charge of paying household bills and other financial responsibilities.
If both parties are across budgets and other financial interests, this isn't typically a problem, Ms Filipich says.
But if you've taken a back seat, she says it's a good idea to get up to speed anytime — and not just ahead of ending a relationship.
"Have a conversation. Sit down and work out who is paying for what and how much," she says.
Dr Zeka says we often let our "financial guard down" in relationships, and once we become solely responsible for our finances, some things can take us by surprise.
"Really take an inventory of your financial position," she says.
"What is my economic financial standpoint? Where are there vulnerabilities? What actions need to be taken to protect myself from those?"
She says you should also think about what you might like to do in some circumstances, such as if you own property together.
"Am I going to buy them out, so I keep it? Or am I going to sell my share?"
Dr Zeka also suggests looking at finer details such as what assets are in your name only, versus those which are jointly owned.
Starting over can feel daunting, Dr Zeka says, but being financially prepared can help you feel empowered. (Pexels)
While you need to be across your current budget, it's also a good idea to create a new one that reflects single life.
Ms Filipich says you can take a look at your current budget, and then mark up what you will have to pay for by yourself now, as well as adding new individual costs.
It may be worth reaching out to some providers for quotes also.
For example, going from couples' health insurance to single-person insurance will unlikely be as straightforward as halving the cost.
Dr Zeka says creating a budget can feel empowering and show you where there is room for financial flexibility, or where you need to tighten up.
"It will help you be realistic about how you will manage life on your own," she says.
Dr Zeka says separation can be overwhelming and emotions may run high — which without good preparation — may cost you.
"You can end up putting yourself in a more financially vulnerable position because you are ready to walk away and sever those ties."
Superannuation is a common example. Women often walk away with less than they are entitled in divorces or during separations in de facto relationships.
Ms Filipich says because women are much more likely to retire with less superannuation than men, it's important they get advice on what they are entitled to.
"Women who have been at home caring for children often think, 'He earned the money. It's not mine.'
"I really want them to get past that. The work you did at home was unpaid, which enabled him to get paid. Don't forfeit it."
Ahead of ending the relationship, you could also consider speaking to your partner about evening up your superannuation before you split.
When financial planner Rebecca Pritchard was starting her family, she used a little-known strategy called contribution splitting to keep her super ticking over.
There are several options for support when it comes to finding your financial bearings.
Financial counselling is a good place to start, Ms Filipich says.
"They are free, and there to help with the nitty gritty.
"They can't give specific advice on legal entitlements, but anything to do with budgeting, planning, [letting you know] what resources are out there — they are the heroes of the financial ecosystem."
She says Relationships Australia also has resources that can help with an "amicable break-up, rather than going through court".
The government website MoneySmart also has a variety of online tools that can help with budgeting and planning.
Dr Zeka says a financial therapist can provide both financial and emotional support.
"Financial coaches are also great — and more accessible than a traditional financial adviser," she says.
She says many banks also offer a free chat to discuss different ways to "help protect your finances", and many superannuation funds offer free consultations to review your contributions.
While starting over can be daunting, Dr Zeka says to remember there are many people willing to help.
"There are a lot of resources you have at your disposal that you can leverage to help you."
This article contains general information only. You should consider obtaining independent professional advice in relation to your particular circumstances.

title: Labor demands Coalition costings and claims $1b in deficit reduction
content:
A crackdown on consultants will help fund the lion's share of Labor's $10 billion in election commitments, according to government pre-election costings released on Monday in a bid to pressure the Coalition to publish its own accounts.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the budget would be about $1 billion better off over four years compared to the March budget, which forecast more than $150 billion in deficits over the same period.
The updated figures include a claimed saving of $6.4 billion through reduced use of consultants, and $740 million in additional revenue from student visa application fees.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
The savings come on top of $4 billion in offsets accounted for in last month's budget.
Released on the same day that one of the world's top ratings agency warned both sides of politics that spending roaring towards post-war highs could threaten Australia's coveted AAA rating, the figures again confirm the nation faces a decade of ongoing deficits caused by increased promises on welfare, military outlays and tax benefits.
"We call on the Coalition to release their costs and cuts immediately," Mr Chalmers told reporters in Brisbane on Monday.
"It is long past time for the Coalition to come clean on their secret cuts to pay for nuclear reactors.
"We've made it very clear what our costs are and how we will pay for the commitments that we have made in this election campaign."
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the government spent about $100 billion a year on procurement and contracts and that it saw "room to make further reductions in that area".
That suggests the savings on consultants announced on Monday would be equivalent to about 1.6 per cent of those outlays.
"That's a significant commitment and it shows that responsible economic management that we've brought to our budget processes," Senator Gallagher told ABC's Afternoon Briefing.
"We want to find further whole-of-government savings."
However, she added that they were "modest in the overall spending of government services".
"They don't affect programs or people, and that's a real contrast, I think, with what the opposition are saying, which is … in the order of $28 billion worth of cuts and 41,000 jobs they want to sack from the public services. We've taken a different approach."
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Labor's demand for immediate Coalition costings follow the traditional political pantomime of election campaigns in their dying days. Three years ago Labor held off releasing its costings until the Thursday before polling day.
The Coalition has made a series of major spending and tax promises during and prior to the campaign, but has yet to reveal a full picture of its likely budget outcomes if it wins government.
Figures released by Labor's campaign claim the Coalition's election promises amount to more than $62 billion, including plans to allow mortgage interest deductions and fuel excise cuts.
Shadow Treasurer Angus Taylor said Labor's costings revealed it had "no plan for the budget and no plan for the economy".
"There is a better way. We can get this country back on track and that means we need to beat inflation by cutting waste and slashing red tape," he said.
Ratings agency S&P warned Australia's AAA credit rating may be at risk if a swathe of spending promises lead to larger budget deficits and greater debt.
S&P analyst Anthony Walker said the budget is "already regressing to moderate deficits" as spending hits "post-war highs, global trade tensions intensify, and growth slows".
Labor and the Coalition have now laid out nearly all their major commitments for what they would do if they win the May 3 poll. Find out what Anthony Albanese and Peter Dutton are promising.
"How the elected government funds its campaign pledges and rising spending will be crucial for maintaining the [triple-A] rating," he wrote in a note on Monday.
S&P also cautioned that the increased use of "off-budget" funds for investment in projects such as the NBN and clean energy is "increasingly obfuscating" Australia's budget position and borrowing needs.
Mr Chalmers said Labor has "demonstrated" in Monday's costings that it has "found the room for our election commitments".
"The budget is stronger at the end of the campaign than it was at the beginning."
He said the biggest risk to the triple-A rating "is Peter Dutton and the Coalition".

title: More Aussie sheep meat will be sent to China as trade wars continue
content:
More Australian sheep meat will be sent to China, as the country looks for new opportunities amid its trade war with the United States.
Ten Australian sheep and goat abattoirs were granted access to the lucrative market for the first time over the weekend.
Abattoirs need to be individually approved by the Chinese government and the agreement process is prolonged and difficult.
The Australian Meat Industry Council (AMIC) said it was the biggest expansion in Australian sheep meat access to China in many years.
AMIC general manager of trade Sam Munsie said it had "been a long time coming" and was "extremely welcome news".
"It's a huge market. It can be quite valuable and lucrative, and it also provides a good counterpoint and balance for where we're sending our meat around the world," he said.
Seven of the abattoirs with new contracts are in Victoria, and there's one each in Tasmania, New South Wales and South Australia.
Another seven processors also had their contracts renewed over the weekend.
Meat industry analyst Simon Quilty from Global AgriTrends believes the new deals are the result of the tariffs announced by US President Donald Trump.
"Without a doubt, tariffs have created a degree of uncertainty and we've also got China wanting to spread its risk and these new licences that have just been issued are part of that," he said.
Mr Quilty said the new deals also gave Australian farmers some relief from the 10 per cent tariffs imposed on their exports to the US.
"This adds really important competition to the marketplace to allow lamb to progress and those tariffs, I believe, to have minimal impact," he said.
Australian mutton is popular in Chinese cooking.  (ABC archives)
China is already the largest buyer of Australian mutton, taking 37 per cent of our exports and it's Australia's second largest buyer of lamb.
"In lamb in particular, it takes all cuts and it takes all weight ranges so it's kind of like the go-to in the marketplace when looking to move carcasses of all different sizes," Mr Quilty said.
"I think these 10 operations, particularly for Victorian farmers and processors, it's a welcome situation that's arisen and I think will play a critical role in increasing overall demand for Australian lamb and mutton over the next 10 years."
The meat industry is optimistic about further Australian red meat opportunities in China.
"We're hopeful that this signifies progress and there might be further progress to come in areas such as beef access, and also potential to expand access for other products, such as tripe," Mr Munsie said.
The JBS abattoir in Cobram is among 10 Australian abattoirs to be granted approval to export sheep meat. (ABC News: Gaye Pattison)
The Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins has welcomed the news.
"It represents another win for our red meat industry and Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry officials, who have worked tirelessly for this outcome," she said.
"This is a win for Australian farmers and processors and comes on the back of multiple successes delivered by the Albanese Labor Government over the past 12 months.
The ABC has contacted the Opposition for comment.

title: Proposal for 4,000 new Darwin homes relaunched years after rejection
content:
The company behind a controversial planned housing development in Darwin's rural area that was rejected due to local opposition has relaunched its bid to build thousands of homes on undeveloped pastoral land.
Melbourne-based real estate developer Intrapac Property has written to Planning Minister Josh Burgoyne requesting an amendment to the Northern Territory’s planning scheme to allow a new development named Lloyd Creek Rural Village.
The proposal would see about 4,000 homes built on a site south of Humpty Doo, a rural area suburb 36 kilometres south of Darwin, in an area currently zoned for rural living.
It comes as the NT capital, like many Australian cities, is facing an ongoing shortage of housing, with a recent report showing the city's rental vacancy rate is just 0.6 per cent — well below the national average.
Lloyd Creek is being proposed by Melbourne-based developer Intrapac. (Supplied: Intrapac)
Intrapac chief executive Maxwell Shifman said his vision for Lloyd Creek "speaks to that local, rural character".
"One of the things we're aiming to do here is really deliver some housing typologies and some lot types you haven't seen in the territory for a long time — really bringing it back to that sort of local, tropical-style housing on a slightly larger lot," he said.
The proposed site of the Lloyd Creek housing development is currently bushland. (ABC News: Sam Parry)
In 2014, Intrapac Property proposed another development on the same parcel of land — a precinct called Noonamah Ridge that would have featured 4,200 homes.
That proposal was rejected by former planning minister Eva Lawler in 2020, following opposition from residents and former local member of parliament Kezia Purick.
Mr Shifman said the new plan for Lloyd Creek Rural Village responded to previous community concern about potential impacts on the local rural lifestyle, and now proposed housing connected to town water instead of bores.
Noonamah Ridge was rejected by the former NT Labor government. (Supplied: Intrapac)
"We've now got the Strauss Water Treatment Plant that's under construction and we'll be able to tap in and deliver potable water to the site, so that takes up one of the key criticisms of the proposal," Mr Shifman said.
The application also said the rural village's proposed land offerings would range from about a quarter-acre up to five acres, with no more than 1.5 dwellings per hectare on most of the site.
Darwin, Australia's smallest capital city, has been ranked the country's second-most-expensive place to rent a house, along with Canberra.
However, in two higher-density sections the proposal refers to as "rural activity centres", that number could be as high as 10 dwellings per hectare.
Many residents in the surrounding area live on much larger acreage.
Ms Purick said the proposed Lloyd Creek village was the "wrong kind of development" for the rural area, and pledged to support other locals as they relaunched their fight against the proposal.
"They have stock animals, they have farming activities, they have mango orchards and the like, and that comes with certain activities," she said.
"Having small, urbanised blocks right across the road from you will bring a clash of cultures. There's no doubt about it.
"If Intrapac is so keen to have a presence in the territory, [it should] go and talk to the NT government about developing Weddell, which already has big chunks of major infrastructure in place."
Kezia Purick says the proposed Lloyd Creek development would clash with existing rural blocks in the area. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)
Weddell — a proposed satellite city 30 kilometres south of Darwin — has been flagged as a potential development since 1984.
Labor had plans to establish Weddell while in government in 2009, before the Country Liberal Party shelved the project after taking power in 2012.
In response, Mr Shifman said his company was not competing with Weddell.
"It's a very different offering. Weddell would need significant infrastructure upgrades before it's up and running," he said.
"It's not a simple matter of, 'there's land there, develop it'."
Max Shifman says the proposal suits Darwin's rural area. (Supplied)
Intrapac's application to the government is out for public feedback until May 16.
The company behind the proposed Noonamah Ridge development in Darwin's rural area begins its charm offensive to win support.
Asked whether he supported the proposal, Mr Burgoyne said it was "important for consultation processes to run their course to ensure that community expectations are being met".
"We promised to rebuild the territory economy and as the minister responsible for the Planning Act and NT Planning Scheme, I will not rule project proposals in or out until all information and necessary feedback has been considered," he said.
Intrapac has estimated the Lloyd Creek Rural Village would inject about $3.5 billion into the NT economy during the construction phase and create about 300 ongoing jobs.

title: Fishers struggle to find banana prawns in ocean after rain comes too late
content:
It is the season of banana prawns in northern Australia, but trawler operators in the Gulf of Carpentaria say they are coming back to shore with not much in the nets.
Queensland's late wet season devastated towns and agriculture across the state, and the latest victim is the banana prawn industry, which is grappling with the worst season many have ever seen.
Whether consumers will feel the pinch is yet to be determined.
Bryan Van Wyk says he has not ever seen a banana prawn season this poor. (Supplied: Bryan Van Wyk)
That is because much of last year's bumper season is sitting in freezers across the country, according to Bryan Van Wyk, who manages Austral Fisheries' northern prawn division.
"There's still a lot of leftover prawn stock around on the market from previous big years," he said.
"We've got the worst of both worlds … a market that is reasonably full, which means lower prawn price, and the lowest productive season we've ever seen."
Prawn sales tend to skyrocket twice a year — Christmas and Australia Day.
Banana prawns are usually flushed into the Gulf of Carpentaria with the first downpour early in the year. (ABC Rural: Abbey Halter)
As this season's banana prawns hit the shelves, private Carpentaria and Northern Prawn Fishery trawler manager Greg Albert urged people to consider seafood as a protein source when grocery shopping, especially as steak prices had risen.
"The price of prawns has basically been the same for the last five years in the supermarkets, yet I think it's just the habits of the consumer," he said.
"They're more economical than some of the other proteins."
Greg Albert wants more people to eat prawns to support the local industry. (Supplied)
Mr Van Wyk said Queensland's month-late wet season flushed out many of the prawns, leaving few for trawlers to snag.
"We're basically looking at probably one of the, if not the, worst banana prawn season start we've ever had in history," he said.
Banana prawns typically settle into northern rivers, and the first downpour of rain during January or February flushes them into the Gulf, Mr Van Wyk said.
But since the big wet came later in March, many prawns failed to escape and became prey for other animals in the rivers.
Banana prawn season in northern Australia runs from late March to mid June, but the 2025 season started late. (Supplied: Michele Burford)
He said the ones that did get out were smaller than ideal.
Mr Van Wyk said the season was likely to close early, and 20 per cent of the northern prawn fishery chose to not head out at all.
"We currently have the lowest amount of vessels that have ever participated in the northern prawn fishery banana season of all time," he said.
Fewer vessels are heading out into northern waters this year because prawn numbers are expected to be so low. (ABC North West Queensland)
But he was confident the tide would turn for the boom-and-bust industry.
"There's still a bright future ahead, we've just got to get to that bright future," he said.
Raptis fleet manager Phil Robinson echoed Mr Van Wyk's sentiment and said he had not seen a worse season in 25 years.
"The late wet season has very much impacted the banana prawn season," he said.
He said the deluge in March was far too late to prompt any meaningful catches for fishers, and sizes were down, but the quality of prawns would remain high.
Prawn fishers are concerned about the late wet season in the gulf. (Supplied: Austral Fisheries)
Mr Albert said the late wet season impacted the aggregations, and his catch so far was "pretty average".
He said he had left one trawler out of the Gulf waters, with high fuel prices, lack of mother shipping and low sale prices all factors in the decision.
"We can only go out and catch what's there and try and get it to market in the best quality we can," he said.
author: Abbey Halter

title: Artist and miner saves a life with powerful, 16m-high message
content:
For Brisbane-based artist Vondelini, the blank surface of a 16-metre-high tank at Evolution Mining's Mungari Gold Mine in Western Australia was too good to pass up.
"I was working there as a fitter … and I walked past this tank every day for like four months," he said.
"Every day, it looked back at me.
Vondelini was inspired by the blank canvas the tank offered. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)
Vondelini joked with a construction manager that he could paint the tank.
"He came back to me four or five days later and he was like, 'Do you have any ideas?'" he said.
Having been given the green light Vondelini wasn't going to miss the chance to spread his important message.
"It's essentially a reason for the guys to go home," he said.
"Everybody's isolated, we're away for like three weeks at a time, sometimes you just need that prompt to go, 'That's why I'm going home.'"
The mural says "Family, you're not alone" in order to remind workers they will be home soon. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)
After three months of planning and six days of painting involving 1,000 spray cans, the mural was complete.
"A week after I painted it, we all received a message that someone had not [died by] suicide because of the message that's on the picture there," Vondelini said.
Vondelini was invited to speak at Evolution Mining's Mungari mill opening, along with managing director Lawrie Conway. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)
In 2024, a University of Western Australia (UWA) and MATES in Construction study found those working in fly-in, fly-out (FIFO) and drive-in, drive-out (DIDO) roles were at a much higher risk of having suicidal thoughts than the rest of the population.
"We looked at loneliness compared to job insecurity, workload, financial troubles, marital problems, being a minority person," UWA lead researcher Joseph Carpini said.
"Even when we compared it, loneliness came up as number one factor."
Dr Carpini said one in five workers who reported feelings of loneliness also had suicidal thoughts.
In comparison, for workers who did not classify as feeling lonely, one in 20 experienced suicidal ideation.
"This isn't feeling lonely at lunch and you know, 'Buck up mate,'" Dr Carpini said.
FIFO and DIDO workers are far more likely to feel lonely than other employees. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)
Self-leadership coach Lachie Samuel spent 12 years in the construction and mining industries and experienced how dangerous the FIFO lifestyle could be.
"I had a couple of [friends] take their lives," he said.
"Then I got evacuated from site for being suicidal."
Since then Mr Samuel has forged a path in the mental health space and hopes that by sharing his experiences, he can help others.
Lachie Samuel quit FIFO work and now helps others improve their wellbeing. (Supplied: Lachie Samuel)
He said loneliness among FIFO workers was more complex than simple homesickness.
"A lot of people … [if] they're not feeling connected to the people that they love, they either avoid them or they try and spend time with other people that they might not actually connect with," he said.
Mr Samuel said workers often started to avoid their colleagues.
"It just keeps getting worse and worse," he said.
"You come back home, you feel disconnected, and then you take it to camp or site with you.
Dr Carpini says there has been a strong response to the report, but more needs to be done. (ABC News: Aran Hart)
MATES in Construction said several organisations had sought to implement suicide prevention practices and policies since the release of the report last year, which made a host of recommendations.
Dr Carpini said he appreciated the "incredible response" but would like to see more action.
"I wish it was more, to be honest," he said.
"We know that there's still such a long way to go."
MATES in Construction says the report has gained some traction within the industry. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)
Mr Samuel said prospective FIFO or DIDO employees should carefully consider whether the work was the right fit before signing up.
"I don't think that lifestyle is suitable for everyone," he said.
"There are people who need to be around other people, who need to be connected.

title: Major parties have pledged tax relief. Calculate what it means for you
content:
In an election campaign dominated by the rising cost of living, few voters would turn down the promise of extra money.
It's why both the major parties are promising tax relief measures in a bid to grab your attention.
Labor is offering cuts to the lowest marginal tax rate, and an instant $1,000 tax deduction for work expenses.
The Coalition is pledging a one-off tax offset for low and middle income earners, and will cut the fuel excise from 50.8 cents a litre to 25.4 cents for one year.
Try our tax calculator for a rough idea of how these measures might impact you:
Our calculator assumes you will claim the $1,000 instant tax deduction, and compares what you would already be claiming as work expenses this financial year to what you could save with the full $1,000.
The cost of living has dominated politics for three years, and will be top of mind when voters turn up to the ballot box. But how much blame should the federal government really wear?
For example, if you already claim $1,000 or more in work expenses, your savings under the new deduction would be zero.
But if you already claim something like $300, your saving would be calculated on the extra $700 accounted for in Labor's policy.
Our calculator also only examines the impact of promised changes to the tax system.
It doesn't account for other tax breaks on offer for specific groups of voters, such as instant asset write-offs for small businesses, or the Coalition's tax deduction on mortgage repayments for first home buyers.
It also doesn't account for other policies targeting Australia's rising cost of living.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
Labor's latest federal budget proposed a permanent cut to the lowest marginal tax rate, costing about $17.1 billion in the first four years.
To find out more about how it works, read this.
The change effectively means if you're earning more than $45,000, you will see a tax cut of $268 a year when the rate is 15 per cent, and $536 a year when the rate is 14 per cent.
But if you earn between $18,000 and $45,000, you will get a little less than that.
Our tax calculator assumes these legislated tax cuts will be repealed by the Coalition.
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Labor is offering an automatic $1,000 instant tax deduction for work expenses, for things such as uniform or equipment.
Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app.
There's no need to keep receipts or paperwork for deductions less than $1,000 — just tick the box when lodging your tax return.
To be clear, that doesn't mean you'll receive up to $1,000 in your bank account.
Rather, that sum will be deducted from your taxable income.
Labor estimates the average amount of annual tax relief for those who benefit will be about $205.
This tax promise is expected to cost about $2.4 billion.
The Coalition is proposing tax relief for low and middle income earners for one financial year only, in mid-2026.
It's a rebadging of a measure introduced in 2018.
Dubbed the 'Cost of Living Tax Offset', the policy means Australians with taxable incomes between $48,000 and $104,000 will get a one-off rebate of $1,200.
Other taxpayers with incomes below $144,000 will get smaller rebates.
The Coalition says these tax measures would save the average two-income family about $2,400.
The Coalition is proposing to halve the fuel excise from 50.8 cents a litre to 25.4 cents for 12 months, starting in July.
The excise is effectively a tax paid by petrol suppliers, which is passed on to customers at the pump.
You might remember the Morrison government temporarily reducing the fuel excise in 2022 in response to high fuel prices caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The opposition claims the cut would save a motorist who fills up a 55-litre tank each week about $14 a week, and says Australia's competition watchdog will ensure service stations pass the full discount onto customers.
Our tax calculator sets the average weekly fuel usage at 24 litres, based on the latest data for average fuel usage from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Of course, not everyone will benefit equally from this measure.
The saving depends on how far someone regularly drives and the fuel efficiency of their vehicle.
The measure also won't help drivers of electric vehicles.

title: The dying trade critical to keeping Australian manufacturing alive
content:
Australia's manufacturing industry has been in terminal decline for decades as increased labour and energy costs, combined with worker shortages, have made local production uncompetitive with overseas options.
It's a problem the Albanese government has tried to address with its 'Future Made in Australia' policy, which has set aside billions to support a handful of industries, with an eye on helping Australia transition to net zero.
Beyond incentives for the handful of companies who end up receiving grants, there's another factor that needs to be addressed — keeping alive the rapidly-shrinking trades needed to keep local manufacturing up and running.
Ron Conry is a veteran of the industry, known globally for his invention of an energy-efficient compressor for air conditioners, which has a 60 per cent market share globally.
Conry Tech founder and chief technology officer Ron Conry. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)
Mr Conry returned to Australia during the pandemic, after moving his business to North America in 2000 when his company was offered a $26 million grant from the Canadian government.
"COVID had hit, and we decided that we would come back to Australia and try this new concept and make it Australian, an Australian company," the founder and chief technology officer at Conry Tech tells ABC News.
His latest invention, and one he hopes to produce here, is a new air-conditioning system which promises to cut energy bills by 40 per cent, and can be retrofitted into commercial buildings.
The problem is, Mr Conry says, despite all the talk about a 'Future Made in Australia', the challenges he faced in the 1990s when trying to commercialise his product remain.
"Australia is a very good place for getting brain power and getting new concepts and innovations done, but it's a very hard thing to make products.
"It's very attractive to go back overseas, but we're still trying to complete the whole project in Australia," he says, citing difficulties raising capital and rising labour and energy costs.
Conry Tech is an air conditioning company focused on sustainability. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)
Mr Conry and his business partner Sam Ringwaldt are now warning of another challenge facing the Australian manufacturing industry — the decline of a little-known but critical trade in the supply chain: toolmaking and engineering pattern-making.
Once a thriving trade, toolmaking and engineering pattern-making has been shrinking since the early 2000s, and in serious decline since the closure of the Australian automotive industry in 2017.
Toolmakers and engineering pattern-makers make and repair tools, dies, jigs, fixtures and other precision parts and equipment for machine tools and other production machinery. The trades also construct full-size engineering, models for prototype developmental products and the working pattern to make parts.
File photo of Toyota Australia's car manufacturing plant at Altona, Melbourne, July 5, 2013. (AAP: Joe Castro)
"Even to make the simplest plastic component, you need to make a tool that you can then inject molten plastic into, or you need to make something out of metal, it's the same thing," explains Sam Ringwaldt, the co-founder and chief executive of Conry Tech.
"There used to be quite a strong industry in Australia, supported largely by the automotive industry.
"But what we've seen as we've come back is that there's very few operators left.
"In fact, even those companies that advertise that they can make tools for you, we've found when we've pushed into them further to say, please introduce us to your tool maker, we find that those companies here are also getting the work done overseas," Mr Ringwaldt says.
According to the latest Census, there are only 2,220 toolmakers and engineering pattern-makers left in Australia — that's a 70 per cent decrease between 2006 and 2021.
Only 411 of these jobs are held by people under 40.
"It's a real skill set that's missing, which means that we're almost at the point where it's going to be impossible to do 100 per cent manufacturing process in Australia from raw materials," Mr Ringwaldt says.
Conry Tech founders Roy Conry and Sam Ringwaldt. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)
The toolmakers and engineering pattern-makers that are still operating in Australia are struggling to keep up with demand, resulting in long wait times and manufacturers needing to go offshore to source vital components.
"You're going to have to get stuff done overseas and then bring it in, and essentially become an assembly nation, rather than a manufacturing nation," Mr Ringwaldt says.
Alan Cooke is the national vice president at the Australian Foundry Institute, which represents the local metal casting industry.
He says the number of foundries in Australia, which make metal castings, has approximately halved since 2000.
Alan Cooke of the Australian Foundry Institute says there aren't enough training opportunities for the next generation of foundry workers. (ABC News: Rhiana Whitson)
"The amount of activity in our industry at the moment is not the real issue. The real issues are around our ability to attract and find skilled people," Mr Cooke says.
"We need young people to come in at the apprentice level, at technician level, at management level, to be able to have the future owners of the industry of these small- to medium-sized enterprises."
According to the Australian Foundry Institute, nationally, there is only one accredited TAFE apprenticeship training program in Queensland for engineering pattern-making, and one program run by a Victorian private registered training organisation (RTO).
However, Mr Cooke says that RTO has been affected by Victorian government funding cuts to new placements.
"It means that our businesses that have previously had some funding support to put on apprentices — that's gone," he says.
Melbourne metal casting business Beckwith Group employs about 100 people across its three sites, and provides toolmaking and engineering pattern-making services, all of which is produced locally.
Chief executive Rob Dalla Via says Beckwith Group could easily employ another 50 staff, if the workers were available.
Beckwith Group CEO Rob Dalla Via and Australian Foundry Institute national vice president Alan Cooke. (ABC News: Rhiana Whitson)
"We've got an aging workforce, and a lot of the young people coming through," he says.
"Yes, they might be excited to see molten metal being poured and so forth, but once a lot of them spend a couple of days, they [say], 'it's not for me, it's too hot, it smells' and so forth."
While the company has been able to invest time and training in some young staff that have persisted, it is still forced to turn away business it doesn't have capacity to take on.
Industry figures say the global uncertainty triggered by US President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs on imports has highlighted the need for Australia to strengthen its manufacturing industry.
From toy brands to fashion labels, some Australian firms are facing tariffs way above the 10 per cent "baseline". Company owners say they are not getting enough support as they navigate soaring tariffs to send Chinese-made goods into the US.
"I think the world is in a lot of turmoil at the moment," Mr Ringwaldt says.
"We see things happening in China, we see things happening in the US, more and more, it's clear that we need to have capability onshore in Australia.
"If we are reliant 100 per cent for any given industry offshore, then we really have no bargaining power.
He says it's a short-term reality that most manufacturing will end up occurring overseas.
"When you're making those raw components overseas, when you're making the tools overseas, and then you're making those initial parts overseas — then it almost becomes a question, well, is it worth bringing that part in to assemble it here, or should we just end up making it overseas?"
The companies that need to go offshore for critical components expose themselves to the risk of intellectual property (IP) theft.
"Every time that you send a drawing out to overseas, every time you send something out to be manufactured overseas, you are opening yourself up to more risk," Mr Ringwaldt says.
Ron Conry fell victim to intellectual property theft in China in the 1980s and won the case, but argues while legal protections such as patents offer some protection, they only go so far.
"Larger companies have teams of people just tracking IP infringement, if you're a small person, and just trying to do it, it's very, very hard.
"If it's a an obvious thing, then you'll be able to see it, but if it's a component, you'd never know that that component is being used."
Workers at this iron and steel foundry in Melbourne manufacture castings for industries from auto and motorsports to mining. (ABC News: Rhiana Whitson)
Manufacturing as a share of economic output fell from 14.9 per cent in 1990 to 5.9 per cent last year.
Indeed, Australia ranks last in manufacturing self-sufficiency among the world's developed economies.
Several major manufacturers have closed their Australian operations in recent years, including major fertiliser producer Incitec Pivot, the nation's only local architectural glass manufacturer Oceania Glass and our last major plastics manufacturer Qenos.
"We now have to go overseas to get those supply chains. And that makes a difference to everybody," Victorian head of the Australian Industry Group Tim Piper says.
"We do need to be producing goods here.
"We need to do it for our own Australian psyche, but we need to do it for the supply chain, and we need to do it because there could be times when we can't get product overseas."
Ron Conry and Sam Ringwaldt have not ruled out moving their latest venture overseas, and have already received offers from New York and China. Much like patents to protect intellectual property, they say, patriotism, also only goes so far.
"We can only bang our head against this wall for so long before we're going to have to make a decision," Mr Ringwaldt says.
For the moment though, Conry Tech is still hopeful it can produce its product for the global market here.
"There's a lot of debate about whether manufacturing should be done or whether it can ever be economical enough to do it here in Australia.
"But I think that's the wrong lens … The high cost of labour in Australia, for example, whilst it's an issue, it's not necessarily an issue when you have a high tech product that really solves problems.
"And so that's where the investment needs to be … Invest in startups, invest in the entrepreneurs."
"Slogans, unfortunately, don't fill shelves. We need to see some tangible action that will help support and rebuild this industry."

title: Sauna proposal for Pemberton comes as region pivots for wellness dollar
content:
As tourism operators look to market Western Australia's South West as the ultimate "wellness tourism" destination, a developer is eyeing off the icy waters in Pemberton's historic pool for a Nordic-style floating sauna.
Steamy saunas and cold plunges have long been part of Nordic culture and have been introduced to tourists through sauna boat attractions in places like Oslo, Norway.
Sauna business owner Nigel Reeves said "sauna culture" was taking off in Australia.
He has already set up a floating sauna in Derby in northeast Tasmania and has approval to set up on Lake Burley Griffin in Canberra.
His latest proposal, which is open to public comment, would see people rent out sauna cabins for an hour on the historic 100-year-old Pemberton pool and take a plunge in the cold water.
"I'm hoping for a positive outcome," Mr Reeves said.
"The Australian sauna culture is very young but since I started up in Tasmania there's been three other sauna businesses start up similar to mine set up.
"People are looking for a wellness-type experience on their holidays now and they're making decisions about where to go based on what wellness experiences and back-to-nature type experiences they can have."
The saunas have been popular with mountain bikers in Derby.
A floating sauna has already been set up at Lake Derby in Tasmania. (Supplied: Jason Charles Hill)
It comes after local tourism body, Australia's South West, outlined a plan to make the region the "leading destination" for nature-based tourism in Australia by 2034.
Destination Wellbeing's Lisa Spencer developed the strategy.
"Wellness tourism is growing faster than tourism overall," she said.
Lisa Spencer says "wellness travellers" spend more and stay longer. (Supplied: Lisa Spencer)
"Wellness travellers they travel out of season. They stay longer and they spend more.
"They're a really attractive target market for the region when we're looking to get people down there in the quieter months like winter.
"You've got your nature-based trails already existing but now we're seeing things pop up like bathhouses and spas across the region as well as experiences in nature like guided meditation and forest bathing experiences."
The Global Wellness Institute expects wellness tourism to grow dramatically around the world and bring more than $1 trillion to economies in 2028.
The Pemberton pool is a popular spot for locals and for visitors. (Supplied: Australia's South West)
The plan floated for saunas in Pemberton is yet to be given the green light on a local level but the WA government has already indicated its support by awarding the company a $170,000 timber transition grant.
The fund was set up to help grow industries in timber towns like Pemberton after the ban on native logging was put in place.
The head of the Pemberton Tourism Association Graeme Dearle said he was "cautiously" excited about the plan.
Graeme Dearle says a decision needs to be made in the community's best interests. (ABC South West: Jacqueline Lynch)
The Pemberton Pool is a man-made, community-maintained waterway that was built more than 100 years ago.
It holds a special place in the hearts of locals and is also a popular Instagram spot for visitors.
Mr Dearle said consultation with locals was key.
"It's [also] a community asset and we've got to try and make the best decisions we can for the interests of the community," he said.
The Pemberton pool has been a much-loved community place for more than 100 years. (Supplied: Ransom Offroad-Travel Aus)
Tourism operators have been worried about the future of tourism in Pemberton following the closure of its famous climbing trees.
It was recently revealed the famous Gloucester tree would re-open, but the attraction would eventually close for good.
Mr Reeves said he would work with the community and hoped to give back to the pool if the endeavour went ahead.
"There's actually no impact on the environment," he said.
Nigel Reeves has been setting up floating saunas across Australia. (Supplied: Nigel Reeves)
"If, for example, it was a complete failure and no one wanted to do it, we could simply dismantle and crane the infrastructure out of the water.
"I can't see any reason why it couldn't proceed."
