title: US' most-populous state files lawsuit against Trump's tariffs
content:
The United States' most populous jurisdiction, California, and its Governor Gavin Newsom are suing the Trump administration in a lawsuit aimed at blocking President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs on foreign trading partners.
In the lawsuit filed in the US Federal Court, the state is accusing Mr Trump of abusing his executive powers and inflicting harm on California and the country.
California Governor Gavin Newsom and the state's Attorney-General Rob Bonta have announced a lawsuit has been filed in the federal court against Donald Trump's tariffs. (AP: Noah Berger)
"Today I announced a lawsuit on behalf of the state of California suing the Trump administration. California's the largest manufacturing state in our union, one of the largest trading partners around the globe," Mr Newsom said in a post on X.
"No state will be impacted more than the state of California as it relates to the unilateral authority that's been asserted by the Trump administration to impose the largest tax increase in modern American history."
Mr Trump imposed 10 per cent tariffs on goods from all countries and higher tariffs for countries the administration says have high barriers to US imports, most of which he later paused for 90 days.
He also imposed a 145 per cent tariff on China, with exceptions for certain electronics, while China retaliated with a 125 per cent tariff against the US and the European Union approved its own retaliatory tariffs which have since been paused.
The US Constitution vests the authority to impose tariffs in Congress, and the law that Mr Trump cites as authority for his new tariffs — the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) — does not allow the president to "tax all goods entering the United States on a whim," California said in its lawsuit.
"President Trump's new tariff regime has already had devastating impacts on the economy, creating chaos in the stock and bond markets, wiping out hundreds of billions of dollars in market capitalisation in hours, chilling investment in the face of such consequential Presidential action with no notice or process, and threatening to push the country into recession," the lawsuit said.
The legal move from California marks the strongest pushback yet against a tariff roll-out that has sent global stock markets into meltdown, and left businesses across the US fretting about uncertainty.
"One of the most self-destructive things that we've experienced in modern American history."
With 40 million people California would be the world's fifth-largest economy if it were an independent country and is the largest importer of goods among US states. The state also accounts for 14 per cent of US GDP.
Mr Trump's tariffs could cripple the state's 12 ports, which take in 40 per cent of goods imported to the US and provide steady tax revenue.
The retaliatory tariffs from China and other nations could also harm California's agricultural exports, which totalled $US23.6 billion ($37.1b) in 2022, potentially costing thousands of jobs, the lawsuit says.
White House spokesman Kush Desai said on Wednesday that Mr Newsom should focus on addressing crime, homelessness, and high prices in his state instead of trying to block Mr Trump's tariffs.
"The entire Trump administration remains committed to addressing this national emergency that's decimating America's industries and leaving our workers behind with every tool at our disposal, from tariffs to negotiations," Mr Desai said.
Amid fears that the so-called reciprocal tariffs could cause a recession for the US, here's what it means for the global economy.
In executive orders imposing the tariffs, Mr Trump had invoked laws including the IEEPA, which gives presidents special powers to combat unusual or extraordinary threats to the US.
The Republican president said that the United States' net trade deficit relative to the rest of the world is a national emergency endangering its manufacturing capacity and making it dependent on foreign adversaries.
Mr Trump has also long-prized tariffs as a tool to achieve what he says is the urgent task of rebalancing America's trading relationships, and pledged on the campaign trail that he would hit imports with extra levies.
Initial punitive tariffs against Mexico and Canada were built on with his self-declared "Liberation Day," which saw onerous charges imposed on scores of countries, including allies and partners.
Many of those duties have since been paused, but their chaotic announcement sent global stock markets into spasms, wiping out trillions of dollars of value.
What impact will tariffs have on the price of electronics?
In California's lawsuit, Mr Newsom and California Attorney-General Rob Bonta — who are both Democrats — asked a judge to bar the Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection from enforcing the tariffs.
The United States has gone in a matter of weeks "from free capitalism to crony capitalism, just like that." Mr Newsom said.
"This is the personification of corruption...this is smash-mouth, in-your-face, every minute of every day, every hour.
"How in the hell are we sitting by and allowing this to happen?"
The Trump administration already faces three similar lawsuits — one in the New York-based Court of International Trade by business advocacy group Liberty Justice Center seeking to block all of the tariffs, one in Florida federal court by a small business owner seeking to block the tariffs on China, and a third filed in Montana by members of the Blackfeet Nation — a Native American tribe that spans Montana and Canada's Alberta province — challenging Mr Trump's tariffs on Canada.
Experts say the tariffs are on shaky legal ground, because the law cited by the president is meant to address "unusual and extraordinary" threats to the US.
"We're asking the court to rein in the president … and uphold the constitution," Attorney-General Bonta said.
"The president is yet again acting as if he's above the law, he isn't.
"It's simple, Trump does not have the authority to impose these tariffs. He must be stopped."
Mr Newsom's lawsuit comes just months after President Trump slammed Californian officials for alleged incompetence in the wake of the deadly wildfires that ravaged Los Angeles.
As blazes ravaged parts of California, the heir apparent of the Democratic Party found himself at the centre of a political firestorm stoked by rival Republicans and Donald Trump.
The fires were the most destructive in southern California's history, with at least 30 people killed and more than 16,000 structures destroyed.
In January, Mr Trump described the disaster as "one of the worst catastrophes in the history of our country" and accused Californian officials of having "no idea how to put them out".
Those comments also led to a heated political stoush between Mr Trump and the Californian governor over crucial water supplies needed by firefighters during the blazes to put them out.
About 40 per cent of the Los Angeles city water comes from state-controlled projects connected to northern California and the state limited the water it delivers this year.
One of Mr Trump's first executive orders signed after being sworn back into office this year was a decree to "immediately restart the work … to route more water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta to other parts of the state for use by the people there who desperately need a reliable water supply."

title: Australia's unemployment rate picks up slightly in March, to 4.1pc
content:
Australia's unemployment rate rose slightly in March, as 32,000 people found employment and the pool of unemployed people increased by 3,000.
The unemployment rate lifted to 4.1 per cent, up from 4 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.
In trend terms - which smooths out seasonal fluctuations in the data - the unemployment rate remained steady at 4 per cent in March, for the fifth month in a row.
But economists say Australia's job market has cooled down noticeably in recent months, with far fewer jobs being added compared to this time last year.
There's almost no chance the RBA will keep rates on hold in May, but the biggest challenge comes from Donald Trump while financial markets are in constant turmoil.
And they say even though employers are still reporting high-than-normal vacancies that need to be filled, that hasn't translated into stronger employment growth this year.
Callam Pickering, Asia-Pacific economist at global job site Indeed, says geopolitical and economic uncertainty could weigh heavily on the jobs market this year and that will be playing on the Reserve Bank's mind.
"Carnage in financial markets, high levels of economic uncertainty and a suddenly weaker economic outlook makes another rate cut in May all but certain," he said.
"Soft employment growth over the past few months will only give the RBA Board more confidence that this is the right path to take.
"While acknowledging that the Trump administration is nothing if not unpredictable, the global economic environment has shifted in such a fashion that I now expect the RBA to deliver rate cuts in each of their next three meetings, with a possibility that they deliver a super-sized cut in May," he said.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) says hours worked decreased by 0.3 per cent in March, falling for the second month in a row, despite the growth in employment.
"A higher than usual number of people reported working reduced hours this month due to bad weather, coinciding with ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred and other major weather events in New South Wales and Queensland," ABS head of labour statistics Sean Crick said.
Mr Pickering said the slow-down in employment growth this year was somewhat-at-odds with the ongoing strength in forward looking indicators of labour demand, such as job vacancies and job advertisements.
He said most labour market metrics remained quite healthy, with some even improving.
As the United States and China continue escalating the trade war, economists say Australian consumers and businesses could benefit from cheaper prices.
For example, the underemployment rate — the share of Australians with a job who would prefer more hours — is currently sitting at its lowest level since August 2008.
However, he said despite employment increasing by 32,000 people in March, that followed a decline in employment of 57,000 in February, which averages out to very little employment growth across the March quarter.
"Over the first three months of the year, Australian employment has increased by just 6,500 people," Mr Pickering said.
"That's a fair slowdown from last year when the job market was regularly adding 100,000 people or more a quarter.
"Given that, it's perhaps surprising that Australia's unemployment rate hasn't increased. The reason though is quite simple: Australia's participation rate has declined by 0.5 percentage points over the past two months, effectively absorbing the impact of low employment growth.
"If the participation rate had held steady, at its record high from January, Australia's unemployment rate would have jumped to 4.7 per cent," he said.
The participation rate was a record-high 67.2 per cent in January, but it slipped noticeably to 66.7 per cent in February and then rose slightly to 66.8 per cent in March.
Citi economists said that noticeable decline in the participation rate within a short period of time was perplexing, and if it rebounded in coming months it could see the unemployment rate rising.
"The ABS noted last month that [the decline] was driven by the older-aged cohort not returning to the workforce," Faraz Syed and Josh Williamson said.
"But there could still be some job-attachment that might see the labour force participation rate rebound in coming months.
The forecasts in the federal budget paint a rosy picture of the future, claiming the mythical "soft landing" is "increasingly likely" for Australia's economy.
"If this does occur, then job-growth will likely need to increase to around 45,000 — 50,000 over those months to keep the unemployment rate unchanged," they said.
They also think the labour market is still tight overall, with conditions suggesting the economy was still experiencing levels of employment that were stronger than the RBA's estimate of full employment.
However, the head of Australian economics at Commonwealth Bank, Gareth Aird, has offered a different perspective, saying the current level for the unemployment rate seems to be around where the true level of "full employment" actually is.
He said NAB's March quarter business survey, released today, shows that labour as a significant constraint on output fell notably in the quarter.
He said that phenomenon is consistent with slowing wages growth in the private sector.
"And in out view provides further evidence that the NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of employment) is likely to be around 4 per cent (i.e. essentially the current level of the unemployment rate)," he wrote.
"If we are correct on our estimate of NAIRU then Australia will be able to run a lower unemployment rate than is currently assumed by the RBA that is consistent with inflation sustainability around the mid-point of the target band.
"The RBA's models continue to imply that the NAIRU is closer to 4.5 per cent. But the RBA is very much open minded to the idea that the NAIRU could be lower than its working assumption.
"Ultimately inflation and wages outcomes from here will help to settle the conjecture around what level of unemployment Australia can run that is consistent with the inflation target," he said.

title: Smashing use found for Australia's tonnes of wasted avocados
content:
Avocados are a breakfast and brunch staple, with Australians consuming upwards of 4 kilograms each year on average.
But strict requirements from supermarkets, as well as picky consumers, leave hundreds of tonnes of the fruit wasted each year.
In the heart of Western Australia's avocado heartland, a local entrepreneur is hoping turn some of that waste around.
Third-grade avocados are often left to rot. (ABC South West: Georgia Hargreaves)
With a background in engineering, Lawrence Cheng noticed how much produce was going to waste at the farm level because it was either undersized, damaged or discoloured.
"I was working previously as a tech advisor in precision agriculture. Every time I would go visit farms I would see a lot of waste," he said.
"I started asking the question, what could we do about this?"
Generally, avocados that do not meet market specifications are destined to either be left in the paddock or sent to landfill.
"[Avocados] are usually left on farm if it's not going to the fresh market — it could be disposed of in a manner they deem environmentally and economically feasible," Mr Cheng said.
The wasted produce is what inspired Mr Cheng to invest in opening an avocado oil processing plant at the start of 2024, to give local producers another option for tackling food waste.
Mr Cheng's avocado oil processing plant opens options for tackling food waste. (ABC South West: Kate Forrester)
The engineer's business is still in its early stages, but there has already been involvement from local growers in Manjimup, a food bowl region well known for its avocado production.
"We are working with packhouses in the region to divert fruit from landfill to be turned into extra virgin avocado oil," Mr Cheng said.
The facility, which was primarily self-funded, has already diverted more than 90 tonnes of waste into oil.
It is the first season avocado oil has been produced at Southern Forest Food Technology. (Supplied)
"We have a production facility that can process up to 2 tonnes of avocados per hour."
Manjimup orchardist Kirsty Fontanini runs a packing shed in the region, where local farmers send bulk fresh produce to be packaged and sent to market.
Kirsty Fontanini grows a wide variety of fruit at her family farm. (Supplied: Craig Kinder Photography)
This season she was able to send several tonnes of third-grade avocados to Mr Cheng's facility.
"It's great because otherwise we would have had to dump them."
Australia wastes 7.6 million tonnes of food annually, according to End Food Waste Australia.
Households are responsible for wasting the most at 32 per cent, with primary production the second highest contributor.
Food waste occurs at every stage of the supply chain. (Supplied: End Food Waste)
Mr Cheng said he planned to use the facility to process and value-add to other wasted produce from the region in the future.
"It doesn't just have to do with avocados, it's whatever the region holds," he said.
"We have plenty of orchards here with plenty of fruit that we're keen to explore and partner with the different growers to see what's possible."

title: Shein, Temu to increase US prices as Trump cracks down on cheap imports
content:
Chinese e-marketplace Temu and fast-fashion retailer Shein will raise prices for US customers from next week.
It comes as US President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs and crackdown on low-value imports push up costs for the companies known for their budget offerings.
In nearly identical letters to US customers this week, the two companies said they will be increasing prices starting April 25, encouraging shoppers to purchase "now at today's rates".
Shein and Temu, sellers of everything from toys to smartphones, had grown rapidly in the US thanks in part to the "de minimis" exemption that allowed duty-free entry for merchandise priced below US$800 ($1255), enabling the companies to keep prices low.
Temu and Shein have been hit by Trump's tariffs on China. (Kate Ainsworth)
However, their business model has come under pressure from a recent executive order signed by Mr Trump that closes the trade loophole and goes into effect on May 2.
"Due to recent changes in global trade rules and tariffs, our operating expenses have gone up. To keep offering the products you love without compromising on quality, we will be making price adjustments starting April 25, 2025," the statements from both companies said.
Shein dresses are currently priced between $9 and $143 on its website, while Temu sells them at anywhere between $3.89 and $330 online.
The rapid rise of ultra-fast-fashion retailer Shein has been so key to the fortunes of a group of urban villages on the outskirts of China's southern metropolis of Guangzhou that they have been colloquially dubbed "Shein villages".
Chinese factories are trying to sell directly to American consumers on social media platforms in a bid to bypass the 145 per cent tariff hike imposed by Donald Trump.
On a recent visit to Shein villages in Panyu District, however, the mood was glum.
Three factory bosses along with four local downstream suppliers said Shein's local orders were in decline, pointing the finger at moves to diversify production to Vietnam.
Factory owner Mr Li has been in business since 2006, manufacturing apparel for both the Chinese and international markets.
He has been working with Shein for five years and says orders from the firm this year have dropped by 50 per cent as more orders have moved to Vietnam.
"The impact is quite obvious," he said.
A move to source more from Vietnam could help Shein to continue sending goods to the US at lower tariff rates or without import duties at all for packages sent under de minimis — though there is no guarantee the threshold will remain in place for goods sent from Vietnam.
But it also creates a Catch-22 situation for the company — a potentially costly and time-consuming one in an industry in which price and time are essential.
"The diversification of its sourcing base and a significant change in its business model will have to go hand-in-hand for Shein," said Sheng Lu, professor of fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware.
Without fundamentally changing the business model of pumping out thousands of new styles in small batches and shipping them quickly to end consumers, Shein can't diversify its supply chain, and without diversifying the supply chain away from South China, it can no longer ship products direct to US consumers at low, tariff-free prices, Professor Lu said.
Want even more? Check out our tariffs topic page
Alison Layfield, is director of product development at ePost Global, which helps businesses manage cross-border shipping and customs challenges.
"The model is really genius when you think about it … but to move that whole business model, that's going to definitely put a hiccup in their turnaround times and their costs," she said.
For Shein and Temu, cost and timing are essential. (AP: Richard Drew)
For Mr Li, the  factory owner, the capital investment involved in a move to Vietnam, combined with what he said was less productive labour there compared with China, makes it an unappealing choice.
"Here we can finish 1,000 pieces of clothing in one day, there it takes a month," he said.
While he plans to lean more heavily on his factory supplying the domestic market, Mr Li said for some of his compatriots there was little option left.
"They have only two choices. One is to go bankrupt, and the other is to go to Vietnam."

Hi Stephen,
According to the RBA Act 1959, the Reserve Bank was responsible for three main things:
That triple mandate adapted itself to big changes in the global economy over the decades.
In 1959, under the Bretton Woods system, when Australia's currency was pegged to the British pound, the "stability of the currency" and "full employment" meant very different things.
We ended up abandoning that old definition of "full employment" in the 1970s and we floated the dollar in 1983.
From thereafter, "full employment" came to be defined as the lowest level of unemployment that was thought to sustainable with low levels of inflation (i.e. which wouldn't contribute to accelerating inflation) through the cycle.
And in a world of floating exchange rates, the "stability of the currency" was going to be best supported by maintaining a low and stable level of inflation.
Over time, however, it seemed as though economic authorities started to put more emphasis on targeting inflation.
That's why the 2023 Review of the RBA recommended that more equal emphasis should be placed on low and stable inflation and full employment.
That's why you may have noticed a slight change in the RBA's communications in recent years, whereby it's now regularly mentioning its "dual mandate" of low inflation and full employment.
During the debates leading up to that RBA review, it was argued that the third goal of monetary policy that was mentioned in the RBA Act 1959 - that the RBA should aim to improve the economic prosperity and welfare of Australians - was self-evident and didn't need to be explicitly stated.

title: Oyster grower claims Australia's most prestigious food prize
content:
The first winner of what is regarded as one of the most prestigious food awards in the country has claimed it for a second time, almost two decades later.
Tathra Oysters has been awarded the 18th annual Royal Agricultural Society of NSW President's Medal at the Sydney Royal Easter Show.
It's not only a shot in the arm for the business, but also for the oyster industry on the NSW South Coast which has suffered through bushfires, flood, emergencies and even an ex-tropical cyclone.
Recovery from the 2018 bushfire in Tathra was slow, and a decline in tourism after disasters often affects oyster growers. (ABC News: Greg Nelson)
Tathra Oysters operates on 20 hectares in Nelson Lake in the middle of Mimosa Rocks National Park.
The town is a jewel in the region's crown, but a disastrous fire in 2018 destroyed 65 homes.
Rebuilding was slow, tourism faded and recovery for Tathra Oysters was made harder by another fire in 2020 that polluted the surrounding coastline and forced the closure of the oyster lease.
Tathra Oysters are grown in Nelsons Lake in the middle of Mimosa Rocks National Park. (Supplied: RAS)
Gary Rodely, the owner and manager of Tathra Oysters, spoke with the ABC prior to the awards about his family's 36-year legacy of oyster farming.
In 2005, they won the inaugural President's Medal.
"Back then the $10,000 [prize] was a big part of our income that year," he said.
Mr Rodely said the business had grown off the back of that early recognition and now produced close to a million oysters a year.
Tathra produces Sydney rock oysters on the far south coast of NSW. (Supplied: RAS)
The solar-powered farm also produces up to 10 million juvenile oysters for other farmers to grow, has a shopfront in Tathra and supplies oysters direct to the Sydney restaurant market.
"Now we have the ability to employ lots of staff, pay good wages and contribute money into the town," Mr Rodely said.
Mr Rodely's son Sam, now a marine biologist, has returned to the family business as the time approaches for Mr Rodely and his wife Jo to hand over the family business.
"We're getting towards the twilight of our career," Mr Rodely said.
"He's taken the business to places we couldn't imagine.
"We're very proud our son Sam has the same passion for it and for Nelson Lake."
Sam, Jo, and Gary Rodely from Tathra Oysters grow Sydney Rock Oysters at Nelsons Lagoon. (Supplied: Dave Rogers)
To qualify for the Royal Agricultural Society of NSW (RAS) President's Medal, producers must have been champions in the previous year's Sydney Royal Wine, Dairy or Fine Food shows.
Tathra Oysters was up against seven other finalists in produce as diverse as olives, pork and gin.
Judge Simon Marnie said the competition was one of a kind.
"It's the only one in Australia that allows us to judge a pork producer against a dairy or beer producer," he said.
The producers are judged not only on their product, but the overall integrity of their production practices, including environmental, economic and social sustainability.
Winning this competition is recognition as well for the oyster industry in NSW, which has had an especially difficult few years.
There are more 2,000 oyster leases in the state, but many have been shut for long periods in recent years due to disease outbreaks, floods, fires, blue algal blooms and other forms of contamination.
Oysters are like the canary in the coal mine.
They are often the first indicator of a problem because they filter the water and are very sensitive to changes.
Leases are closed for safety when water testing shows concerns following flood, fire or contamination.
Widespread flooding in coastal areas of NSW in 2021 shut down many areas and in 2023 floods closed 60 per cent of the oyster growing just before Christmas and the peak selling season.
In 2022 the Port Stephens oyster industry was shut down due to an outbreak of deadly QX disease, which affects Sydney Rock oysters.
Four oyster businesses never recovered from that outbreak.
In 2024, a massive grain spill in the Shoalhaven River triggered a blue-green algae outbreak that shut the oyster industry there.
Mr Rodely said oyster growers were the stewards of coastal areas.
"Here we are with farms on the eastern seaboard of Australia where everyone wants to live, so these are environments under pressure," he said.
"You've got oyster farmers are eking out a living in these environments, so if anything goes wrong they've got their finger on the pulse, and that resonates with the values of this award."

title: Shared living model offers hope amid rental housing crunch
content:
Brooke Kerton is on her way to her monthly housing co-op meeting with a smile on her face.
It's a familiar setting, one that feels more like a family gathering than a formal discussion.
"It's nice, we all get around to Kate's house and have a cuppa and a chat and do our meeting," Ms Kerton said.
"It such a nice little group of friends and you grow into a little family."
Ms Kerton lives in the regional Victorian town of Bairnsdale and is a full-time mum to four children.
She lives in co-op housing, a model that sees a number of renters in smaller homes on a shared block of land.
For Brooke Kerton and her family, security of tenure was a huge factor in considering a housing co-op. (Supplied: Brooke Kerton)
It's a familiar premise, having grown up in a different co-op in the Gippsland town of Moe, often tagging along to meetings with her mum, learning early on the value of community.
Ms Kerton said the security of an open-ended, capped-price lease was a huge factor.
In Copenhagen, housing co-operatives constitute 28 per cent of all dwellingss. (Supplied: Melina Morrison)
Housing co-operatives are a community-led form of affordable housing run by the people who live in them.
Residents can be renters or they can have a stake in the co-operative's equity, and advocates say they could be part of the solution to Australia's rental crisis.
The push for more co-operative housing
In Ms Kerton's case, her rent is capped at 25 per cent of her and her partner's combined salary, a figure that is updated if their circumstances change.
"We've looked at rentals in the market and it's not in our price range," she said.
"We'd be having to pay nearly an extra $400-500 a fortnight to move, whereas here we're not going to be overcharged."
Co-op member Beth Rundle with Common Equity Housing Ltd Managing Director Liz Thomas. (ABC Gippsland: Danielle Pope)
In Australia, co-op housing is less than 1 per cent of the national community housing stock.
The sector is made up of four types — common equity housing co-ops, Aboriginal housing co-ops, and other rental housing co-ops and private equity housing co-ops.
Between them, they have over 8,000 units of housing nationally.
But in some parts of Europe, such as Sweden, Denmark and Norway it is 25-30 per cent of national housing stock.
This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat.
Liz Thomas is the managing director of Common Equity Housing, an organisation that manages 100 housing co-ops with more than 2,000 properties across Victoria.
She said the co-operative model bridged the gap for people who could not afford private rentals.
"In the private rental market, people lurch from 12-month lease to 12-month lease with that threat [of eviction] over their heads all the time," Ms Thomas said.
"That's no way to plan a career, it's no way to plan where your kids go to school.
Community housing providers like Common Equity Housing develop, own and manage the co-ops.
The members live in individual homes and work together to manage the properties including financing, budgeting and organising any maintenance required.
Housing Co-operatives have increasing popularity in Europe. (Supplied: Emily Ouston)
Advocates say the sense of ownership and responsibility for the properties is what sets it apart.
"People living in that housing are empowered by the fact that they have a say in how it's managed, how it's maintained and who are the other co-op members," Ms Thomas said.
"That empowerment, that renter agency, is really a fundamental part of feeling as though you are in control of your living environment.
However, advocates realise that this commitment to being an active part of property management is not for everyone.
"Co-ops function by members taking active roles within the co-op community," Ms Thomas said.
"Not everybody loves the co-op model. You really do need to be willing to be an active co-op member for the co-op to succeed."
Two in five low-income renters were at risk of homelessness last financial year, according to the federal government's latest Productivity Commission report.
But they are not the only ones feeling the pinch.
A new report by from campaign group Everybody's Home last month revealed middle-to-high income earners were also facing rental stress.
Katherine Sundermann, an architect and a Professor at Monash University, said co-operative housing models had proven popular in Europe and could be replicated in Australia.
Katherine Sundermann is an architect and lecturer who studies urban planning. (Supplied: Katherine Sundermann)
"Obviously the current [housing] model isn't working," she said.
"In Australia, we've had a strong reliance on private ownership of housing, and we all know that kind of idea of most people owning their own home is no longer within reach for a lot of people."
Professor Sundermann said there was value in a model that provided quality homes with stability and access to community.
The Australian Co-operative Housing Alliance wants to secure a dedicated community housing funding stream from the government's Housing Australia Future Fund to grow housing co-operatives to 10 per cent of the social housing stock.

Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
The alliance is seeking an extra $250 million over three years to build 500 houses a year.
"As elections come up, there's a really important opportunity for all of us as a community to say it's time housing was the third pillar in every government's policy," Ms Thomas said.
"'It's not optional to have a really rigorous housing policy that has real meat on the bones."
The federal government has promised in this year's budget to fund $49.3 million for prefabricated and modular housing construction and $800 million in additional money for the Help to Buy program.
The Coalition has pledged to spend $5 billion for essential infrastructure to get stalled housing projects underway.

title: 'Sorry for my cynicism': Salmon boss says he has no confidence in new fishery
content:
The chief executive of salmon producer Tassal last year told the Tasmanian government he did not have any confidence in the Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) delivering a proposed sardine fishery.
An email released under Right to Information laws shows in June last year CEO Mark Ryan wrote to Tasmanian Business, Industry and Resources Minister Eric Abetz and NRE's then-acting general manager of marine resources, Will Joscelyne.
"Sorry for my cynicism but I had the same process … relayed to me in 2022 and in 2023 … with the fishery to commence in late 2023," he said.
"So it would be very helpful for me to understand some key timelines within the process please.
Last November, the Tasmanian government announced its intention to set up a new commercial sardine fishery — the first new fishery in state waters in decades.
In the email exchange, Mr Ryan said he hoped there was "a pathway forward for this fishery — its too important for Tasmania".
A study in 2023 identified a sardine population stretching from NSW's south coast to Tasmania could rival the biggest fishery in Australia — and there's a push to make use of it.
"I understand that institutional investors have contacted government about the opportunity — well, we know where that has the abalone, rick [sic] lobster and other segments since their involvement," he said.
"To develop a fisheries [sic], you need to catch, process and sell the products … not just do a one off transaction and own 'rights'."
Mr Ryan also asked if Tassal would be included in industry consultation with the government regarding the fishery's development.
A report produced by the Institute of Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) in 2023 noted that locally sourced sardines have "demonstrable ecological and socio-economic benefits" as a source of fish food for Tasmania's salmon industry.
"The absence of a large-scale small pelagic fishery off Tasmania limits the opportunity for the salmon industry to obtain the tens of thousands of tonnes of forage fish that it needs annually from a sustainable local source," it said.
Responding to questions about the Right to Information email, a Tassal spokesperson told the ABC the company "has no plans to participate in the proposed Tasmanian sardine fishery".
Tassal is owned by Canadian seafood company Cooke and is one of three major international salmon aquaculture companies that operate in Tasmania, along with Brazilian multinational JBS (Huon Aquaculture) and New Zealand's Sealord (Petuna).
Overseas, only a small amount of sardine goes to human consumption, with much if it being turned into food for other fish. (Adobe Stock: Andrea Izzotti)
The Tasmanian government's Fishing Tasmania website says the sardines caught in any future fishery could be used for "high-value human consumption, recreational and commercial bait, pharmaceuticals, fish oil and fish meal".
NRE's development guidelines for the fishery state that it could "allow access to a continued supply of sustainably caught Tasmanian seafood to national and local markets".
Those black, circular things floating in the water off the Tasmanian coastline? They are salmon farms. Here is how many there are — and who owns them.
"As a sardine fishery will produce a range of grades of product, it will be important that these products are all utilised in an economically sustainable way both to maximise the benefits of the fishery and minimise wastage," the guidelines read.
An NRE spokesperson said the development guidelines would "inform the development of a fishery management plan".
"The creation of rules and regulations for a new sardine fishery would involve standard processes, including statutory public consultation, which is expected to occur later this year," they said.
New study confirms potential to establish a large Tasmanian sardine fishery
The ABC first reported on attempts to access the fishery in 2014.
It was not until November 2024 that the Tasmanian government officially announced it was investigating a new commercial fishery.
Since then, community consultations and information sessions were held across the state regarding the fishery's development.
The exact size and location of the fishery, and the overall catch limit, have not yet been determined.
However, the Tasmanian government has indicated a commercial harvest level of a maximum of 15 per cent could be initially applied, based on research provided by IMAS.
The Tasmanian government wants to establish a commercial fishery to exploit the south-eastern sardine resource. (Supplied: IMAS)
The estimated size of the sardine biomass in Bass Strait is roughly 210,000 tonnes, according to the latest report released last December by the Fisheries Research and Development Corporation (FRDC).
The report found the sardine stock could be harvested at an ecologically sustainable level, but the recent discovery of the size of the resource meant a "precautionary approach" should be taken when developing the fishery.
Stateline report on potential for sardine fishery in Bass Strait (Clancy Balen)

title: Dutton's 'struggle street' seat the most marginal in Queensland
content:
It's Queensland's most marginal seat, and it's held by the man vying to be Australia's next prime minister.
The electorate of Dickson, north-west of Brisbane, is part outer-suburban mortgage belt, part rural.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
Opposition Leader Peter Dutton — who's held it since 2001 — clings on by a margin of less than 2 per cent.
Peter Dutton became the opposition leader in 2022, but has held the seat of Dickson since 2001. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)
Labor, the Greens, and a new "teal-like" independent are all in a race to unseat the potential prime minister.
So, is Mr Dutton in trouble?
"Peter Dutton is safe in that seat," political commentator and Griffith University Professor Paul Williams says.
"If the Labor Party couldn't pick up the seat of Dickson at the height of Anthony Albanese's popularity in 2022, they're certainly not going to pick it up now."
An election sign promoting Opposition Leader Peter Dutton in the seat of Dickson. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)
In fact, Mr Williams says it may no longer be marginal after May 3.
"Dutton should get a big swing to him and turn that seat into a fairly safe seat over five or six points," he says.
Professor Williams describes Dickson as a "struggle street" seat.
The vast electorate takes in the outer Brisbane mortgage belt, western rural localities, and large parts of Moreton Bay.
Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage
Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Mr Dutton lives at Dayboro, a rural country town to the west, where he polled strongly at the last election.
The mortgage belt suburbs span from Kallangur down to Arana Hills, which largely split their vote between Labor and the Coalition.
At the Old Petrie Town Markets, down the road from Mr Dutton's home, cost of living, interest rates, jobs and the environment are front of mind for many voters.
The markets are situated in the electorate Peter Dutton has held for more than 20 years. (ABC News: Alex Brewster)
Sharon Hill-Lavender juggles two jobs and began selling at the markets eight years ago.
"We run at a loss here, but it's our dream, so that's why we do it," she says.
"Cost of living has changed everything. No-one's got money for fun stuff, which is a shame because that's what my business is."
Sharon Hill-Lavender at the Old Petrie Town Markets. (ABC News: Alex Brewster)
Labor hopeful Ali France is confident her third consecutive attempt to unseat the Coalition leader will be a success.
"People are getting to see Peter Dutton up close since he's become opposition leader, and I think they're seeing that he doesn't represent the things they need in this community," she says.
Ali France is the Labor candidate for the seat of Dickson at the upcoming federal election. (ABC News: Alex Brewster)
The former journalist and para-athlete says campaigning here for the past seven years has given her a deep understanding of what matters to the community.
"My issues are their issues. I'm a single mother, I have a disability, I have a mortgage, I'm struggling with the cost of living," she says.
Labor is certainly campaigning like it believes it can take Dickson, with the prime minister and a slew of frontbenchers visiting during the campaign.
Ali France is confident her third consecutive attempt to unseat the Coalition leader will be a success. (ABC News: Alex Brewster)
How much of this is tactical compared to real winning confidence is unclear.
Also in the ring for another bout is Greens' candidate Vinnie Batten, who garnered 13 per cent of the vote in 2022.
Vinnie Batten is the Greens candidate in Dickson. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)
Independent Ellie Smith is hoping to do the same as teal candidates who have unseated Coalition strongholds interstate.
Despite receiving financial backing from Climate 200 — the major fundraising group behind many teal campaigns — Ms Smith dubs herself a "maroon".
The first-timer has a background in environmental management, and worked with anti-coal group Lock The Gate.
Ellie Smith is an independent candidate for the seat of Dickson at the upcoming federal election. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)
"There's a lot of sentiment out in the community against both of the major parties," she says.
"They feel neglected by both parties, and they like the idea of having an independent representing them.
"The big challenge is getting the recognition out there into the community over a short period. Peter Dutton has been here for 24 years, and my campaign started in January."
Despite receiving financial backing from Climate 200, Ms Smith dubs herself a "maroon". (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)
Signs promoting Mr Dutton have been swapped out for attack ads, claiming Ms Smith is a Green in disguise — suggesting the Liberals are more worried about her than Labor.
Mr Williams says a teal-like candidate has "zero chance".
"Queensland is not New South Wales and Victoria. It's a very different political culture, and there's no appetite for teal politics, at least outside of downtown Brisbane.
"The seats the teals would have done well [in] are Brisbane, Ryan, and Griffith, but they're already sewn up by the Greens."
In statement to the ABC, Mr Dutton says "he'd never taken the people of Dickson for granted".
Peter Dutton has held the seat since 2001. (AAP: Alan Porritt)
"As opposition leader, I have to balance responsibilities, but people in Dickson know I've always been accessible, I've always listened, and I've always delivered.
"My priority is making sure our community gets the support it needs, and I'll keep working hard to do exactly that."
If Mr Dutton were to be unseated, it would be a historic loss — an opposition leader has never lost their seat at a federal election.
Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app.
Two prime ministers have gone down with their losing party on election night — John Howard in 2007, and Stanley Bruce in 1929.
"We've also seen premiers lose their seat. The Queensland premier, Campbell Newman, lost his seat in ... 2015," Mr Williams says.
In the unlikely event Mr Dutton were to lose, replacing him as Coalition leader would take just a "matter of minutes", he adds.
"That position would be declared vacant after the election, and they would have to hold a meeting of the surviving caucus members, whether the LNP is in majority government, minority government, or in opposition," Mr Williams says.
"There doesn't seem to be an heir-apparent at this stage, but one would think that the most logical leader would be the deputy leader that they have today, which is Sussan Ley."

title: 'I can't get out': How Andrea's country home dream turned to nightmare
content:
When Andrea Martens set out to build a home to retire to in the Victorian countryside, she imagined enjoying the rural serenity with a home loan almost paid off and her troubles behind her.
While a local builder would construct the home, she had a hand in its design, helping craft plans that would maximise enjoyment of the beautiful surroundings.
Five years later, the building is neither a finished home nor an active construction site, but sits in limbo, barely touched after the builder left amid a deepening dispute in December 2020.
Ms Martens says her dream has become a painful nightmare due to alleged defects. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
"This is the part of the house that hurts the most: my beautiful kitchen I can't use," Ms Martens said as she stepped into the house on a recent visit.
Ms Martens and her partner first brought a detailed complaint to Victoria's building watchdog in the second half of 2020, asking it to engage with their surveyor to work through about a dozen alleged potential problems at the site.
In its initial response, the Victorian Building Authority (VBA) reviewed documents and photos before concluding the surveyor had acted appropriately in its attempts to resolve the potential non-compliances.
Ms Martens alleges issues with the slab are among the defects at her home. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
The authority encouraged the couple to raise other issues in further complaints, including one with Domestic Building Dispute Resolution Victoria.
But it closed the detailed complaint they had already made.
The incomplete home in regional Victoria was where Ms Martens had hoped to retire. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
It was 2021 before the VBA inspected some of the site and about another year before it began formally investigating other practitioners (due in part to COVID-era delays and resourcing issues), but it warned the Martens any disciplinary action would only go so far.
"I reiterate that the VBA outcomes will not resolve any outstanding building issues at the site or lead to compensation for damages," wrote an investigator, who encouraged them to pursue contractual issues before VCAT.
Ms Martens says her heart breaks each time she visits the unfinished home. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
Ms Martens's experience is one of several laid out in an independent review of the building watchdog released in November last year.
Many of them sought help with defective or half-finished homes but were failed so badly that the release of the report detailing their experiences triggered a major overhaul of the VBA.
The Martens have asked the state government for compensation to help finish their home. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
Ms Martens's allegation, based on an expert report, that there are major defects in her home's slab, framing and roofing are yet to be tested. A VCAT compensation case the Martens brought in late 2021 has moved so slowly the presiding member recently described its pace as glacial.
In the meantime — with rent, a mortgage and legal costs pushing her closer to financial ruin — Ms Martens has appealed to the state government for compensation over what she called the severe negligence of the VBA.
The review released in October 2024 was only the latest report to confirm the state's critical building regulator was facing major defects of its own.
Co-authored by lawyer and building regulation specialist Bronwyn Weir, it said poor building work standards and unethical conduct had flourished on the watch of an unresponsive watchdog that took a narrow scope to complex complaints.
Complainants who were suffering life-altering financial and emotional stress as their savings and super balances depleted were described as "emotional" or "stirring up trouble" in internal documents.
Matthew Bell says many homeowners tend to give up before they start a claim.   (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
By statute, the VBA's role focuses on matters like builder registration and the enforcement of standards, according to University of Melbourne construction law expert Matthew Bell.
He said that remit could fall short of community expectations of strong protection from a well-resourced regulator.
That can leave homeowners seeking help for shoddy work through other avenues, including potentially lengthy lawsuits in complex legal areas against builders whose livelihoods are at stake, the academic said.
"What we do see is that well-resourced and resilient homeowners can often get a result in VCAT if they take it all the way," he said.
"But there's so many places along the line where people just give up, and quite often it's before they've even started a claim.
"They'll just say, 'I'll put up with that' and just move on, or get it fixed myself, or — probably even worse — fix it myself."
The Martens are one of at least two households featured anonymously in the review to have asked the state government for financial support while complicated matters progress before VCAT.
The second, who for privacy reasons wanted to use the pseudonym Anne, is also embroiled in a years-long saga over an unfinished home and a terminated contract.
Anne* has made several complaints to the watchdog over the years.  (Supplied)
Anne told the ABC she made an initial four complaints to the watchdog, hoping it would use rectification powers to resolve alleged defects such as waterproofing problems that had emerged during the build.
"We thought, I suppose, that the VBA was our saviour. They would be the ones to make it right," she said.
Anne lodged a further 13 complaints over the following years.
While her builder and his company's registrations were cancelled in relation to a number of sites earlier this year (a decision being appealed before VCAT), her home was still incomplete after seven years, she said.
The Weir review was one initiative taken by the VBA's new CEO, Anna Cronin, who is overseeing cultural transformation at the agency and of whom complainants speak highly.
Anna Cronin has been overseeing a cultural transformation of the building regulator. (ABC News)
Letters seeking participation in the review did not specifically mention compensation, but both women believed the government should offer support as the VBA missed critical early opportunities to intervene.
"And if there were any other issues, the builder would've known that the VBA would've been on top of it," Anne said.
The report found most participants believed years of expensive legal action seeking compensation could have been avoided had the VBA "done its job", but noted regulatory action alone may not have solved their issues.
The government's response to both complainants and, later, the ABC's questions focused largely on series of consumer-focused building reforms but did not specifically address the question of compensation.
Legislation before parliament will replace the VBA with a new Building and Plumbing Commission, bringing insurance, regulation and dispute resolution under the one roof.
The watchdog would have powers to direct builders to fix defects after occupants move in, create a "first-resort" building insurance scheme and require a bond deposit from certain developers, as in New South Wales.
"It could really be a game changer as these measures have been in New South Wales: an integrated regulator, so a one-stop-shop," Associate Professor Bell said.
"Even at that first stage for consumers, where you are tearing your hair out and you don't know what to do, if you can at least ring somebody and the phone is answered by a regulator who can then give some advice, pathways, that's very, very helpful."
Water pooling at Ms Martens's home.  (Supplied)
Since its review started, the VBA said it had suspended, cancelled or disciplined seven practitioners involved and is progressing investigations of more than a dozen others, including some involved in Ms Martens's home.
"Some investigations remain open – these are highly complex cases with extensive documentation and we’re working hard to achieve the best possible outcomes,” a spokesperson said.
In late February, Housing and Building Minister Harriet Shing also thanked Ms Martens for participating in the Weir review, saying "the courage and commitment of case study contributors including yourselves have played an important part in informing the VBA reform process".
There's been extensive correspondence between the Martens and the VBA. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
The minister's response was among dozens of emails and letters exchanged between the Martens and various authorities over the past five years reviewed by the ABC for this story.
Despite the extensive correspondence, the report and a formal apology from Ms Cronin, the Martens fear little has materially changed their situation.
One expert estimate said the couple would need to find $670,000 to repair their home, a figure Ms Marten said adds to many tens of thousands of dollars already spent on legal fees and expert reports.
Five years after first complaining to the VBA, Andrea Martens' home is still unfinished.  (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)
Ms Martens described the litigation as a second full-time job, one that comes at a personal cost by day, then keeps her up at night.
"I can't get out of it," she said.

title: 'Gambling without limits': How video games are fleecing kids
content:
Kids playing popular video games are being targeted with harmful design tactics including gambling-like features, which fleece them of cash and trap them in gameplay, according to a new report.
As a result, children were being enticed to play more and spend more, said Erin Turner, CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre (CPRC).
"What really worries me is when we see these gambling-like features in games targeting children," she said.
Researchers from CPRC and Monash University — who authored the report — looked at 20 "dark patterns" which they say deceived and manipulated gamers.
The design features were not in all games but 95 per cent of adult players surveyed had come across them and 83 per cent had suffered negative consequences.
Do you have a story to share? Email Specialist.Team@abc.net.au
Merrick Wolski is a 17-year-old gamer who has tried to take action against gaming companies that use addictive features. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
Of most concern was children being exposed to gambling-like features such as "paid loot boxes" and prompted to buy items with in-game currencies.
Paid loot boxes require a player to pay to open a mystery box in the hope they receive something valuable in the game.
Unlike the electronic gaming industry which has strict rules on how much money is returned to a player who pulls the lever of a pokie machine — Ms Turner said there's nothing forcing video game developers to even disclose that. "This is gambling without limits and real manipulation," she said.
Researchers said paid loot boxes had the potential to "normalise and encourage" monetary gambling among children and young people.
After questioning 800 adult gamers about their concerns, the researchers found close to half spent more money than they intended, felt pressured into buying something or made a purchase by accident, they found.
Merrick Wolski spends his downtime playing and designing games on Roblox. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
They said Australian regulators had failed to keep pace with the industry's rapid expansion — with Australians spending an estimated $4 billion annually — and a substantial overhaul was needed to keep children and adult gamers safe.
Ms Turner has called for a classification system that alerts parents and players to what harmful features are included in games.
However, the Australian industry body, the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association, has argued these design features were different from gambling because the items couldn't be cashed out for real money.
Merrick Wolski says gaming can quickly become "toxic". (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
Brisbane gamer Merrick Wolski, 17, spends his downtime playing and designing games on Roblox — a gaming platform which allows players to create their own games.
Roblox boasts 380 million users, with 42 per cent of them under the age of 13.
"I like making games on the platform, because I find that fun. I like coding and modelling and stuff like that," Merrick said.
Roblox earned US$3.6 billion in revenue in 2024, much of it coming from in-game transactions using the platform's currency Robux.
A recent study found Australian players between the ages of four and 18 spent an average of 137 minutes a day on the platform.
While Merrick is passionate about gaming he says it can quickly become "toxic".
"A lot of games promote gambling content to their audiences… where you can pay to spin a wheel for different prizes."
Merrick Wolski estimated over the last year he'd spent around $150 on Roblox. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)
"I found myself at times when I spin and I'm just that close to it landing on the best reward on the wheel, and it goes, 'Oh, would you like another spin for 50 Robux'."
"Why not? And then I'm 10 spins down."
Merrick estimated over the last year he'd spent around $150 on Roblox.
"It doesn't feel great hearing that number out loud."
Some of the adult gamers surveyed expressed similar concerns.
"Ninety-nine per cent of them are made to create an emotional vortex of dopamine-chasing people, especially young men with a lot of anger, get sucked down, constantly chasing positive reinforcement through micro-transactions and wins while in reality hating the experience," an 18-year-old male said.
Not a gamer but want to understand the lingo? Click here to see our breakdown.
Researchers singled out the popular online game Stumble Guys for criticism due to its use of "trick language".
The game which featured animated characters racing to the finish is marketed to kids but had complex calculations for a "Super Gem Sale" that would be difficult for many to understand, especially children.
Roblox is one of the most popular platforms in the world, but there are increasing concerns over the ability for users to message each other directly through games.
"It has features that look like gambling: a wheel that for anyone who's walked into a casino will look similar to a roulette wheel," Ms Turner said.
"It's got randomised rewards, an overlay of fun, colourful graphics that are really about engaging children, and lots of push to spend."
"There's no way we should be seeing these features in games rated for kids nine and over."
In a statement the game's developer, Scopely, said age ratings were set independently by platform app stores, they followed the store policies for advertising disclosures and parents were able to use controls to limit in-game spending and screen time.
"In Stumble Guys' we take additional steps to limit access to certain features for our younger players, including disabling social media plug-ins and targeted advertising," it said in a statement.
Laura is part of the Heads Up Alliance, a grassroots organisation supporting parents who want their kids to be smart-phone and social media free. (ABC News: Leonie Thorne)
Globally, the industry earned revenue of approximately US$223 billion in 2023 — with around $125 billion due mostly to micro-transactions, in-game ads and product placement, the report found.
Ms Turner said some players spent thousands of dollars on "micro-transactions"
The gamers surveyed revealed they rarely tried to get redress when something went wrong and when they did, they failed to receive help from the game developer or platform.
That's something Merrick can relate to.
He sent complaints to Roblox and the Australian Classification Board about gambling-like features in four games he was exposed to on the platform and believed could violate the platform's rules and breach the classification system.
"They [Roblox] gave me a response that basically just said that there was nothing they could do about them."
Jojo's gaming PC is in the lounge room so his parents can keep an eye on what he's doing. (ABC News: Leonie Thorne)
The ABC put questions about Merrick's complaint to Roblox but it did not answer them.
Roblox said safety was its "top priority" and it took action on reports of content not meeting guidelines or Australian requirements.
Australia has just introduced new minimum classifications for games with gambling-like content.
Games with in-game purchases linked to chance, including paid -loot boxes have an M rating and aren't recommended for children under 15.
Those with simulated gambling are further restricted — rated R for adults over 18.
However, Ms Turner was critical of the ratings only applying to new games and believed the definition of gambling-like content was too narrow.
"It has to physically look like blackjack or poker, it has to look like a casino," she said.
Laura says she tries to monitor her son Jojo's gaming. (ABC News: Leonie Thorne)
Communications Minister Michelle Rowland acknowledged some active games for children still contained these purchases because the changes were not retrospective, she said if those games eventually added new purchases or rewards they would need to be re-classified.
Ms Turner wants the federal government to create an independent body that would adjudicate complaints, called a digital ombudsman — something that already exists for the telecommunications and finance sectors.
But she said that body would only be effective if consumer protections were strengthened — something the Albanese government said it is consulting on.
Dangers still lurk for young social media users in chatrooms like Roblox (Mike Lorigan)
University of Sydney research and game designer Mark Johnson said gaming companies had become incredibly skilled at "dodging and weaving" regulations.
"Depending on the nature of the law, it might be as simple as just changing what something is called. So don't call it a loot box, call it something else," he said.
Peak body, the Interactive Games & Entertainment Association (IGEA) said most games and platforms offered tools for parents and players to manage screen time, spending, interactions and access to content.
It defended the classification system calling it "robust" and stating it provided "clear, age-appropriate guidance on game content, helping parents make informed decisions."

title: Market meltdowns may have been a trial run, insiders warn
content:
Are we nearly there yet? For anyone who has ever gone on a longish road trip with young children, the phrase will have been burned into the memory banks.
It's also becoming the most frequently asked question from investors, most of whom have been seared by the tumult on global financial markets during the past month following US President Donald Trump's scorched-earth policy on international trade.
While the past few days has seen calmness return to markets, many of the financial world's best minds fear further falls — and warn we're nowhere near the end, unless America backs away from its current policy.
In last week's market chaos, traders turned their backs on US government bonds. Is Donald Trump destroying America's "exorbitant privilege"?
JP Morgan chief Jamie Dimon, once a vocal Trump supporter, has shifted stance and called for the US to engage with China, concerned the trade war has begun to chip away at America's credibility.
The US investment banking giant now puts the odds of a US recession at 60 per cent.
Mike Wilson, the influential US stock analyst from rival firm Morgan Stanley, fears further upheaval while investors remain exposed to Mr Trump's unpredictability, and the confusing and chaotic policy shifts.
Tariff impositions, repeated backflips, conflicting messages, temporary reprieves, retaliatory tariff lifts in response to retaliation from China, backdowns on repeated assurances, and clearly amateurish arithmetic to justify the blanket protectionism have shattered investor confidence.
It's also unleashed a growing global feeling of distrust in the very country that controls international finance through its global reserve currency, which, ironically, features the word 'Trust' on its banknotes.
Currency traders haven't been treating the US greenback as a safe haven as they typically do in times of crisis. (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton)
Many rapidly are coming to the same conclusion: this is a pivotal moment in history that could go horribly wrong.
"To be honest, we haven't seen a reordering of the global economic system on this scale since the 1930s," Satyajit Das, one of Australia's foremost minds on financial and economic history, tells The Business..
"That was the Smoot Hawley tariffs, which certainly didn't cause the Great Depression, but were contributors to that.
"Also on the other side, on the financial side, the excesses that have built up over the last 20 years are far greater than I've ever seen before."
Satyajit Das is a former banker and financial risk analyst. (ABC News)
It's a combination that deeply concerns Mr Das.
"I don't know how bad it could be, but all I know, looking at history, is it could be very bad," he says.
Last week, the upheaval spread to the US bond market, normally a safe haven for troubled investors.
Instead of cash flooding into the system, as it ordinarily would in times of a stock market meltdown, it began departing.
And rather than the US dollar strengthening, it began to decline as investors abandoned US debt markets and took their cash out of the country, a deeply disturbing turn of events.
The US president was confronted by a force far greater than his own and the office he now holds overnight. The bond market, an arena where brutality knows no bounds and where the participants take no prisoners.
Luke Yeaman, former deputy secretary of the Australian treasury and now the Commonwealth Bank's chief economist, believes the US president will persist with his tariff policies and argues there are genuine underlying problems the new administration is trying to address.
Mr Yeaman says Mr Trump sees tariffs as the balm for a range of American economic ailments: fixing the budget and trade deficits, on-shoring industry and jobs, and improving national security.
"Is it going to work? I think it's going to be very challenging," he tells The Business.
"Achieving those goals is not easy, and the global economy is quite good at adjusting to changes in tariffs.
"That said, the US is a huge market. It's still the largest consumer market globally, accounting for around 25 to 30 per cent of global demand.
"So, opportunities to avoid these tariffs are going to be quite limited compared to previous trade wars, but it's clearly doing significant damage to the US economy in the meantime."
Luke Yeaman is the new chief economist at the Commonwealth Bank, joining from the federal Treasury. (Supplied: Treasury)
Mr Yeaman sees clouds ahead for the US and global economies.
The speed and extent of the changes to the global system will impact the economy and markets for quite some time, he argues. And there's no guarantee that Mr Trump's goals will be achieved.
Mr Das agrees that the US president appears to be attempting to address serious holes that have emerged in the American economy, its financial system and its place in the world.
But he is stunned at the methods.
From toy brands to fashion labels, some Australian firms are facing tariffs way above the 10 per cent "baseline". Company owners say they are not getting enough support as they navigate soaring tariffs to send Chinese-made goods into the US.
Imposing tariffs is just one part of the program, Mr Das explains.
Another option being looked at is a radical overhaul of the bond markets, forcibly converting some or all of them to perpetual bonds or 100-year bonds with low coupon or interest rates.
Capital controls are also on the table, along with an idea to charge user fees for US Treasuries, representing a complete about-face in the way America has acted in the past half century.
"This is part of a plan, and the problem is we really don't know how many bits of it are going to get actually implemented or when they'll be implemented, because what we've seen is the whole process is entirely erratic," he says.
Want even more? Check out our tariffs topic page
Both men believe Australia is relatively well placed to cope with the impending trade war but, as a trading nation with exports heavily weighted to China, it undoubtedly will feel the pinch if China's already troubled economy takes a hit.
Mr Yeaman expects Beijing to ramp up stimulus if its economy starts to waver, in a bid to defend its five per cent growth target.
"I think China will certainly spend a substantial amount to ensure that its economy remains strong during this period, and we also expect them to front-load that support as much as possible to ensure that the economy doesn't dip too much in the near term," he says.
Should that occur, it will further shield Australia from the impact of a protracted global slowdown as a result of the trade war.
The global trading system is being rewritten, says new CBA chief economist (Kirsten Aiken)
For Mr Das, the potential for longer-term damage from the way in which Mr Trump has attempted to impose his policy are the biggest concerns.
"The loss of trust in the US, the loss of trust in the basic way the US has operated, is very, very critical to understand," he says.
He is concerned that, once lost, that trust will be difficult to win back, that the damage being incurred may be permanent.
"Mark Twain once said that he didn't know about the people who were ruling us, whether they were very smart people putting us on, or whether they were imbeciles who really meant it, and we're still trying to work that out."

title: Pacific island nation gains access to electronic banking for first time ever
content:
For the first time, the Pacific island nation of Tuvalu has access to electronic banking after its first ATM was unveiled.
Officials called it a "transformative" era of modern banking in the remote archipelago.
For years, the nation's 12,000 residents have done all their banking in cash, with workers enduring long lines to withdraw their wages from the bank each pay day.
Now they will be able to withdraw money at the swipe of a card, with five ATMs and 30 point-of-sale terminals installed.
General manager of the National Bank of Tuvalu, Siose Teo, said it was a "great achievement" and "transformative switch" that was many years in the making.
Prime Minister Feleti Teo said it was a "significant milestone" with a "noble objective".
Dignitaries gathered in front of the ATM, on the main island of Funafuti, to mark the occasion with a chocolate cake.
"It will definitely break the barriers and introduce the people to modern and reliable banking services," said Nisar Ali from Pacific Technology Limited, which helped design the machine.
With a landmass of just 26 square kilometres, climate-threatened Tuvalu is one of the smallest and most remote nations on the planet.
An Asian Development Bank briefing from 2019 described its banking sector as "effectively unregulated".
"Key reform priorities are instituting effective banking oversight and expanding access to financial services," it said.
AFP/ABC

title: US and Japan aim for deal on tariffs as Donald Trump joins talks
content:
US President Donald Trump says he will join negotiations with Japan on tariffs, after both countries expressed confidence in striking a deal.
President Trump issued a 90-day pause on his 24-per cent tariffs on Japan last week, but a 10 per cent tariff remains in place.
Japan is the biggest investor into the United States and a close strategic and economic ally.
Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba has described the levy situation as "a national crisis."
The White House meeting with Tokyo's envoy is being closely watched as a possible barometer for talks with other countries, as trade officials line up to negotiate over Mr Trump's punishing tariffs.
"Japan is coming in today to negotiate Tariffs, the cost of military support, and 'TRADE FAIRNESS.' I will attend the meeting, along with Treasury & Commerce Secretaries," Mr Trump posted on Truth Social.
"Hopefully something can be worked out which is good (GREAT!) for Japan and the USA!"
Ryosei Akazawa, Japan's Minister for Economic Revitalisation, is responsible for the country's negotiations with the US on tariffs.  (AP Photo: Hiro Komae, file)
As he left for the White House meeting, Japan's lead tariff negotiator, Ryosei Akazawa, spoke of seeking a "win-win" outcome, while protecting Japanese national interests.
"I am confident that we will be able to build a relationship of trust and conduct good negotiations that will lead to a win-win relationship," Mr Akazawa, Japan's economic revitalisation minister, told reporters.
The Trump administration has imposed steep levies on imports of Japanese cars, steel and aluminium.
Automaker Honda said on Wednesday it will shift production of its hybrid Civic model from Japan to the United States in June or July, but stopped short of saying the reason was US tariffs.
The rationale behind the decision "is not a single issue", a Honda spokesperson said.
"The decision is based on the company's policy since its foundation that we produce cars where the demand is."
The vehicle, however, represents only a small part of the Japanese company's annual output.
Donald Trump's tariffs have targeted Japan's car makers, causing significant concerns for the country's export economy. (Reuters: Issei Kato, file photo)
Mr Akazawa will also hold talks with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during his trip.
Purchases of US defence hardware and natural gas from Alaska could be up for negotiation, analysts said.
The minister, who studied at a US university and is close to Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba, said he wants to "protect our national interests" in the talks with Mr Bessent and Mr Greer, who are "fond of Japan".
The Daiwa Institute of Research warned that Trump's reciprocal tariffs could cause a decline of 1.8 per cent in Japan's real GDP by 2029.
US officials are also set to hold talks with South Korea and others, but Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management called the discussions with Japan a "canary in the tariff coal mine".
"If Japan secures a deal — even a half-baked one — the template is set. If they walk away empty-handed, brace yourself. Other nations will start pricing in confrontation, not cooperation," he wrote in a newsletter.
And "don't forget the elephant in the vault: Japan's still the biggest holder of US Treasuries. And that, my friend, is a whole lot of leverage", he added.
Chinese factories are trying to sell directly to American consumers on social media platforms in a bid to bypass the 145 per cent tariff hike imposed by Donald Trump.
Top Japanese officials including Mr Ishiba have brushed aside claims that Tokyo may have deliberately created volatility in the US Treasury market to force Trump's pause of reciprocal tariffs, saying that is not what allies would do.
Mr Ishiba called Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and French President Emmanuel Macron in separate calls on Wednesday to discuss the impact of US tariffs and China's retaliatory actions.
Japan's prime minister told Mr Anwar that "the current situation is serious for Japanese companies operating in South-East Asian countries" and that he was willing to listen to the voices of South-East Asian countries, according to the foreign ministry.
Mr Macron and Mr Ishiba also discussed the impact of the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs "on the global economy and the multilateral trade system," and "affirmed that it is in the common interest of Japan and France to maintain and strengthen a free and open international order based on the rule of law," the ministry said.
Meanwhile, China has announced a new trade negotiator as it battles the US in an escalating trade war.
Beijing announced that Li Chenggang had replaced Wang Shouwen.
Mr Wang was involved in previous trade negotiations with the US in 2020.
It wasn't clear what prompted the change.
Prior to his appointment as trade negotiator, Mr Li spent about four-and-a-half years as China's ambassador to the World Trade Organization, the body that governs global commerce.
Beijing has appealed to the body in its tariff dispute with the US.
The timing of his tour through South-East Asia couldn't be better for Xi, who is trying to court as many countries as possible to form a united diplomatic front against Trump's tariffs.
Earlier on Wednesday, China announced its economy expanded at 5.4 per cent annual pace between January and March, supported by strong exports.
Its exports helped it achieve a 5 per cent annual growth rate in 2024, but analysts forecast the world's second largest economy will slow in coming months as US tariffs take effect.
Asked about the possibility of talks with the US, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said America started the tariff war and China was only taking "necessary countermeasures" to defend its rights and interests.
"If the US truly wants to resolve the issue through dialogue and negotiation, it should stop using maximum pressure and stop threats and blackmail. For any dialogue to happen, it must be based on equality, respect and mutual benefit," Mr Lin told a daily briefing.
President Xi Jinping has been making the case that China is a source of "stability and certainty" in global free trade as he tours South-East Asia this week — implying that China is a more reliable trade partner than the US.
On a visit to Malaysia, President Xi said "China and Malaysia will stand with countries in the region to combat the undercurrents of geopolitical … confrontation, as well as the counter-currents of unilateralism and protectionism."
"Together we will safeguard the bright prospects of our Asian family," he added.
ABC/wires
