title: Darwin Airport records rise in passengers too drunk to fly
content:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) are warning travellers in Darwin to behave after an increase in passengers too drunk to fly attending the city's airport.
Both the Darwin International Airport and the AFP have recorded a recent increase in "obnoxious, abusive" drunk passengers at the facility.
In the past 12 months, AFP officers have turned away 30 intoxicated travellers from the gate and been called to remove a further six passengers from planes.
Rob Porter, executive general manager of the Airport Development Group, which operates the Darwin Airport, said he anticipated the upcoming Easter holidays and peak tourism season could cause those numbers to rise.
The AFP will be increasing its presence near the airport's terminal gates and licensed bars. (ABC News: Lillian Rangiah)
"There's some really aggressive behaviour that's unacceptable at the airport, and for the safety of everybody who flies, we'd like to see that end," he said.
"We want you to come and have a great holiday, but we don't want those obnoxious, abusive behaviours."
In response, AFP officers will be ramping up their presence near the terminal gates and licensed bars leading into the busy period.
While it may be easy to chalk up the over-intoxication to the Northern Territory's laid-back reputation, AFP Superintendent Greg Davis said he didn't believe that was the case.
Rather, he said drinking at the airport was a particular problem in Darwin because so many flights occurred overnight.
Sky-high airfares, poor flight times and unexpected scheduling changes have become standard in the NT capital of Darwin.
That means it isn't uncommon for holiday-makers to head straight from the city's pubs and clubs to the airport.
"Our observations are, particularly with the late-night flights, people have already been out — perhaps they're celebrating or [having] farewells with their family — then they come to the airport," he said.
Airline staff have the authority to prevent a passenger from boarding a plane, if they are overly intoxicated and unruly.
Once a person is on a plane, Superintendent Davis said it was an offence to disobey directions from the cabin crew.
Refusal to comply can result in fines and charges.
Greg Davis says late-night flights at Darwin Airport appear to be contributing to the rise in drunken behaviour. (ABC News: Lillian Rangiah)
Superintendent Davis said in most cases, disruptive passengers ruined the experience for others.
But in the worst cases, they could become threatening or violent towards staff.
"Nobody wants to be threatened or sworn at, when they're just doing their job," he said.

title: Owner of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit completes $5bn gold takeover
content:
Australia's biggest gold miner Northern Star Resources will add the country's largest new gold find to its portfolio after shareholders in De Grey Mining overwhelmingly voted in favour of a $5-billion takeover.
The owner of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine announced its proposed acquisition of De Grey in December in a bid to get its hands on the six-million-ounce Hemi discovery in Western Australia's Pilbara region.
A shareholder meeting held in Perth on Wednesday afternoon saw 99.64 per cent vote in favour of the deal, which valued De Grey at $2.08 per share.
The takeover was effectively locked in after WA miner Gold Road Resources, which holds a 17.26 per cent stake in De Grey worth more than $1.03 billion, confirmed its intention on Monday to vote in favour.
The Federal Court will be asked to approve the takeover next Tuesday.
The takeover comes amid record gold prices and increasing activity in the mergers and acquisitions space.
The Australian dollar gold price surpassed $5,000/oz for the first time on April 1, 17 years after it first topped $1,000/oz in January 2008.
Driller Zakary Kelly working at De Grey Mining's Hemi project in 2020. (Facebook: Topdrill)
De Grey chairman Simon Lill said no superior proposal had emerged in the five months since the takeover was announced.
"We had regard to the costs and risks associated with continuing to develop the Hemi project on a standalone basis and assessed the scheme consideration against a range of valuation benchmarks," he told the meeting.
Since the takeover was announced late last year the company's shares surged from $17.51 to $22.09 at Wednesday's market close.
De Grey's stocks also rose from $1.52 prior to the takeover announcement to $2.61 at Wednesday's close.
Mr Lill was asked at the shareholder meeting why De Grey's board was still recommending the takeover after its share price had surpassed the offer price.
He said the De Grey shares were "inextricably linked" to Northern Star shares and noted the gold price had "moved significantly".
Open pit manager Sean Davies at Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)
The Hemi deposit, about 85 kilometres from Port Hedland, was discovered in late 2019 but the scale of the find became clearer after a major exploration campaign that saw as many as 10 drill rigs turning in 2022.
The cost of bringing Hemi into production is estimated at $1.3b, but a definitive feasibility study estimated payback on that investment could be achieved in less than two years.
Those studies were conducted at an Australian dollar gold price of $2,700/oz, which has since almost doubled.
The mine is slated to have an initial 12-year life and is expected to create 900 construction jobs and 600 operational roles.
The addition of Hemi is expected to increase Northern Star's production from a forecast two million ounces next financial year to 2.5m ounces a year by 2028-29.
Northern Star chief technical officer Steve McClare and Kalgoorlie Consolidated Gold Mines general manager Nick Strong at the Fimiston Mill. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)
Canaccord Genuity analyst Tim McCormack has said the addition of Hemi would notably reduce Northern Star's exposure to the Super Pit and Mt Charlotte operations, which are forecast to represent more than 40 per cent of its production from 2027-28.
The Fimiston Mill at the Super Pit is half-way through a $1.5b, three-year expansion, which is set to increase production from the operation to 900,000 ounces a year towards the end of the decade.
Northern Star's managing director Stuart Tonkin has described the Hemi project as a "low-cost, long-life and large scale gold mine in a tier-one jurisdiction".
"The mill expansion is the largest Australian gold project in over 10 years and provides Northern Star with the unique opportunity to de-risk the Hemi development pathway through our experience and relationships with contractors and suppliers," he said.
author: JBy Jarrod Lucas

title: 'Going to China with an empty suitcase': US shoppers swap tips to beat tariffs
content:
Chinese factories are trying to sell directly to American consumers on social media platforms in a bid to bypass the 145 per cent tariff hike imposed on Chinese products by US President Donald Trump.
From furniture and appliances to laundry pods and home decors, a growing number of Chinese sellers are showcasing their products in English on platforms like TikTok and Rednote, targeting US users with captions such as "factory price for Americans" and "no middleman, no mark-up".
In another clip, a factory worker pitches ultrasonic cleaning products with the line, "Trust me, trust me, Chinese people never cheat," while a Guangzhou wholesaler claims through captions, "only 10 yuan for clothes that cost hundreds."
Views on these posts often climb above 200,000, and some hit over half a million.
Consumers talk about how cheap products manufactured in China are on TikTok.
The trend has also sparked a wave of quirky, engaging content from American users, with one TikToker declaring, "finding out I can get 20 laundry capsules for a single dollar is making my brain short-circuit."
Another joked about "reverse daigou" — referring to the practice of buying goods in China on behalf of American consumers.
The viral spread of these videos allowed US consumers to directly compare prices and connect across borders, making visible the once-invisible layers of profit between factories and shelves.
Many users said they realised how much middle businesses and US-based companies have inflated prices for everyday goods.
Ashley Dudarenok, founder of China research firm ChoZan told the ABC that while consumers can save on small purchases, they're still required to declare goods upon re-entry to the US and pay duties if they exceed exemption limits of $800.
She said the manufacturers' invite for American buyers to visit "captures attention", but was a symptom of trade tensions.
Buyers are expected to save a significant amount of money by buying directly in China, but they will still pay the tariff on the cheaper products.
What differentiates the current trade war with the 2018 US-China trade war is that Chinese businesses explored diversifying exports away from the US rather than looking at directly selling to US consumers.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has landed in Malaysia after visiting Vietnam, as he tries to secure more support from South-East Asian neighbours amid the trade war with Donald Trump.
The first US-China trade war hit a wide range of export-heavy Chinese sectors, particularly electronics, textiles, toys, furniture, and machinery.
According to Chinese government figures, nearly 1.9 million jobs were lost in manufacturing, and industries heavily reliant on the US market — such as those producing low-cost consumer goods — were among the hardest hit.
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which make up the bulk of exporters in China, struggled to adapt to sudden tariff hikes and shipment delays.
Back then, sellers tested drop shipping, online marketplaces, and influencer partnerships.
This time, they are leaning on short videos, livestreaming, and personalised messaging to tap into Western markets.
Now, many of those same industries are back in the spotlight. Household goods, soft furnishings, clothing, and basic electronics are once again bearing the brunt of the renewed tariffs.
Factories in Guangdong, Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces, which serve as major manufacturing hubs for these products, are among the most active in turning to platforms like TikTok and Rednote to promote direct-to-consumer sales.
Experts say this model of bypassing intermediaries may help some exporters offload surplus inventory, but turning viral reach into sustained sales will require more than digital visibility — it depends on fulfilment logistics, payment systems, and consumer trust.
Companies manufacturing in China caught out by US trade war | The Business | ABC News
Dr Cheng Mingming, a digital marketing professor at Curtin University, believed the direct selling trend's implications are still symbolic.
"Manufacturers in a way let US consumers realise that China provides a lot of cheap products that can meet their needs, so that they would feel that America's trade tariffs actually created inconvenience in their life.
An industrial park where many clothing manufacturers are located, in Guangzhou. (Reuters: Casey Hall)
"It might affect how US customers perceive tariffs and the policies that Mr Trump promotes, which argue tariffs are good for the US."
Meanwhile, on Rednote, China's lifestyle-sharing platform, live streamers have launched promotions under hashtags like #saveourfactory and #shopinchina, urging local consumers to buy goods originally destined for US customers.
Some sellers have filled their livestream sets with boxes bearing English shipping labels and barcodes, claiming they were forced to clear out warehouses because of the US tariffs.
In a post, a seller offered steep discounts on small home appliances such as rice cookers, juicers and toasters, while lamenting that US companies "cancelled our contract".
"Now it's all 90 per cent off!" the post wrote.
Some users even urge Americans to visit China in person for cheaper shopping, playing on both sarcasm and a growing sense of cross-border frustration.
"Come to China, buy direct, save big!" reads one post on TikTok, layered over footage of a factory floor.
While the message may resonate with frustrated shoppers, experts say it is unlikely to bring a surge of American shoppers to Chinese factories.
He added that the passport ownership rate in the US is relatively low compared to other developed countries, and international travel remains inaccessible for many.
But the goal, he believes, is not necessarily tourism.
Ms Dudarenok agrees the videos are a savvy marketing strategy.
She said while it's unlikely they will inspire a wave of inbound shopping tourism, they could fuel greater demand for direct-to-consumer platforms.
"Failure to declare goods or pay applicable duties could result in fines or confiscation of items."

title: Footwear chain Wittner hopes for new buyer after collapse
content:
Australian footwear chain Wittner is the latest local retailer to face closure, with administrators appointed to manage the 113-year-old company.
Its collapse follows the closure of Jeanswest stores and chains under company Mosaic, including Katies, Rivers and Noni B.
This spate of insolvencies has already led to the loss of thousands of retail jobs nationally.
Wittner has 20 standalone stores nationally, and 25 stores that sit inside the floors of department stores Myer and David Jones.
Its management said while online sales were up this year, so too were its costs.
Are you a Wittner worker? Confidentially email our journalists on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me
Wittner's administrators say they will keep the stores trading, while they try to sell or restructure the footwear business.
"We understand the appointment of administrators will be particularly concerning to Wittner's employees," Deloitte's Sal Algeri said in a statement.
"Please be assured that trade will continue on a business-as-usual basis as we conduct an urgent review of the group's finances.
"And seek expressions of interest (EOI)s from parties interested in the sale or recapitalisation of this iconic Australian brand."
Wittner was first founded as a mail order business back in 1912.
Deloitte did not say how many employees it has today.
The Retail and Fast Food Workers Union says it represents a small number of members at Wittner, and as well as some from Jeanswest and Mosaic.
“It is an ongoing concern for us particularly because these boutique brands are heavily feminised," the unions Josh Callinan told ABC News.

title: Operator of trouble-plagued power plant 'understated the gravity' of explosion
content:
The operator of the trouble-plagued Callide Power Station has conceded it "understated the gravity" of an explosion at the facility, and that there has not been "adequate reporting of serious issues".
One of Central Queensland power plant's generators will be offline until the end of May after a blast on April 4.
Energy Minister David Janetzki has come under fire for not disclosing the incident to the public during a major address days after it occurred.
The CEO and general manager of the trouble-plagued Callide Power Station have left the company after an explosion earlier this month.
On Sunday, the government accused operator CS Energy of failing to communicate how serious the incident was.
Two senior employees have since exited the company.
This week, the government released documents, including briefing notes, outlining communications from the operator following the incident.
However, the opposition accused the government of a "cover up" after it was revealed CS Energy drafted two media releases about the explosion on the day of the incident and the day after, which were not publicly issued.
Shannon Fentiman says the government needs to explain why CS Energy media releases about the incident were not made public.
In a statement released today, the CS Energy board acknowledged the company had "major cultural issues", and the draft media releases were its responsibility.
"The recent incident has once again highlighted the deep-seated cultural problems at CS Energy that have not been addressed," the statement said.
"There has not been adequate reporting of serious issues to senior management, the board and relevant ministers.
"The board confirms that briefings and holding statements by CS Energy to the energy minister's office understated the gravity of the incident and the release of public statements is always a decision for CS Energy management."
In a statement released last night, Mr Janetzki said any claim that his office "prevented CS Energy from releasing holding statements is categorically false".
The government said it would now require energy companies to provide real-time updates following an outage — as Energex and Ergon do — to prevent a repeat of the communication failings.
Mr Janetzki said any claim that his office "prevented CS Energy from releasing holding statements is categorically false". (Supplied: AAP)
"The board welcomes the relevant ministers' response to introduce real-time outage reporting, seeking a full briefing into how advice is provided to relevant ministers and their offices, and a review into the operation and culture of government-owned corporations," the CS Energy board said.
The Callide power station made headlines in 2021 after an explosion left nearly half a million homes without power.
Callide Power Station is operated by CS Energy. (ABC News: Scout Wallen)
A long-awaited report by forensic engineer Dr Sean Brady, released last year, found the operator had "substantive and longstanding issues" with safety.
"The Brady Report flagged major cultural problems at CS Energy and the new board is determined to fix them," the statement from CS Energy said.

title: Zuckerberg considered 'spinning off' Instagram in 2018 amid antitrust scrutiny
content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg considered spinning off popular photo-sharing app Instagram in 2018 over concerns about the growing risk of antitrust scrutiny, according to a document shown at a trial in Washington on Tuesday.
The document was shown during Mr Zuckerberg's second day of testimony at the high-stakes trial, in which the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is seeking to unwind Meta's acquisitions of prized assets Instagram and WhatsApp.
"I wonder if we should consider the extreme step of spinning Instagram out as a separate company," Mr Zuckerberg said in the 2018 memo.
Tech giant Meta used pirated books by Australian authors including Hannah Kent and Charlotte Wood to train its AI language model.
At the time, Meta was mulling plans to reorganise the social media company and link its apps together more closely.
Mr Zuckerberg pushed back in the memo, saying consolidation was likely to yield "strong business growth" but cautioning that it also could erode the value of flagship app Facebook's social network, with scant promise that the company would get to keep its full "family of apps" in the end.
Meta ultimately did not spin off Instagram, instead proceeding with the plan to integrate its apps the following year. But the fact that Mr Zuckerberg even considered the idea is a stunning sign of how seriously he took the threat of precisely the type of antitrust trial proceeding now.
"As calls to break up the big tech companies grow, there is a non-trivial chance that we will be forced to spin out Instagram and perhaps WhatsApp in the next 5-10 years anyway," he wrote then, noting the possibility that the "next Democratic president" could take action to break up tech companies.
"This is one more factor that we should consider since even if we wanted to keep those apps together we may not be able to," he said.
The courthouse in Washington where Meta platforms and the Federal Trade Commission are facing off in an antitrust trial. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)
The FTC ultimately sued Meta in 2020, during President Donald Trump's first term. Mr Trump's antitrust enforcers sued Alphabet-owned Google the same year, accusing it of monopolising search.
Mr Zuckerberg also downplayed the impact of a spin-off on the company's fortunes at the time in his memo, although Meta has argued publicly since then that attempts to break it up would be damaging.
"While most companies resist break ups, the corporate history is that most companies actually perform better after they've been split up. The synergies are usually less than people think and the strategy tax is usually greater than people think," he wrote.
Mr Zuckerberg's testimony comes as Meta is defending itself years after the release of other damning statements plucked from Facebook's own documents, like a 2008 email in which he said "it is better to buy than compete".
The FTC accuses Meta of holding a monopoly on platforms used to share content with friends and family, where its main competitors in the United States are Snap's Snapchat and MeWe, a tiny privacy-focused social media app launched in 2016.
Platforms where users broadcast content to strangers based on shared interests, such as X, TikTok, YouTube and Reddit, are not interchangeable, the FTC argues.
The case is widely seen as a test of the new Trump administration's promises to take on Big Tech companies.
Mr Zuckerberg testified earlier in the day that Meta bought Instagram because it had a "better" camera than the one his company was trying to build at the time.
The Meta CEO acknolwedged in 2018 that separating Instagram into its own company would be an "extreme step".
  (Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration)
The acknowledgement likewise appeared to support allegations by the FTC that Meta had used a "buy or bury" strategy to snap up potential rivals, keep smaller competitors at bay and maintain an illegal monopoly.
Asked by an attorney for the FTC whether he thought fast-growing Instagram could be destructive to Meta, then known as Facebook, Mr Zuckerberg said he believed Instagram had a better camera than the one his company was building.
"We were doing a build vs. buy analysis," while in the process of building a camera app, Mr Zuckerberg said. "I thought that Instagram was better at that, so I thought it was better to buy them."
The company argues that his past intentions are irrelevant because the FTC has defined the social media market inaccurately and failed to account for stiff competition Meta has faced from ByteDance's TikTok, Alphabet's YouTube and Apple's messaging app.
Mr Zuckerberg also acknowledged that many of the company's attempts at building its own apps had failed.
"Building a new app is hard and many more times than not when we have tried to build a new app, it hasn't gotten a lot of traction," he told the court.
"We probably tried building dozens of apps over the history of the company and the majority of them don't go anywhere."

title: Video of 'disgusting' youth disturbance in Big W fuels police probe
content:
Tasmania Police is investigating a disturbance that broke out on Tuesday at a department store in Hobart's northern suburbs, as a video of the affray reaches hundreds of thousands of viewers.
The video, circulated on social media, shows a confrontation involving a large group of youths inside the Glenorchy Big W store.
The young people are shown shouting in the tech area, with some jumping onto the service counter and one seen throwing punches.
A Tasmania Police spokesperson said it is believed the disturbance involved two youth groups known to each other.
The ABC spoke to one witness who was shopping in the store when the incident happened.
Wanting to remain anonymous, the customer described it as "disgusting".
"My friend and I were doing some Easter shopping and were at the front of the shop and heard some kids yelling," she said.
"About five kids ran out of the shop stealing things.
"One of the staff said [the youths] had just bashed someone up.
"We continued shopping and were heading to the back of the shop when about 15-20 kids strolled in in one big line.
The customer said she saw staff members being pushed, kicked and abused.
"We couldn't stand there and watch, so we got in the middle and [were] trying to split it all up, also other people were helping as well," she said.
A Woolworths Group spokesperson said team members who witnessed the incident were given access to counselling services.
The customer said she wanted to see more police patrolling shops, and said she feared shops would close down because of "kids like this".
"If nothing is done I can see the public taking things into their own hands."
Tasmania Police has a specific taskforce to target shoplifting and anti-social behaviour in Glenorchy known as Operation Swipe.
Police, Fire and Emergency Management Minister Felix Ellis said he was "appalled at the behaviour displayed last night".
"Tasmanians deserve to not only feel safe, but be safe when they are going about their business.
"Our government will continue to be tough on crime, and tough on the causes of crime to keep our communities safe."

title: Restaurant industry spooked by vow to crack down on immigrant workers
content:
Restaurateur Amanda Scott says the process of employing skilled immigrant workers is slow, expensive, and maddeningly bureaucratic.
The cafe owner fears the process will become even harder as both major parties vow to reduce immigration levels if they win the upcoming federal election.
The Kedron Farm House owner said few Australians were studying cookery, with venues becoming increasingly dependent on immigrant workers.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
She said this could be partly due to the "Gordon Ramsay effect", with Australians viewing hospitality as a brutal, difficult, and unfriendly career path.
Ms Scott said overseas chefs had been filling those roles instead, but the worker visa approvals process was becoming increasingly onerous.
She said skilled visa applications were now taking several years to be processed while costing upwards of $8,000 in paperwork.
"It was successful until this year, but now something's happened with both sides of politics using this as an election ploy," Ms Scott said.
"It's such a disincentive to go into restaurants these days because it's so complicated — you have to be a visa expert, a payroll expert, an immigration expert."
Brisbane cafe mogul Philip Di Bella said the industry was badly hit when the Labor government capped the hours international students were allowed to work.
Phillip Di Bella says the foreign worker cap is driving an illegal trade. (ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)
Student visa work restrictions were scrapped in 2022 and brought back in 2023, preventing international students from working more than 24 hours per week.
The Coffee Commune owner said this had served to embolden the illegal cash-in-hand market and made it more difficult for venues to fill their rosters.

Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen
Mr Di Bella said he believed immigrants were unfairly blamed for taking Australian jobs at a time when the unemployment rate was only around 4 per cent.
"The international students didn't take all the jobs and cause unemployment," Mr Di Bella said.
"If they do cap international students and migrants, it will have a big effect."
Australian Hotel Association (AHA) chief executive Stephen Ferguson said the Coalition's proposed caps on foreign workers would hurt local businesses.
Stephen Ferguson says there is a shortage of chefs that cannot be filled domestically. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)
"The AHA is very concerned regarding the Coalition's disappointing announcement that it will decrease foreign workers by 100,000 each year," Mr Ferguson said.
"Political parties often talk about the need for productivity, but in a labour-intensive industry like hospitality, a reduction in available workers will cause a severe downturn in productivity."
The Hospitality Industry Award shows minimum wages for chefs have not kept up with the pace of inflation in the last five years.
A casual entry-level chef earns $31.23 per hour, which is lower than the casual award for traffic controllers ($35.04 per hour), and bus drivers ($32.25 per hour).
The Department of Homes Affairs was contacted for comment.
Venezualan accountant José Gomez said it took 10 years to get his worker visa approved.
José Gomez says it was an exhausting 10-year battle to get full worker rights. (ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)
The Kedron Farm House accountant said he had his visa denied and delayed several times before it was eventually approved.
"We had anxieties and worries because we couldn't go and buy a car, we couldn't buy a house because nobody will lend you money when on a visa with no stability or rights to extend your stay in a country," Mr Gomez said.

title: China halts orders of US-made Boeing jets, scrapping deals worth billions
content:
China has reportedly ordered its airlines to pause all incoming deliveries of American-made Boeing aircraft in response to Donald Trump's 145 per cent tariffs on Chinese goods.
The three main Chinese airlines were expected to take delivery of 179 Boeing planes between now and 2027 — more planes than the entire Qantas main fleet — in deals worth billions of dollars.
But that plan has been put on hold, according to reports from Bloomberg News.
In his first public comments about the US-China trade war, President Xi Jinping says there are no winners in a tariff war.
International aviation consultant Neil Hansford said China would be the biggest loser from this latest trade spat.
"In the end China is cutting off its nose to spite its face because [the country] has a shortage of aircraft after COVID," he said.
Mr Hansford said the upheaval meant Boeing could focus on sending planes elsewhere.
"It'll assist Boeing because they can actually start bringing deliveries to other customers," he said.
"Everybody is short of equipment, we're all trying to give maintenance to aircraft.
"So for the rest of the aviation world it's a good thing."
Mr Hansford said China would still have access to jets from elsewhere, "but they need Boeing's because COVID set us years behind in the building of aircraft".
The larger trade war between China and the United States shows no sign of cooling.
US tariffs on China stand at 145 per cent and in return China has imposed 125 per cent tariffs on American goods entering its borders.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said his country was open for business.
"We will continue to expand our circle of friends in trade, strengthen the gravitational field of investment, and inject more stability and positive energy into the world economy through high-quality development and high-level opening-up."
Meanwhile, a Communist Party official in Hong Kong, Xia Baolong, has clapped back to a recent reference to Chinese "peasants" made by US Vice President JD Vance.
"The repeated attempts of the US to contain and suppress Hong Kong will only result in the end of its agents in Hong Kong, and will backfire, and harm itself," he said.
"Those peasants from the US will soon be crying tears in front of China's 5,000 years of civilisation."
Donald Trump attends a bilateral meeting with China's President Xi Jinping during the G20 leaders summit in 2019. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the US president was waiting on China to come to the table.
"The president has made his position on China quite clear," she said.
"The ball is in China's court — China needs to make a deal with us, we don't have to make a deal with them.
"There's no difference between China and any other country except they are much larger and China wants what we have … they need our money.
"The president has made it quite clear that he's open to a deal with China, but China needs to make a deal with the United States of America."
Most countries are facing a 10 per cent tariff, except for some goods from Canada and Mexico.

The S&P/ASX200 closed down just 2.8 points Wednesday to 7,758.9 after being higher for most of the day on Chinese economic data beating analyst estimates.
The White House said US President Donald Trump was open to making a trade deal with China but that the ball was in China's court.
Escalating tensions between Washington and Beijing have hit the tech sector, with Nvidia shares sliding in after-hours trade on Wall Street after revealing it will take a $US5.5 billion ($8.7 billion) hit on restrictions of chip exports to China.
By Stephanie Chalmers
Shares in Star Entertainment have bounced around this session, its first back trading on the ASX since it was suspended for failing to lodge its financial results on Februrary 28.
The stock surged out of the gates, gaining more than 10 per cent in early trade, but has since swung between losses and gains.
Currently it's up 4.6 per cent.
It's worth noting that Star shares last closed at 11 cents, so it's moving between around 10 and 12 cents during today's trade.
Yesterday, the embattled casino operator reported a half-year loss of more than $300 million.
"Star equity valuation will remain challenged, given significant levels of net debt," Jefferies analysts said in a note on Tuesday.
They cut their price target on the stock to 9 cents from 15 cents and retained the "underperform" rating.
Star shareholders will vote in June to approve an investment by US gaming giant Bally's, which will give it a controlling stake in the company.
Star has already received the first $100 million of the $300 million rescue funding provided by Bally's and pub investor Bruce Mathieson.
Reporting with Reuters
By Nassim Khadem
Are markets near breaking point? This is a question that many are asking as the impact of US President Donald Trump's tariff war continues to play out.
Jamieson Coote Bonds chief investment officer Charlie Jamieson says Trump's "tariff escalations, unpredictable rhetoric, and regulatory pivots have disrupted financial markets in a deliberate attempt to reset the system".
"By first crushing investor confidence and dampening growth, the aim appears to be cooling inflation expectations, which opens the door for the US Federal Reserve to cut rates and enable refinancing of pandemic-era debt," he noted.
"This would be followed by fiscal stimulus, likely in the form of tax cuts ahead of the US midterms."
But he says the ongoing uncertainty has triggered "a sharp tightening in financial conditions".
"Markets have hit an inflection point, with risk now shifting from interest rates to equity and credit," he said.
"Liquidity has evaporated in parts of the credit market, spreads have widened dramatically, and traditionally defensive income assets have become pro-cyclical.
"Unlike previous periods of market stress, there's little expectation of timely support from monetary or fiscal policy. Investors are now navigating a highly fragile and volatile environment."
He suggests portfolios need to be reassessed. He says this can be done "through a lens of liquidity, credit risk, and policy inaction — where diversification, quality and agility are essential to managing through the next phase of the cycle".
By Stephanie Chalmers
A quick check in on how the share market is travelling an hour out from the end of the session.

By Nassim Khadem
The Australian dollar has rebounded from last week's cyclical low of 59 cents, but CBA thinks it could still go lower.
The Aussie dollar is currently trading around 63 US cents.
"While it is tempting to think AUD/USD is now past its low point, we think that the downside risks to AUD/USD remain heightened," CBA said in a research note.
"A weak global economy, inherent volatility, and bad news about the Chinese economy will weigh on AUD/USD.
"Consequently, we judge AUD/USD could easily set a new cyclical low in coming months."
By Nassim Khadem
Shares in buy now pay later company Zip are trading 21.3 per cent higher at $1.80 following the release of the company's third-quarter update.
The company reported a 219 per cent year-on-year increase in cash earnings before tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBTDA) of $46 million.
Zip also upgraded its guidance for FY 2025, forecasting it will deliver cash EBTDA of at least $153 million, up from prior guidance of at least $147 million.
As at March 31, Zip has 6.3 million active customers, up 4.2 per cent year on year.
While merchants using Zip's platforms increased by 7.2 per cent to around 83,300.
Zip Group CEO Cynthia Scott noted the company has delivered the largest ever quarterly cash earnings in Zip's history of $46 million, underpinned by material operating leverage.
"Our US business continues to deliver significant growth, with TTV (time to value) and revenue increasing 40.2 per cent and 44.1 per cent year on year respectively, driven by deeper customer engagement," she said.
"Momentum in the ANZ business continued, with TTV increasing 12.6 per cent year on year."
Some shareholders missed out on gains in the share price when -  at the end of 2023 - Zip announced it would buy out many of its small shareholders. You can read more about that here:
By Nassim Khadem
Mining giant BHP has gained approval for NSW's largest coal mine to remain open for a further four years until 2030.
BHP has partnered with renewable energy and infrastructure company ACCIONA Energía to explore the development of a pumped hydro energy storage project at Mt Arthur Coal.
The approval comes some 15 years ahead of previous plans to shut the coal mine which has a 2000-strong workforce.
In 2022, BHP announced its decision to transition Mt Arthur Coal to closure in 2030, based on the mine reaching the end of its economic life.
As part of the planned pathway for closure, BHP has gained approval from the NSW Government to extend mining activities at Mt Arthur Coal for an additional four years, from July 2026 to June 2030.
BHP says its conceptual studies show that a pumped hydro energy storage project at Mt Arthur Coal has the potential to support around 1,000 jobs within the Upper Hunter in the construction phase and contribute to ongoing economic activity.
Over the next twelve months, ACCIONA Energía will carry out due diligence on the possibility of converting part of the Mt Arthur site into a pumped hydro energy storage project.
"Mt Arthur Coal sits on more than 7,000 hectares and we are working hard to explore alternative land uses for the site that will continue to support jobs, investment in the region, and the local economy," BHP President Australia Geraldine Slattery said.
"The community have told us they want to see Mt Arthur repurposed when mining ends. This study will examine the role pumped hydro at the Mt Arthur site could play in the region's future."
By Nassim Khadem
China's economy grew by 5.4 per cent in first quarter as the world's second biggest economy braces the full impact of an escalating trade war.
"According to preliminary estimates, the gross domestic product in the first quarter reached 31,875.8 billion yuan, up by 5.4 per cent year on year at constant prices," Beijing's National Bureau of Statistics said.
The result was above analyst estimates of 5.1 per cent, and came before some of the US government's steep tariffs took hold.
US President Donald Trump last week announced a 90-day pause on higher tariffs on all countries — except China.
US levies imposed on China have risen to 145 per cent, and Beijing has set a retaliatory 125 per cent tariff on US imports.
China's bureau said "the national economy got off to a good and steady start", but that "we should be aware that the external environment is becoming more complex and severe".
"The drive for the growth of effective domestic demand is insufficient, and the foundation for sustained economic recovery and growth is yet to be consolidated," the bureau said.
Beijing is aiming for economic growth of around 5 per cent this year, but some analysts say that is an ambitious target given the ongoing trade war, as well as a continuing domestic property crisis.
By Nassim Khadem
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has slashed forecasts for global oil demand this year amid the escalating trade war.
And in its first detailed assessment of 2026, the IEA predicted a persistent supply surplus.
It slashed projections for 2025 demand growth by 300,000 barrels a day to 730,000 barrels a day, according to its monthly report.
Half of the reduction was concentrated in the US and China, which are engaged in an ongoing trade war.
The IEA forecast consumption growth will be even slower in 2026, at 690,000 barrels a day, due to "a fragile macroeconomic environment" and the rising popularity of electric vehicles.
Global oil prices tumbled in March and early April in the wake of US tariffs and mounting recession fears.
"The decision by some OPEC+ members to accelerate the unwinding of extra voluntary production cuts added to the bearish momentum," the IEA said.
The Paris-based agency said while imports of oil, gas and refined products were given exemptions from the tariffs announced by the US government, concerns that the measures could stoke inflation, slow economic growth and intensify trade disputes had weighed on oil prices.
Brent futures are trading near $US65 a barrel after earlier hitting their lowest levels in more than four years to below US$60 a barrel.
"With negotiations and countermeasures still ongoing, the situation is fluid and substantial risks remain," the IEA said.
"With arduous trade negotiations expected to take place during the coming 90-day reprieve on tariffs and possibly beyond, oil markets are in for a bumpy ride and considerable uncertainties hang over our forecasts for this year and next."

By Nassim Khadem
Nvidia will take a quarterly charge of about $US5.5 billion after the US government limited exports of its H20 artificial intelligence chip to China, a key market for one of its most popular chips.
The news sent its stock price sliding about 6 per cent in after-hours trading.
The H20 is currently Nvidia's most advanced chip for sale in China.
Nvidia said the US government informed it on April 9 that the H20 chip would require a license to be exported to China, and on April 14 told Nvidia those rules would be in place indefinitely.
It's a big hurdle for Nvidia, which earlier in the week said it was planning to build AI servers worth as much as $US500 billion in the US over the next four years.
Tech stock analyst Daniel Ives from Wedbush said Nvidia now faced "massive restrictions and hurdles in selling to China", which had been building during the Biden Administration.
"The Trump administration knows there is one chip and company fueling the AI Revolution and its Nvidia ... and put a 'Do Not Enter' sign in front of China for Nvidia and Jensen (Huang CEO of Nvidia) with this restriction," Mr Ives said.
"The financial impact is small relatively, but the strategic blow is the focus of the market as Nvidia now has massive blockades going after the China market in the middle of this raging US/China tariff battle."
Mr Ives notes Nvidia is a "key strategic asset" for the US and the Trump Administration during this very tense period with China.
"And the White House is going to make sure Jensen and Nvidia's chips do not land in China for now and help Beijing in the AI Revolution," he added.
"The Street will take this news with clear nervousness worried these are the first shots fired in the tech battle between the US and China and Beijing/Xi are not just going to take this news and walk away."
Mr Ives said there would likely be "a major back and forth between the US and China as the market and the economy is caught in the middle with this tariff battle royale."
"While the Nvidia news is concerning it's not a shock as we are in the middle of a trade war between the US and China and expect more punches thrown by both sides before cooler heads prevail and negotiations in some form can start to get these 145 per cent reciprocal tariffs down to a digestible level," he said.

By Daniel Ziffer
Hard Rock sells blank apparel to retailers on a wholesale basis and directly to consumers via its online store.
But... they made false or misleading representations about consumers’ rights to return faulty or incorrect products and tried to rig what retailers could sell the gear for.
The ACCC has a court-enforceable undertaking from it where it admits breaking the Competition and Consumer Act and the Australian Consumer Law, commits to issue corrective notices to resellers and remove misleading representations about consumer guarantees from its website, and implement a compliance program.
Hard Rock has admitted that between 20 June 2024 and 11 September 2024 it required certain resellers to sell Hard Rock products within a specific price range.
No way, says ACCC Chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb.
“Hard Rock has admitted that it sent written communications to ten resellers requiring them not to sell their products below 10 per cent of Hard Rock’s recommended retail price.
“In addition, Hard Rock told resellers that if they did not agree, it may adjust pricing or cease supplying its products to them.
“Suppliers cannot maintain price premiums in an anti-competitive way by setting minimum prices for resellers.”
Hard Rock’s undertaking, which the ACCC has accepted, is in effect for three years.
By Daniel Ziffer
Does it seem like everyone is "calling for" something at the moment?
It's a febrile moment, with almost a huge proportion of Australians set to cast their vote early at this election, and those pre-poll facilities about to open on April 22.
Peak body ASFA, which advocates on behalf of superannuation funds, is asking the next government for "certainty and stability in superannuation policy" as its key ask.
ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty says it wants to build on the stability that has helped superannuation become one of the biggest pools of capital in the world.
(My recent report on this is tagged at the bottom).
“Our superannuation system is working well for the 17 million Australians with superannuation accounts by delivering strong retirement outcomes: it builds our prosperity, and delivers greater financial security for retirees, stable capital for investment, and economic resilience for the country”
But it doesn't want stasis either, calling for expanding the Low Income Superannuation Tax Offset to improve retirement outcomes for working Australians, implementing 'payday super' (getting paid it at the same time, something that has passed into law) without delay so that all Australians get their superannuation entitlements on time and protecting people from scams, among other items.
By Daniel Ziffer
Half of all investment properties are being resold within two years of tenants living in them, according to new data from the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI).
The research, based on data from a large and long-running survey by the Melbourne Institute, shows people aged 25-34 years are more likely to buy a rental property compared to other age groups, but also more likely to sell quickly.
This article from my colleagues Adelaide Miller and Emilia Terzon puts some bones on the vibe we've had around instability for the one-in-three Australians who rent - and why the housing crisis has such substantial and broad impact in society.
By Daniel Ziffer
Who says the minors can't make it?
Bank of Queensland shares are up +4.4% at the time of writing on the release of strong half-yearly profits.
It holds 210,000 mortgages and has 500,000 deposit customers, the report says.
It has closed a substantial amount of branches, detailing the "early conversion of 34 branches" and the "consolidation of 20 branches" in its network.
As of now, shares are up +4.4% to $6.78.
By Stephanie Chalmers
With home ownership further out of reach than ever for younger Australians, some are pondering whether their locked-away retirement funds would be better off used now, to buy a house.
Jordan Davies is one young person who views home ownership as out of reach, despite the 28-year-old feeling that he is relatively well-off, with a decent job and stable salary.
"It's still difficult to obtain finance in the amount that is needed to purchase a property," he told ABC News.
Should first home buyers be able to use super to buy a house? (Nadia Daly)
Yet Mr Davies is on the fence about a policy being put forward by the Coalition, ahead of the federal election on May 3.
The scheme proposes that Australians should be allowed to take up to $50,000, or 40 per cent, of their superannuation fund to buy their first home.

title: Mount Gambier airport passengers face 'unsustainable' $90 fare hike
content:
Tickets for flights out of the biggest city in regional South Australia will rise by an "unsustainable" $90 if the council is not able to get assistance to pay for installing security screening.
Mount Gambier airport, in the state's south-east, is currently exempt from security screening, but has been told it is nearing passenger number thresholds that would trigger mandatory screening.
The District Council of Grant, which operates the airport, has said security screening will cost in excess of $1.5 million up-front, and $300,000 each year.
Council chief executive Darryl Whicker said increasing flight costs to Adelaide and Melbourne by $90 would risk making the airport unsustainable.
"Airports need to have frequency of flights and affordability," he said.
"Any impact that increases ticket prices substantially will reduce affordability which means people won't travel and therefore airports become unsustainable."
The Mount Gambier airport will soon need to add security screening due to the number of passengers. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)
Australian Airports Association (AAA) chief executive Simon Westaway said he had heard similar concerns across the country on a recent tour of regional airports.
"A lot of these airports are council-run and owned, and the margins are finite," he said.
"Fifteen per cent of the overall Australian market for air travel is regional flying.
"The reality is if [costs] go up, they need to be managed."
Former senator and current SA Senate candidate for the Jacqui Lambie Network Rex Patrick said regional passengers paid significantly more per flight for security screening than their city counterparts.
"At Port Lincoln Airport, passengers pay about $15 per ticket, $45 at Whyalla, and, as will be the case soon, $90 per passenger at Mount Gambier," he said.
"Yet passengers in Sydney pay only 70 cents."
Rex Patrick (second from left) met with the Grant District Council to discuss the cost of security screening. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)
Implementing the fee in Whyalla caused a significant drop in passengers, from 1,500 per week to 900 per week.
Rex Airlines also halted services to Whyalla.
Mr Whicker said a reduction in flights to Mount Gambier would impact a number of critical services for the region.
"We can attract teachers, doctors, nurses and allied health professionals from Melbourne and Adelaide," he said.
The Whyalla airport experienced a drop in passengers when it added the cost of security screening. (Supplied: Whyalla City Council)
If successful in the federal election, Mr Patrick and Senator Jacqui Lambie promised to introduce a bill to share the costs of security screening between all passengers in Australia.
"We need to have a regime in Australia where each passenger pays a levy for security screening costs, and that levy is used to fund the security screening costs all around the country," Mr Patrick said.
"What that means is people in Sydney who now pay 70 cents per passenger might have to pay a dollar.
"But it means that the people in Mount Gambier, instead of having to pay $90 will also only have to pay a dollar.
Mr Westaway said the AAA would push for more support for regional airports with the next federal parliament.
"We need to see a more sustainable commitment of funding to support both capital and operational requirements at our regional airfields," he said.
A spokesperson for the Department for Home Affairs said it worked with airport operators to ensure appropriate security measures were in place.
"Within the aviation security framework, airports and airlines are responsible for delivering aviation security requirements and managing day-to-day security operations, including the associated costs," they said.

title: The ABC's first Elder-in-residence wants to see a future without racism
content:
Amid a hum of clacking typewriters, office chatter and the urgent jangling of telephones ringing, a crackle of tension cuts through the haze of cigarette smoke hanging in the air.
It's 1972 and along the corridors of the ABC's Toowong headquarters in Brisbane a sense of change is being ushered in. The streets are awash with anti-Vietnam war protests, while on TV scenes of the Aboriginal tent embassy in Canberra being broken up by police leap from the screens.
Flags fly in front of the Aboriginal Tent Embassy outside Parliament House, Canberra, in 1972. (National Archives)
And a 16-year-old Jackie Huggins is also making history as she travels from the Brisbane suburb of Inala to Toowong to take up her first job as a typist for the nation's revered broadcaster. It was not something many Indigenous people had ever achieved.
Warning – this story includes the names and images of people who have died. Readers are advised the story also contains the a racial slur used for historical context.
Professor Jackie Huggins at 16 years old, around the time she started her job as a typist at the ABC. (Supplied: Jackie Huggins)
"I was the only Aboriginal employee in those times in the '70s in Brisbane," says Professor Huggins. "Prior to that my cousin, Lillian Holt, rest in peace, was the only person I knew [who] had worked at the ABC."
In 1962, Holt was the first Aboriginal person to be employed at the ABC in Queensland.
She spent four years working in the Brisbane office and then another four in Sydney. Holt went on to have a distinguished career in education and gained international acclaim before her passing in 2020.
The drive to push boundaries seems to be a family trait.
Now, more than 50 years since Professor Huggins first stepped foot inside the ABC, and with a lifetime of lessons learned, she is returning as the corporation's inaugural Elder-in-residence.
"My new role is something that I never imagined I would do when I started my employment at the ABC when I was 16 years of age," says Professor Huggins, who is a Member of the Order of Australia (AM) and a fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities (FAHA).
"It's come the full circle now that I'm heading towards my 70s and I'm in a different space, different part of my whole life's journey."
'I never give up': Jackie Huggins appointed ABC's inaugural Elder in Residence (ABC News Breakfast)
The position of Elder-in-residence was created in response to criticism from Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) employees who have experienced racism while working at the broadcaster.
In October 2024, the ABC publicly released an independent report, Listen Loudly, Act Strongly, into the media organisation's systems and processes in response to staff experiences of racism.
The report included submissions from past and current employees of Indigenous and CALD backgrounds, of whom 120 gave details of their experiences. All but one had shared direct exposure to racism during their employment at the ABC.
The report made 15 recommendations, with the ABC promising to respond to all and to track their progress. Among them was recommendation 14.i: "ABC Leadership should look at systemic approaches to improve cultural safety, such as establishing a First Nations Elder-in-residence program."
Kelly Williams, the ABC's Acting Director of First Nations Strategy, says Jackie Huggins is a natural fit for the role of elder-in-residence. (ABC)
Kelly Williams is the ABC's acting director of First Nations strategy, also a new role for the broadcaster. The Bundjalung woman has been integral to creating Professor Huggins's new position.
"Professor Huggins is able to bring her lived experience to what has changed and what hasn't — and provide advice on how to move that conversation forward," Williams says.
She is a natural fit for the role, Williams says. As well as her work at the ABC as a young woman, Professor Huggins brings decades of work in the reconciliation movement, experience as a regular contributor across ABC platforms and a strong connection to Indigenous young people, she says.
For Professor Huggins, "being the first" is a hallmark of her life.
But it was far from the expected path for the Bidjara and Birri-Gubbu Juru woman whose father died at 38 from injuries sustained as a prisoner of war on the Thai-Burma railway. Professor Huggins ended up leaving school early to help keep her mother and siblings out of poverty.
Jackie Huggins: my father Jack
"We grew up very poor," she recalls. "I remember the one dress I had to wear all week to school. No shoes. And I thought, there's got to be a way out of this."
The "way out" meant taking up a fight that has endured across the fields of media, public service, academia, writing and reconciliation.
From her start as a 16-year-old at the ABC, Professor Huggins went on to work for the Department of Aboriginal Affairs in Canberra.
The late 1970s was a period of massive change for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leadership and the advancement of Indigenous rights. Community-led organisations were starting to form, land rights were being recognised and land councils were taking shape.
"I left the ABC at the age of 24. I went to Canberra and met Charles Perkins and his angels, they used to call them the angels," Professor Huggins remembers.
The "angels" Professor Huggins refers to included men such as Vince Copley, John Moriarty, Joe Croft, Ben Mason and others.
Freedom rider Charles Perkins, right, talks with Aboriginal residents of Moree. (Supplied: State Library of NSW: The Tribune)
Always at the forefront was Perkins AO, the Arrernte and Kalkadoon man who had shot to fame in 1965 in the Freedom Ride that drew public attention to the inequalities faced by Indigenous people in Australia.
"I was the only young Indigenous woman in the room at times where I'd be taking minutes," she says. "They really progressed my career."
Charles Perkins's Freedom Ride bus in 1965. (Supplied: University of Sydney)
In 1978, Perkins was the assistant secretary of the Department of Aboriginal Affairs. He quickly recognised Professor Huggins's potential. She was a quick study in those heady days of Black politics. From writing up the minutes of department meetings Huggins rose quickly and was heading up DAA's first women's unit by the time she was 28.
"That was my first kind of big leadership role and I was in charge of around 50 women," says Professor Huggins.
Another key mentor was Dr Evelyn Scott AO, a woman synonymous with Australia's reconciliation movement from her time serving as chair of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation (CAR) and whose work with the council culminated in the Walk for Reconciliation across the Sydney Harbour Bridge on May 28, 2000.
Evelyn Scott, a former chair of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, here with former PM John Howard, was a mentor to Jackie Huggins. (AAP: Alan Porritt)
"It was a cold and windy morning. I had all my family there," Professor Huggins recalls. "And I just remember seeing those trains coming to North Sydney. Seeing them packed as. And then they went back empty. I thought, oh, they can't all be coming here, you know. Yes, they were."
"Sharing Our Future" was the theme for Reconciliation Week that year and 250,000 people showed they shared a belief in the future when they walked over the bridge together that day. Throughout the week, multiple events were held across the country marking the biggest collective demonstration of public support that has ever taken place in Australia.
Following Dr Scott's lead in the reconciliation movement, Huggins joined Reconciliation Australia in 2001, taking the position of co-chair. She was also awarded the Australia Medal that year, in recognition of her work on reconciliation, social justice, literacy and women's issues.
In 2000 the Walk for Reconciliation across Sydney Harbour Bridge attracted tens of thousands of participants.  (DG/PB (Reuters))
As the ABC responds to Listen Loudly, Act Strongly, engages with the findings and supports staff who have faced racism in the workplace, it's an opportune time for Professor Huggins to reflect on her experiences.
"You never forget those times when people scar you or inflict that racism upon you," she says. Whether that's being asked: "What's it like to live in a traditional Aboriginal society?" by a university lecturer when you're the only First Nations student in the room, or having a colleague say to you over a cup of tea "Do you speak the boong language that they speak at [Brisbane's] West End?".
"I just feel like I've got this armour. This absolute armour," says Professor Huggins. "And I'd like to see every employee of the ABC stand up, name it and really have those conversations."
Professor Jackie Huggins says "You never forget those times when people scar you or inflict that racism upon you" but she now has "armour". (ABC News: Liz Pickering)
The ABC's new managing director, Hugh Marks, has highlighted the importance of the responsibility to respond meaningfully to Listen Loudly, Act Strongly.
"With Professor Huggins and Kelly's leadership, and with so many other contributors around the ABC, we are well placed to act strongly. We should do our work well, we must have an ambition to reach far, and we must ensure our approach reaches into every part of the organisation," Marks says.
"I intend it to be a real priority for me in my new role as MD."
Professor Huggins believes the response should be a guide for other organisations.
"I think it's become a blueprint for other organisations to follow too," she says, always looking further ahead to push what's possible.
Professor Jackie Huggins took her first leadership role at age 28 and has pushed boundaries throughout her career. (Supplied: Syrenne Anu)
In an already impressive career, Huggins describes her appointment as the ABC's Elder-in-residence as "one of my highest badges of honour".
She is looking forward to "taking care of, speaking up for and mentoring" those around her. Just as her Elders did for her.
"I had, of course, my mother, father and my mother's brothers and sisters," she says. "They'd mostly growl at me because they loved me. I find that I'm doing that too to a lot of people. So, we do growl because we do love you and we want to put you on the right path."
Professor Jackie Huggins, on left in pink dress with her family, including her mother Rita Holt, seated. (Supplied: Jackie Huggins)
Not one to rest on her laurels or measure success through individual achievement, that "right path" for Huggins stretches beyond the ABC.
Like the ABC, SBS also has an Elder-in-residence. Widjabal Wiyabal Bundjalung woman Rhoda Roberts AO was named inaugural Elder-in-residence at the broadcaster in 2021.
Roberts has carved out her own exceptional career in media, the arts, social justice and health.
It comes as no surprise Roberts and Huggins know each other well and will bring their collective wisdom to this new phase for Australian public broadcasting.
"We go back 40 years at least. I call her a Tidda-girl," says Huggins, referring to the expression of womanhood among First Nations women.
The two women hope to collaborate. "You've got to have the other mob and their point of view," Huggins says.
For Roberts, the chance to closely align their work is an opportunity she relishes, describing Huggins as a "ground breaker".
"To have her as ABC Elder-in-residence with not only her academic qualifications but her passion for our people, particularly women, being able to write and look at our activism and unpack it and then talk to you without judging you, I mean, it's a certain style of leadership that I would always call our kinship leadership," says Roberts.
Rhoda Roberts is the elder-in-residence at SBS and hopes to collaborate with Jackie Huggins, her ABC counterpart.  (ABC Arts: Anna Kucera)
It's precisely this way of working which has placed Huggins at the interface of race, reconciliation and justice in Australia, serving as a beacon for the way forward.
With the 25th anniversary of that blustery bridge walk just weeks away, and the theme for this year's Reconciliation Week, Bridging Now to Next, there is an added symmetry to this moment which is not lost on Professor Huggins.
"That's the most important thing, that we move on, together, as a nation."

title: Labor and the Coalition are promising to help first-time buyers. This is what's missing
content:
After years of house prices rising faster than young Australians can catch them, political parties entered this election contest under more pressure than ever to help first-time buyers.
Now both Labor and the Coalition have unveiled their big ideas, we have a clearer picture of how they intend to solve Australia's generations-long housing affordability problem.
Both agree that billions of extra cash is needed, which experts say could impact both the supply and demand for housing.
Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues
They also say there is an elephant in the room — with neither party wanting to talk about big structural reforms to tax incentives for property investors, there is a risk housing market trends will continue in the same vein they are now.
While the assessment from economists is that the policies on offer will have a moderate impact, they come at a time where the most intense cost pressures on the system are easing.
In the words of UNSW professor of housing research Hal Pawson: "there is light at the end of the tunnel".
How the housing offers by each of the major parties plays into the market is still emerging, and some key details that help to understand that remain missing.
In the simplest terms, both parties are offering measures that will lift demand, measures that would improve supply and measures that will in time add to the construction workforce — exactly how the ledger is ultimately balanced in terms of whether demand or supply is pushed up faster remains to be seen.
There are two significant new commitments by Labor: $10 billion to build 100,000 homes over eight years, exclusively for sale to first home buyers, and an expansion of a scheme allowing first home buyers to purchase a home with just a 5 per cent deposit — without having to pay a costly insurance penalty.
Grattan Institute housing policy director Brendan Coates says on the Labor end: "In the long-term the policies will boost supply, in the short term they will probably also push up prices, because the First Home Guarantee scheme in particular will put upward pressure on prices, although that effect should be pretty modest."
Dr Nick Garvin, research manager at economics institute e61, agrees that it will push up prices, hurting future first home buyers.
"I don't think it's going to have much of a dent, it's going to temporarily help first home buyers ... that is going to come at the cost of higher house price pressures," Garvin says.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Housing Minister Clare O'Neil say they will make it easier for first home buyers to get onto the property ladder. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)
Pawson says all demand-side instruments have some inflationary impact on house prices, but the 5 per cent deposit scheme shouldn't be something to worry about, since it already exists and hasn't resulted in a significant change to house prices.
The supply side of the equation is more complex, but Pawson says there are a few things going on.
First, he says the government has laid the foundations for new supply that is only just beginning to get moving now, in both the 30,000 social housing properties promised under Labor's $10 billion Housing Australia Future Fund, and more affordable rental apartments via tax incentives legislated late last year under the Build-to-Rent program (the Property Council estimates that will deliver about 80,000 additional units over a decade).
Then, the government's 100,000 new home program being dubbed 'Build to Buy' could make a measurable if "modest" difference to the market for two reasons: first, by partnering with state governments and councils those homes could be built faster and without requiring pre-sales, getting those projects moving sooner.
Second, Pawson says, is if they are sold at cost price those properties could be listed as much as 20 per cent cheaper, which could also slow the speed at which prices in the rest of the market increase.
Labor's housing policies would push up prices in the short term, housing experts say. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)
If those policies all work as intended, they could grow annual supply by about a tenth above what it is now (assuming there is a workforce to deliver them).
On the Coalition's side, Pawson, Coates and Garvin all say their major policy offerings of tax discounts for mortgage interest payments and allowing people to use up to $50,000 of their super to buy a home will have the greatest benefit for higher income earners.
The First Home Buyer Mortgage Deductibility Scheme would allow first home buyers who buy a new build to deduct their mortgage interest payments from their income tax.
Coates says those policies along with the Coalition's own boost allow more people to buy a home with a 5 per cent deposit "will have a greater impact on house prices" than Labor's proposals, putting more upward pressure on prices — though Garvin suggests that would lead to more homes being built, which then puts downward pressure on prices.
"But on the costs side there are other important questions, like who does it really help?" Garvin asks.
Under the Coalition's mortgage discount scheme, top earners being taxed at higher rates stand to gain more — Coates says for example someone earning $240,000 with a $650,000 mortgage could receive a benefit of up to $87,000 over five years, while someone on an income of $60,000 with a $250,000 mortgage could receive a much smaller $23,000 benefit over five years.
Similarly, Pawson says the people most able to benefit from accessing their super are likely those earning more who have actually been able to accrue enough to withdraw the full amount.
Coates notes it was an idea no "serious" tax or housing experts had been calling for.
But Pawson says while the mortgage deductions would be a "regressive" tax policy, there is merit to easing the burden on the toughest years of a mortgage for first homebuyers, and that countries like the United States have similar measures — they just also balance the other end of the scale by fully taxing capital gains when a home is sold.
The Coalition has not shown any intention of winding back capital gains tax discounts, and Coates says that makes it another tax loophole that eats at the nation's tax base — with the largest benefit going to those with the highest incomes.
"What is the social outcome that is being achieved here? the cohort of people for whom you are giving this benefit are precisely the people that are likely to buy a home anyway," Coates says.
The Coalition's housing promises would be expected to push up house prices, housing experts say. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)
What Pawson says is largely missing from the Coalition's offerings is a significant supply side measure.
The party is promising a $5 billion fund to build enabling infrastructure like streets and sewage at greenfield sites — but Pawson says the suggestion that could lead to 500,000 new homes being built is "surprising", given the fund equates to about $10,000 per property if divvied up evenly.
He says in combination with the tax discount for people buying new builds, the policies will direct more growth at the outskirts of capital cities, something that has environmental and economic consequences.
Coates says if the Coalition can cut net overseas migration — the actual number of people coming into Australia — by 100,000 and sustain it for a decade it could lead to rental prices being about 6 per cent lower than otherwise.
"But there has been no government that has ever gotten net overseas migration down to that level since the mid-2000s," Coates says, and while the party's promised caps on international student numbers will help to get there, "they would need to announce further changes".
Garvin says migration cuts would reduce housing demand, but it would come at costs to Australia's workforce and productivity.
"It seems a bit counterproductive to tailor immigration policy to try to achieve housing market objectives," he says.
Neither side are offering well-targeted measures, Pawson and Coates say, with many first home buyers benefiting from these schemes who would likely be able to buy a home anyway.
"There will be a lot of people benefiting from all of these, the Labor side and Coalition side, who strictly speaking — it's not the difference between becoming a home owner and never becoming one at all," Pawson says.
"They're not very well targeted. Economists would say there is a lot of 'dead weight' in the spend."
What they will do, he says, is take years off of how long those same people would need to save before they can buy a home, and that would make the market accessible to new people at least in the short term.
Find out how you compare with the politicians on that issue by taking the ABC's Vote Compass. Follow the link to take the survey.
But while he criticises the unfocused approach of these policies Pawson says he has been surprised at the "sourness" of some reactions to both of the party's major offerings in terms of how they might affect prices.
"It's not as economically illiterate as Australia's housing policy has been for first homebuyers until quite recently," he says.
"This is the first federal election in a long time where both parties are actually competing over trying to build more housing," Coates adds.
"They're still obviously offering giveaways to first homebuyers as they have every election this century, but this is the first time we are also competing on supply."
What remains the single largest button to be pushed on housing that will set supply running again is one the government cannot press: interest rates.
Over the past term of government, inflation and post-COVID supply chain issues led to the cost of building materials soaring, which combined with rising construction sector wages outpaced the rise in value of housing, especially apartments.
That has made the business case for new developments harder, and new dwelling constructions have been sluggish, falling tens of thousands below their long-term average — particularly in apartment construction where developers must take on huge up-front costs.
Pawson says the proof that viability is a key issue was that there were about 75,000 homes already approved to be built in Greater Sydney alone as of the end of last year, but they hadn't commenced, often because the business case couldn't be stacked up.
The prognosis is looking better: in just the last six months construction costs have been falling relative to inflation and if that continues it will allow more supply to come online.
A new report says a national shortage of construction workers is impacting on Australia's housing supply, with the issue shaping up to be a key concern for voters this federal election.
Alongside that, if the Reserve Bank keeps cutting the cash rate (and RBA-watchers reckon it could do so another four times this year), that will also lower the barrier to new supply being built.
"Housing construction is a bit like trying to turn around the Titanic, it just takes time — and hopefully it ends better than the Titanic as well," Coates says.
"There has not been a worse time to build housing in the last 20 years than in the last two years, construction costs went through the roof [and] interest rates rose sharply.
"And the RBA's research is clear, every 100 basis point increase to interest rates slows housing approvals by 7 per cent the following year, and interest rates rose by 400 basis points. That does a lot to explain why housing construction is so slow."
However there is skepticism of any chance Australia can build the nationwide target of 1.2 million homes by July 2029.
What's more likely, Pawson says, is that Australia can reach the pace required to build that many (about 240,000 a year, while Australia is currently building about 165,000 a year) by the decade's end.
Coates says both party's policies will get more houses built, but not at the pace of what is needed at least in the short-term.
Does this all mean that the three years will look better than the last?
"I think the trajectory will be pretty similar to what it has been in the past," Garvin says.
"Australians really like to use housing as a way to build wealth, it's like a secondary objective. As long as the system is sped up for people to look at housing that way ... we are likely to keep seeing fairly strong house price growth."
Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app.
Coates, Pawson and Garvin all say that doesn't change unless there is structural tax reform.
"To be honest, we really need a much bigger readjustment of the tax settings for all housing property ownership. The elephant in the room here of course is the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing [for investors]," Pawson says.
Garvin says governments don't like to talk about those incentives because they are used to build wealth, but that wealth only grows if house prices increase, which widens the gap young people have to jump to make it onto the property ladder.
Coates says halving capital gains discounts and winding back negative gearing would cause house prices to fall by less than 1 per cent and remove about 16,500 new homes over five years — something that could be easily offset with just a portion of the recovered revenue.
"Negative gearing and capital gains tax reform could in fact be a pro-supply policy heading into the next term of parliament," Coates says.
"It's hard to see how else you could do it," Garvin says.
This story is part of the Your Say: Housing special. You told us that housing affordability was a key election issue for you and we're focusing on the issue today to help you better understand the context of the current crisis, the policies on offer and other ideas to solve it.
Join us at noon to follow the housing debate between Housing Minister Clare O'Neil and opposition housing spokesperson Michael Sukkar then have your questions about the housing crisis answered by our panel of experts. Follow our live election blog.
